title: Supreme Court rejects effort to revive Khalid Sheikh Mohammed plea deal
summary: The Supreme Court has rejected an effort to revive a plea deal for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the September 11 attacks
story: The Supreme Court has rejected an effort to revive a plea deal for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the September 11 attacks
WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an effort to revive a plea deal for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.
The agreement would have spared Mohammed the risk of execution in exchange for his guilty plea and a sentence of life in prison without parole.

Mohammed is accused of developing and directing the plot to crash hijacked airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon 25 years ago. Another of the hijacked planes crashed into a field in Pennsylvania.
The plea agreement was approved by military prosecutors and the Pentagon’s senior official for Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, before then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin stepped in.
Austin threw out the deal in 2024, saying a decision on the death penalty in an attack as grave as Sept. 11 should only be made by the defense secretary.

Relatives of the Sept. 11 victims were split on the agreements for Mohammed and two co-defendants. Some said a trial is the best path to justice, while others saw it as the best hope for bringing the long, painful case to a conclusion.
Defense attorneys had argued that Austin, who served under President Joe Biden, acted too late. But a divided appeals court panel found Austin acted within his authority.
A trial date has been set for 2028.

title: Iran live updates: Russia says it won't stop cooperating with Iran
summary: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Russia does not intend to abandon its agreements with Iran in the economic and investment spheres.
story: Russia's foreign minister said they won't abandon economic and investment deals.
President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government and infrastructure sites.

Despite a memorandum of understanding signed by both countries in June aimed at ending the war, talks broke down and the U.S. and Iran renewed strikes, with the strategic Strait of Hormuz as the primary flashpoint.
Across the region, fighting in Yemen between the Iranian-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has intensified. The militia group also launched strikes on Saudi Arabia.
Key Headlines
3:12 AM EDTUS urges Americans in Middle East to exercise 'heightened vigilance'
3:12 AM EDTUS urges Americans in Middle East to exercise 'heightened vigilance'
Russia says it won't stop cooperating with Iran
Russia will not stop cooperating with Iran amid the conflict in the Middle East, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday.

"Despite the difficult situation that has already been mentioned more than once, Russia does not intend to abandon its agreements with Iran in the economic and investment spheres," Lavrov said during a press briefing in Tehran, according to a readout from his office published by Russian state media.  Lavrov mentioned that Russian specialists are "gradually returning to the Bushehr nuclear power plant" in Iran, and that Russian engineers are expected to soon begin construction on the Rasht–Astara railway being developed jointly by Russia and Iran.
US urges Americans in Middle East to exercise 'heightened vigilance'

The Department of State’s Bureau of Consular Affairs warned Americans in the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance due to the complex security environment," saying Iran or its proxies could target Americans or U.S. interests "throughout the world."

"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," the department said on Monday. "The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area."

title: Shawn Oliver pleads not guilty to OUI charge after crash
summary: Shawn Oliver has pleaded not guilty to charges of operating under the influence and other related offenses after suspending his campaign for lieutenant governor of Massachusetts
story: Shawn Oliver has pleaded not guilty to charges of operating under the influence and other related offenses after suspending his campaign for lieutenant governor of Massachusetts

New Bedford City Councilor Shawn Oliver pleaded not guilty to a charge of operating under the influence of alcohol in New Bedford District Court Monday morning, in a case that has led to him suspending his campaign for lieutenant governor.

Oliver entered the courthouse shortly before 9 a.m. as arraignments began. His lawyer, John Hendrie, greeted him warmly and led him into the lawyers’ lounge, where they stayed for a few minutes before walking into the courtroom together. Oliver sat quietly next to his wife, Emerald O’Driscoll-Oliver, near the back of the courtroom as he waited his turn to be called, watched intently by more than half a dozen journalists and photographers.
“I have no comment at this time,” he told a Light reporter.
When Oliver was called forward, he pleaded not guilty to all charges: operating under the influence, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, speeding and a marked lanes violation.

At the prosecutor’s request, the court released Oliver on the condition that he not drive while his case is pending. He was released on personal recognizance, meaning without bail. His next court date is Nov. 16.

The crash, which occurred Saturday around 11:40 p.m. on Dartmouth Street in New Bedford, involved an overturned car that damaged five vehicles, two of which sustained “extensive damage,” police spokesperson Holly Huntoon said.
Oliver, 42, was taken to St. Luke’s for treatment of injuries and then placed under arrest.

He suspended his campaign for lieutenant governor Sunday, a few hours after his release from Ash Street Jail in New Bedford. But voting has already begun, with Oliver on the ballot as the running mate of Republican candidate for governor Mike Minogue.
Minogue said Sunday that if he is elected, he would ask Oliver to resign.

Oliver has been placed on restricted work duty at his job at the Massachusetts Treatment Center “while all facts and circumstances are reviewed,” Scott Croteau, a spokesperson for the state’s Department of Correction, told The Light in an email. The medium-security facility in Bridgewater houses criminally sentenced male sex offenders and people civilly committed as sexually dangerous persons.
The office of the superintendent at the Massachusetts Treatment Center declined to provide any information regarding Oliver’s employment status.
Court records released after Oliver’s arraignment describe what police say they encountered at the scene of the crash.
When officers arrived on Dartmouth Street near the South End Stop & Shop on Saturday night, they found Oliver’s Lincoln Navigator upside down with no one inside.

They also noted a Toyota Camry “with extensive damage, pushed over the curb, across the sidewalk, and onto the grass.” A red Camry “also had extensive damage and was pushed back causing it to collide into another parked vehicle.” Five cars in all were affected.

New Bedford Police Officer Andrew Parker arrived and found Oliver standing on the sidewalk, talking on his cell phone. The officer noticed Oliver was bleeding and had a cut behind his ear. Parker asked Oliver how he was feeling.
“OK,” Oliver told him, according to the officer’s narrative. “It’s been a long day.”
Oliver told the officer he was meeting with friends in Dartmouth and was heading north on his way home.
Oliver asked twice “if everyone else was OK” and told the officer he had been “burning both ends of the wick,” the narrative said.

A witness who wanted to remain anonymous told Officer Orlando Franco they were in a vehicle behind Oliver’s Navigator at a set of lights on Dartmouth Street, south of Rockdale Avenue. Both were heading north.
“The witness stated that when the light turned green, the Navigator remained stopped, he then had to put his car in reverse in order to see if the light was green,” the officer’s narrative said.

Then, the Navigator accelerated through the intersection and veered right and left as it continued north on Dartmouth Street. After Oliver’s car passed through the intersection with Rockdale Avenue, it drifted left into the opposite lane where, traveling at high speed, it hit the parked cars on the west curb and flipped over, the anonymous witness told police.

Franco followed the ambulance that brought Oliver to St. Luke’s Hospital. According to the report, that’s where Oliver told Franco he’d had “at least 2 alcoholic beverages earlier in the night at Black Bass Grill. He then had gone to a friend’s house located in Dartmouth.”
Oliver’s eyes were “bloodshot and glassy,” and he smelled like alcohol. Franco observed.
“After speaking with Shawn, it was determined that he was under the influence of alcoholic beverages (and) should not have been operating a motor vehicle,” Franco wrote.
The officer told Oliver he was under arrest and handcuffed him to the hospital bed, but not before Oliver vomited, according to the narrative.
Oliver wasn’t able to perform sobriety tests because of his injuries and refused an evidentiary blood draw, the police reports said.

In 2003, Oliver faced charges of operating an unregistered motor vehicle and “number plate violation to conceal identity” in Mattapoisett. Wareham District Court records show he admitted to sufficient facts in the concealment case, and the judge found sufficient facts but continued the case without a guilty finding. (A continued without a finding disposition generally results from completion of probation.)
The records suggest Oliver paid $50 in court costs and a $21 per month probation service fee.
The law to which Oliver entered a plea can apply when someone attaches the wrong license plate to a car, obscures the numbers on a plate, or fails to display a plate.
This story was originally published by The New Bedford Light and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press.

title: Midterm vote is about 'what's best for my family': Voters talk 2026 midterms
summary: ABC News spoke with voters in Alaska, Iowa, New Hampshire and Maine.
story: ABC News spoke with voters in Alaska, Iowa, New Hampshire and Maine.

Josh York, a retired Army major who now works in health care administration in Anchorage, Alaska, has seen firsthand how high prices for fuel have kept Alaskans off the road. In the far reaches of America’s largest state, prices are as high as $24 per gallon.
“The gas prices don't seem to be coming down, and believe me, I watch,” York, a three-time Trump voter, told ABC News.

“Recently, we were out in the middle of rural Alaska, and we were paying $8.99 a gallon for gas,” York said, blaming the higher prices on the Iran war. That war has substantially slowed traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, experts say, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas transited before the war.
The economy is on Americans’ minds across the country ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3, when voters in a handful of key states will wield outsize impact on control of the United States Congress.

ABC News traveled to those states -- Alaska, Iowa, New Hampshire, and Maine -- finding many Americans who are frustrated with their personal finances and aware their vote would be a referendum on President Donald Trump’s job performance.

Trump traveled outside the continental United States this week to boost Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who faces a reelection challenge from Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola – one of four seats the Democrats hope they can capture to win control of the U.S. Senate.
The president defended the war against Iran, telling Alaskans the war would end soon and prices would come down when it did, and said his opponents had made the election about affordability.

“Every time they want to try and get me, they say 'affordability, sir. This and that.' I said, 'They caused the problem,’ he said at a rally in Wasilla, 45 miles north of Anchorage. “But we have reduced it very substantially.’”
The Senate race – analyzed as a toss-up in a state where Trump won by 13 points in 2024 – is reflecting the price pressures of voters.
The president’s polling numbers have plummeted to record lows in recent months. Just over half of Americans, 52%, strongly disapprove of Trump, according to a new ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll.
Sullivan, who is aligned with Trump and has backed the Iran war, acknowledged the conflict was causing higher prices and said it should end “soon.”
One voter said heating costs in Fairbanks had even exceeded mortgage costs.

York told ABC News’ Martha Raddatz, co-anchor of "This Week with George Stephanopoulos," that even though he’s voted for Trump, he disapproved of the president across the board: in his handling of the economy, the Iran war and the overall direction the president was taking the country.
York, unsure about his decision between the candidates, said his vote would come down to the economy.

“I know that they both have their ideas for Alaska and how they want to do things. And I'm not gonna say one's right versus the other being wrong,” he said. “But at this point, I've got to look at what's best for my family. I've got to look at what's best for my kids.”
In America’s heartland, voters told ABC News energy prices and the president’s trade policy were animating discussions around the midterm elections, including in a competitive Iowa senate race.
The rising diesel prices have crunched farmers who rely on diesel for transport.
“Our tanks over there hold 3,500 gallons. It costs $20,000 now to fill them. A year ago it cost [about] $12,000,” said cattle farmer Dan Pederson, who voted for the president three times.
“The ripple effect – hauling cattle, pickups, trucks, everything [is] just-- it's just astronomical. It's crazy,” he said.

Pederson said among his “staunch Republican friends” there was a lot of “wavering” on Trump. The Republican candidate for the Senate seat, Rep. Ashley Hinson, has broken with the president, urging him to bring the Iran war to an end.

The president announced an extraordinary remedy to the price of diesel last week, saying in a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin that the two leaders had agreed to a “diesel deal” that would allow Russian diesel, largely blocked by sanctions and trapped because of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, to enter world markets.
Many Republican lawmakers said the president’s move would benefit an autocratic government that invaded its neighbor, Ukraine.
“We need to lower gas prices in this country,” Hinson said. “We need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it.”
In neighboring Nebraska, Republican congressman Don Bacon, who is stepping away from his own seat, said Republicans’ formula of backing Trump could prove costly.
The Republican worries about his party’s odds in traditionally red Nebraska and Kansas, midwestern Senate races where Democrats hope to manage surprise victories, he told Raddatz.
He credited his own independent streak with his own election victories.
“You got to be able to show that you're your own person and you represent the district,” he said.
In an X post this week, Bacon said Trump’s deal with Putin was a betrayal of Ukraine.
The president was “propping up a dictator’s invasion and throwing an ally under the bus,” he wrote.
In the country’s Northeast, independent voters wield considerable influence.
Democratic-leaning states here have continued to elect Republicans – like Maine’s five-term Sen. Susan Collins, who is seeking a sixth election.
Collins is one of the few Senate Republicans who regularly breaks with Trump, saying in a recent debate she “voted nine times against the president on the Iran war.”
Voters pointed to her role as the top appropriator in Congress, overseeing the key funding mechanisms that Mainers say gives them a crucial voice in Washington.
In a polarized era, voters said it’s Collins’ independent brand that has won her respect.

“I think that objectively speaking, she is the most bipartisan member of the Senate, and I think we need more Susan Collins, not fewer,” said self-described life-long Democrat Mary Anne Lynch. She plans to cast her ballot for Collins this November.
Brenda Garrand has been in Collins’ camp before, voting for her three times – but she says she won’t in 2026.
“I would say, for me, the most important reason to vote for Troy Jackson is to make sure that there is a Democratic Senate,” Garrand said.
Collins was not doing enough with her powerful perch, she argued.
“She has gone a step too far … [I’m] deeply disappointed in her behavior as a woman who has really reached the apex of an ability to make a difference,” Garrand said.

The Democratic senate nominee in neighboring New Hampshire sees the same dynamics at play in his state. Congressman Chris Pappas told Raddatz that Democrats’ margins in the Granite State had improved since Vice President Kamala Harris’s narrow victory there in 2024.

“I'm meeting Republicans every day that are opposed to what they see this administration doing,” he said. “I'm meeting libertarian-minded voters in the ‘Live Free or Die’ state that don't support the disgraceful immigration overreach with respect to [Immigrations and Custom Enforcement.]”
Pappas faces a known name brand in New Hampshire politics: John Sununu, the brother of Republican Gov. Chris Sununu.
Chris Ager, a former chair of the New Hampshire Republican party, called Sununu “that quintessential New Hampshire politician – very pragmatic, very common sense, very independent of Washington.”
He added, “I think that's going to sell very well on Nov. 3.”

title: Dems lead GOP in House vote choice as Trump's approval rating hits record low: Poll
summary: Half or more Americans call every household purchase category measured "unaffordable."
story: Half or more Americans call every household purchase measured "unaffordable."

Just over two-weeks out from consequential midterm elections, a record share of Americans disapprove of President Donald Trump, about 7 in 10 say gasoline is unaffordable and that the country is headed in the wrong direction, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted using Ipsos’ KnowledgePanel.

By an 8-percentage point margin, likely voters support the Democratic candidate in congressional district elections over the Republican candidate, 52% to 44%. That margin remains 8 points among registered voters overall, 50% to 42%, an improvement from a July Washington Post-Ipsos poll for Democrats, when just 3 points separated the Democrats from the Republicans.

Although control of the House will ultimately be determined in votes for individual candidates in individual congressional districts across the county, the generic House question is a useful barometer. For example, before the last midterms, a fall 2022 ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll found registered voters nearly split and Republicans went on to win Congress. In a fall 2018 poll, Democrats had an 11-point lead over Republicans among registered voters and Democrats went on to win the House that year.
Overwhelming shares of partisans support their party’s candidates – 98% of Democratic likely voters and 96% of Republican likely voters each support their party candidates.
Democrats are bolstering their lead among independent likely voters, who support Democratic candidates by a 21-point margin, 56% to 35%.

Democrats are also benefiting from the fact that there’s more enthusiasm from their supporters. More Democratic voters (72%) than Republican voters (65%) say they are absolutely certain to vote and more Democratic voters are following the midterms “extremely” or “very” closely than Republican voters – 44% to 31%.

About 9 in 10 of the roughly half of likely voters who strongly disapprove of Trump plan to vote for the Democratic candidate in their congressional district. And over 9 in 10 of the likely voters who approve of Trump plan to vote for Republicans. But the roughly 1 in 10 voters who somewhat disapprove of Trump support the Republican candidate over the Democratic one by a double-digit margin, 58% to 34%.

Half or more Americans call every household purchase category measured “unaffordable” in the latest poll, including 71% who now call gasoline unaffordable, up from 28% who said the same in February, before the war in Iran drove up fuel costs. The national average gas price has topped $4 a gallon for a record 158 days in 2026 so far.
An increasing share of Americans also call healthcare unaffordable (65%, up from 56% in February) along with home energy and utility costs (57%, up from 45%) and rent or mortgage (50%, up from 37%).
And 60% call groceries unaffordable, also up from February (45%) but less than July (66%).

Growing shares of Americans call relative luxuries unaffordable, too. A 61% majority of Americans call going out to dinner unaffordable, up from 49% in February. Even more, 69%, say a weeklong vacation is unaffordable, up from 60%. And 80% call a new car unaffordable, up from 74% in February.

In all, 75% of Americans rate the nation’s economy negatively, including 35% who call it poor. Roughly half, 48%, say they are “not as well off” as they were when Trump became president, a high over both of his presidential terms.

Likely voters who rate the economy poorly support Democrats over Republicans in the generic ballot by 72 points. Likely voters who say they are not as well off support Democrats over Republicans by 60 points.

Beyond just the economy, Americans are unhappy with the direction the country is moving in: 72% say things in the country are headed in the wrong direction; just 26% say things are heading in the right direction.

Trump’s weak approval ratings do not bode well for his party given that midterms are often a referendum vote on the president. And Trump’s approval rating has reached a record personal low of 33% percent in the ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, lower even than after the Jan. 6, 2021, attacks on the U.S. Capitol when 38% approved. Today, 66% of Americans disapprove, a record high over both terms.
Just over half of Americans, 52%, strongly disapprove of Trump, matching his strong disapproval rating after the Jan. 6 attack, and a record high for his second term, according to the poll.
Over both of his terms, a record-low 22% of independents approve of Trump and a record-high 76% disapprove, including 58% who strongly disapprove – another record high over both of Trump’s terms.

Among Republicans, 79% approve, down just slightly from a July Post-Ipsos poll but down significantly from 88% near the beginning of his second term. And a record-low 39% strongly approve of Trump, down from 63% in February 2025. Today, 21% of Republicans disapprove, up from 12% in February 2025. That includes nearly half of non-MAGA Republicans (47%) who disapprove today.

A majority of MAGA Republicans strongly approve of the president, 55%, but that’s down from 65% in February. About 6 in 10 Republicans consider themselves supporters of the MAGA movement, both now and in February.
Among registered voters overall, Trump’s overall approval rating is slightly better: 37% approve and 63% disapprove.
Majorities of Americans also disapprove of how Trump is handling every issue measured, and for many issues, Trump is at or near record-low approvals.

His worst issue is handling the cost of living in the U.S. -- perhaps the defining issue for the 2026 midterms -- and his ratings are similarly low to what they were in the ABC/Post/Ipsos poll in April. Now, just 21% approve while 77% disapprove.
Trump has similarly low ratings on handling inflation: 23% approve and 75% disapprove, a worse margin than in April when 27% approved and 72% disapproved.

On the economy overall, 28% approve of how Trump is handling things and 70% disapprove, a record-low approval and a record-high disapproval over both of Trump’s terms. In a July Post-Ipsos poll, 33% approved and 65% disapproved. His approval rating on the economy peaked at 56% in January 2020.

On Iran, 27% approve of how Trump is handling the situation and 70% disapprove, virtually the same as in a July Post-Ipsos poll. A 65% majority of Americans say it was a mistake for the U.S. to use military force against Iran.

On relations with U.S. allies, 30% approve of how Trump is handling things and 68% disapprove. A 58% majority of Americans say the U.S. should either reduce military support to Israel (25%) or end it completely (33%).

Trump’s best issue is immigration, where 38% approve and 61% disapprove, slightly down from his July approval ratings on the issue. A 56% majority of Americans say Trump is “going too far” in deporting undocumented immigrants while 15% say he is “not going far enough” and 28% say he’s handling it about right.
On how Trump is managing the military, 35% approve and 63% disapprove.
About two-thirds of Americans say since taking office, Trump has “gone beyond his authority as president;” about a third say he has acted within his authority.

Majorities of Americans say Trump is “not committed” to respecting the authority of Congress (68%), protecting freedom of the press (67%), respecting the authority of the courts (66%), free and fair elections (61%) or protecting freedom of speech (61%). Shares of Americans saying that Trump is not committed to protecting freedom of the press, free and fair elections and freedom of speech are all up from last October.

A record-high 66% of Americans say Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, up from 62% in February and 56% in September 2025. Majorities of Democrats (94%) and independents (73%) along with just over a quarter of Republicans (27%) say Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself.

Wide majorities of Americans also say that it is “inappropriate” for Trump to push to have his name put on the Kennedy Center (80%, including 59% who say it is “totally inappropriate”), including majorities across partisan groups. Even 57% of Republicans say it is inappropriate.

And when it comes to the federal government paying for TV ads promoting Trump and his policies, 74% say it is inappropriate, including 55% who say it is totally inappropriate. Trump has said he would pay for the ads from political fundraising coffers, but the ads continued to air with a line saying they were "paid for by the U.S. government." A federal judge has ordered the government-funded ads to stop running.
About 6 in 10 Americans say Trump is focused too much on building projects in D.C. (59%); just 11% said he’s focused too little and 27% say he’s focused “the right amount” on building projects.
Most Republicans and Republican-leaning independents say the party should follow Trump’s leadership going forward (61%), with 37% saying the party should go in a different direction.
By a wide margin, Americans prefer that the next Congress be controlled by Democrats, to act as a check on Trump (59%) than by Republicans, to support Trump’s agenda (35%).
Americans trust Democrats over Republicans to handle 10 out of 12 issues measured in this poll.

U.S. adults trust Democrats over Republicans by 23 points to handle healthcare and by 14 points to handle education, the cost of living and inflation – all by wider margins than they have recently. Americans trust Democrats over Republicans by 11 points to handle the situation with Iran, by 9 points to handle reducing corruption in the government and transgender issues. Americans trust Democrats by 9 points to better handle the economy, the largest margin they’ve had on the issue since 2022 – previously they’ve been about tied with Republicans or were at a deficit to them. Adults trust Democrats over Republicans by 7 points to handle taxes along with the situation with Israel and Gaza.
The public is roughly divided on whether they trust Democrats or Republicans to do a better job handling immigration.

Americans trust Republicans more than Democrats to handle just one issue, crime, for which they prefer Republicans by a 5-point margin. Still, that’s a recent high mark for Democrats, who have trailed Republicans on the issue by double digits dating back four years.

Americans feel negative toward both the Democratic and Republican parties, but while the Democratic Party is just 10 points underwater on favorability (44% favorable and 54% unfavorable), the Republican Party is worse at 28 points underwater (35% favorable and 63% unfavorable).

Double haters, those who are unfavorable toward both parties, who make up about 2 in 10 voters, favor the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate in the generic ballot by 26 percentage points, 58% to 32%. This has been a key swing group in previous elections dating back to 2016.
More Americans call Trump and the Republican Party “too extreme” – 66% and 55%, respectively – than the Democratic Party (36%).
The MAGA movement is underwater by 41 percentage points, with 28% favorable and 69% unfavorable. Among Republicans, 70% are favorable and 28% are unfavorable.
Democratic socialism is underwater by 22 points, 37% of Americans are favorable and 59% are unfavorable. Among Democrats, 70% have a favorable view of democratic socialism and 27% are unfavorable.

Likely voters who plan to vote in different ways have different vote preferences. Voters who plan to vote in person on Election Day make up about 4 in 10 voters and support Republicans over Democrats by 11 points.

But the other ways voters plan to vote have a Democratic advantage: Those who plan to – or who have already voted early by mail – who make up just under 3 in 10 voters, support Democrats over Republicans by 26 points. About a quarter of likely voters plan to vote early at a polling place or already have, and they favor Democrats by 14 points. And about 1 in 10 voters plan to or have dropped off a ballot before Election Day and they support Democrats over Republicans by a wide 50-point margin.
See PDF for full results and detailed methodology.

Methodology: This ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll was conducted via the probability-based Ipsos KnowledgePanel Oct. 9-13, 2026, among 2,545 U.S. adults including 2,032 registered and likely voters and has an error margin of +/- 2 percentage points overall and +/- 2.2 points among registered and likely voters. All registered voters were assigned a probability of voting to produce likely voter results. Error margins among most other subgroups are larger.
ABC News’ Liz Schreier contributed to this report.
Email ABCNEWS.Polls@abc.com to be added to ABC News’ polling distribution list.
More ABC News polls can be found at abcnews.com. Media contacts: Jeannie Kedas and Van Scott.
