title: Transcript: Sen. Kevin Cramer on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 18, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Kevin Cramer, Republican of North Dakota, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 18, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Kevin Cramer, Republican of North Dakota, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 18, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Welcome back to Face the Nation. We go now to North Dakota Republican Senator Kevin Cramer, who joins us from Bismarck. Good morning to you, Senator.
SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER (R-ND): Good morning. Good to be with you.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to ask you about Ukraine. I know you just recently traveled there. A number of your departing, some retiring, Senate Republican colleagues have made clear they were very upset with President Trump's decision to waive the Lindsey Graham sanctions off of Russia and buyers of Russian oil. Senator Cornyn said Lindsey would be appalled. Senator Tillis said it is beyond irresponsible, unconscionable to capitulate to Vladimir Putin. Where do you stand?

SEN. CRAMER: Well, Margaret, on this topic and a whole bunch of others, I think capitulating to a bully generally means they're going to make more demands going forward. That's the problem with taking sort of a business negotiation approach to negotiating with a thug, which is what Vladimir Putin is. So I share those colleagues' positions on it. However, I also have to acknowledge that we are few weeks or a couple weeks from an election. One of the important topics of the election is the cost of diesel fuel. It's really an important issue here in North Dakota.

As Representative Turner pointed out, and I was cheering him on, our allies throughout Europe have been buying energy from Vladimir Putin and funding his war machine for decades and they should stop right now. Having said all of that, I expect this will be a short-term pause, and I certainly hope so, because one of the things that President Zelenskyy asked of us when I was with him on last Thursday, I think it was Thursday or Friday, was that the president would fully enforce the Lindsey Graham sanctions bill. And I still take that position.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. And some European Union countries do continue to buy fuel products. India and China would be the largest purchasers who would be hit by these tariffs. So do you think the president would actually even post-election trigger the tariffs on China?

SEN. CRAMER: Well, I certainly hope that he does, Margaret. Again, speaking of thugs who will never agree to terms, or at least not continue to agree to terms that would be negotiated, Xi Jinping is another one. I think we have to start approaching our geopolitical negotiations the way that we ought to, and not the way that you do in a boardroom. You know, this is not a finality outcome to a dictator. The outcome of a negotiation with a dictator is more, you know, asking for more demands. And we have to start playing nice with our friends and treating our adversaries like they are adversaries.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You just met with President Zelenskyy. As you know, President Trump publicly blasted him again this week and said Ukraine needs another new president. Let me ask you something specific about how they defend themselves and conduct this war. Starshield is a U.S. military program which Ukraine says that they use to fire into Russian-held territory. Last night, Secretary Rubio said Ukraine does not currently have access to it, but they have asked to use it to fire deep inside of Russia. When you were in Ukraine, as I understand it, you were presenting a proposal to President Zelenskyy to allow for Starshield access expansion if Ukraine stops striking Russian energy assets. What can you tell us about that proposal and what is the status of it?

SEN. CRAMER: So that, you're right, that was a proposal we brought to President Zelenskyy. Senator Wicker, Roger Wicker, the chairman of the Armed Services Committee, came up with that idea. President Zelensky was enthusiastic about it. He said, I'd do that tomorrow. I would absolutely stop attacking Russia's energy facilities if I could have access to targeting capabilities, which is what Starshield would provide them, to go deep into Russia and attack their attackers, in other words, their launch facilities, kill the archer, not the arrows. Of course, the third thing he asked for was the capacity to get licensed to jointly produce, co-produce Patriot missile interceptors, which would help him defend against these much faster now jet-powered drones and missiles coming into Ukraine.

So his requests were three. They were simple. And I agree with all three of them. So I would hope we can get to that point where- remembering that what President Zelenskyy is protecting are civilians. Russia has chosen to go after civilian populations, while President Zelenskyy has simply gone after the launchers and, more importantly, the war machine's funding source, which is energy.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right, bringing us back to where we started here. Ukraine has resumed, just even overnight, hitting Russian oil refineries. They hit the St. Petersburg oil terminal. Russia has been targeting the energy infrastructure inside of Ukraine. Secretary Rubio said there are talks ongoing. Have you talked to Secretary Rubio about your exchange with President Zelenskyy? Who in the administration is actually trying to bring this to a close?

SEN. CRAMER: So I have not talked to Marco, although as I was watching your previous segment, I just said to my staff, I wish I would have called Marco. But obviously he and others are involved with it, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. I thin– but I worry, Margaret, that there's a disconnect. Once again, I go back to my earlier illustration. There's a disconnect between traditional, mutually beneficial negotiations between business people and the difference between somebody's protecting humanity itself versus somebody who wants to take humanity down. And so I worry about that. So who exactly is negotiating these things? I don't know who's calling shots. But at the end of the day, I think the president is, you know, it's where the buck stops. And I think he accepts that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So is Senator Wicker presenting this deal to the White House? What are you doing with what you negotiated?
SEN. CRAMER: Oh yeah, yes, for sure. I mean, we had talked to people in the White House at the Department of War and to the State Department even prior to meeting with President Zelenskyy.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So do you join your colleagues, Senator Tillis and Senator Shaheen, in calling for an investigation of what has happened here in terms of whether U.S. government officials knew that Starlink was going to be interrupted, which impacts Ukraine's ability to use its drones and defend its people?

SEN. CRAMER: Well, I certainly support investigating what was the source of that decision, if in fact it was a decision at all. It may very well have been some sort of a technical glitch. I don't know for sure or whose call it was. So far, nobody's taking credit for making that call or the blame for it. So I do support some sort of an investigation. Certainly Congress itself could and should investigate. I think the letter that Senator Shaheen and Senator Tillis are talking about would be an inspector general investigation, perhaps.

But, sure, we want to get to the bottom of it. In the meantime, what's more important is that that power is put back on full scale and that we actually enhance Ukraine's ability to hit these launch facilities inside of Russia, deeper inside to like 300 kilometers, I think is what President Zelenskyy was asking for.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. President Zelenskyy said today that it has been restored, but has been throttled back. And in terms of that Starshield expansion, as you say, no deal yet. Let me ask you about something closer to home. You said this summer that you "hate," that was the word you used, President Trump's decision to import foreign beef tariff-free because it's not America first, wrongheaded and threatens the future of U.S. food production. The White House did not reverse course, despite those tough words from you. How negative has that been for your state? And is that going to infect- affect- I should say, the enthusiasm for voters to show up in November? Are these ranchers just so ticked off they're not going to vote?

SEN. CRAMER: Well, first of all, Margaret, it won't have any effect in North Dakota in the election cycle. We don't have a governor up. The president's obviously not up. We don't even have a senator up. And we're gonna have an overwhelming Republican victory here. Having said that, it's very discouraging to our ranchers. Again, I think there's a misunderstanding of commodity cycles, commodity economic cycles. Ranchers rebuild their herds when prices are high. Their herds are obviously made much smaller when prices are low. That's why- that's why the countercyclical effect of commodity prices are well known to us, and why it's discouraging when we reduce or eliminate the barriers to to importing somebody else's beef, which is not nearly as safe or as high quality, at the cost of- at the cost of- our local ranchers. They rely on these higher prices. And by the way, I doubt that bringing in a bunch of Argentine beef is going to bring the price at the grocery store down--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --It hasn't--

SEN. CRAMER: --It has not. But it will hurt the market price of the cattle themselves. Now, ranchers are going up against lots of other problems as well, including the concentration of meat packing in the United States, where about a third or more is literally owned by the Chinese and the Brazilians. So they're going up against a lot of things, but their input costs are also higher. They don't come down because the price of a cow goes down. But yeah, so I still strongly oppose it, and I think it was wrongheaded.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. Well, I wanted to get your insight on that because we're seeing that dynamic in other states as well, including Kansas. So, Senator, thank you so much for your time today. We're going to have to leave it there. We'll be right back.

title: Transcript: Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 18, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 18, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 18, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Florida State Representative Angie Nixon. She is the Democratic Party's nominee for Senate, and she joins us from Gainesville. Good morning to you.
ANGIE NIXON: Good morning. Happy to be here with you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it's good to talk you.
ANGIE NIXON: And to the nation.

MARGARET BRENNAN: It's good to talk to you. You identify as a progressive, but I know this past June you joined the Democratic Socialists of America during your primary bid. Our CBS polling shows 42% of Americans have a somewhat or very negative view of socialism. I'm wondering what elements of the Democratic Socialist platform drew you to it. How do you define your vision here?

ANGIE NIXON: For sure. So first of all, thank you for having me on the show today, and I think it's really important for me to lay the groundwork because a lot of people—this is my first introduction to them. I am someone who is a lifelong Floridian, having worked in the state of Florida as a community organizer and a union organizer, and our campaign is on fire. We actually had over 4,000 people show up yesterday at rallies, and some in deep red counties, and we are on fire. We were able to outfundraise our opponent by over $2 million in this past quarter, and I know in regards to my joining that organization, it's not about letters, but it is actually about the fact that we are fighting to ensure that there's access to quality health care for everyone, and access to fully funded public schools, in addition to ensuring people have a roof over their head, my opponent, Ashley Moody, actually voted to end health care for over 440,000 people here in the state of Florida, which also jacked up premiums for private people—private insurance, and so I just want to make sure that people don't go bankrupt simply because they're trying to live or go to the doctor.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so on the specifics with your platform, you call for Medicare for all, a national rent stabilization standard, raising the federal minimum wage, abolishing ICE, and a 5% annual wealth tax on billionaires. If you win, you would have two years here in Congress with a Republican president in office. What areas of agreement do you see, if any? How would you work across the aisle with Republicans?

ANGIE NIXON: You know, I would work across the aisle with whoever wants to put hardworking everyday people at the forefront. I mean, right now, what we're witnessing in D.C. and with my opponent Ashley Moody is a culture of corruption. Ashley Moody is someone who has enriched herself in the tune of $2 million because she is trading stocks, and of which she actually has the opportunity. She's sitting on committees, health- healthcare committees, where she has access to insider stock trading information. She also has been able to—she also has actually been able to, she's just not listening to what Floridians want. She is rubber stamping everything that Donald Trump wants as well. You know, she's deporting—she's okay with his deportation policies, locking people up in cages, and it's something that I would work to stop when I become the next United States senator.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You made reference to a number of things there in regard to your opponent. There was a grand jury finding that the DeSantis administration misappropriated taxpayer funds to a charity called Hope Florida, but there were no charges brought against the senator. She has denied any wrongdoing. But moving along to issues in this campaign, you have talked about some frustration that you're not getting more support from the Democratic Party. You told MS Now in September they could do a lot more to help you. You pointed out Florida has a very large black population, and you said "Folks are a little gun shy because Vice President Harris lost as a black woman, and so people are very hesitant in terms of funding black women in the South." You did just campaign with Bernie Sanders. Senator Chris Murphy was just down there as well. Do you think now you are getting support from the National Party?

ANGIE NIXON: You know we are excited with all of the folks that are coming down, helping to ensure that we get this W in November, and I'm excited that folks like Leader Schumer as well as Senator Gillibrand have decided to host fundraisers, and we're getting support. We always want even more support. But again, I'm also excited because this is a people-powered campaign, and we've had over 300,000 contributions, and those average donations are around $31. So that lets people know that your regular, everyday working people are supportive of this campaign. Look, we are not the little engine that could. We have been on the ground organizing, doing the work, building diverse coalitions all across the state of Florida. Previously, with very little help, and I have led those efforts from doing things like expanding and increasing the minimum wage to $15 an hour here in this state, and that is what we are going to take part in and you know incorporate here on this campaign those coalitions of people, and that's how we're going to be able to win come November.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you think you are getting the help you need now?
ANGIE NIXON: We're getting help, but we always can use more. As a matter of fact, people can go to angienixon.com to donate to our campaign.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I just want to move on to some other issues here on your platform, but you did when you were talking about your opponent—I want to come back to language here because you have said you want to keep funding the police. You said that's wrong for your opponent to accuse you of trying to defund the police.
ANGIE NIXON: Yeah, absolutely.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You've said she should be locked up and punished in jail. Given in the past that Democrats have expressed discomfort with some Republicans using that kind of language, do you worry that that sounds like a desire to weaponize the justice system?

ANGIE NIXON: It's not language to weaponize the—It's not a desire to weaponize the justice system. It's designed to actually hold corrupt politicians accountable for what they're doing. Again, I want an investigation done. I would like the Department of Justice to investigate because nearly $10 million was stolen from sick kids, and people are pointing the finger saying they don't know who did it, and so we need to bring that in. Look, this is Donald Trump 2.0 here in the state of Florida, and we really need to work to push back. I'm wondering how many kids are going to die because $10 million was taken from Medicaid that was supposed to make sure that those sick kids had the treatment that they needed here.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, well, as we mentioned, Senator Moody has denied wrongdoing. But thank you for your time. It's good to meet you, Angie Nixon. We will be watching your race in November. We'll be right back with a lot more. Face the Nation. Stay with us.

title: Transcript: Rep. Mike Turner on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 18, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Mike Turner, Republican of Ohio, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 18, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Mike Turner, Republican of Ohio, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 18, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're joined now by Ohio Republican Congressman Mike Turner. Good morning, and thanks for being here in person. A lot to get to with you, but let's start on politics. Ohio has been reliably Republican, but you've got a competitive gubernatorial race and Senate race in Minnesota, in Iowa, in Michigan, and in Maine. Republicans have been positioning themselves as independent of the president on some issues. Take a listen.
[START SOUND ON TAPE]
MICHELLE TAFOYA: When Trump is right, I'll work with him. When he's wrong, I'll stand up for Minnesota.
ASHLEY HINSON: We need to lower gas prices in this country. We need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it.
MIKE ROGERS: Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now.
SEN. SUSAN COLLINS: I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: I know you've been endorsed by President Trump. You did appear at a rally with him, but do you feel it would help to create some distance, like they did?

REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, as you know, I don't run with the president. I don't run from the president. It's one of the reasons why you have me on this show because of the fact that- that I have my- my own agenda, and I think what's important, as your pollster has- has indicated, he's in- he's talking of- of trends. What's most important, as he ended his presentation, as Anthony said, this is about who gets out to vote, and everybody needs to get out and vote. You know, Margaret, my very first race, I won by 244 votes out of 44,000. It's really, really important as to who gets out and votes. So, my message would be to everyone, is to get out and vote. And also, when they go to the polls, they need to make certain that they vote in every race. It's amazing the number of drop-offs that people have as they go down the ballot. People need to vote in every race, and they need to get out and vote.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But clearly, those candidates felt they needed to say that. Fox had a poll this week showing six in 10 respondents were extremely concerned about government corruption. AP had one that said six in 10 adults believe Trump is illegally profiting from the presidency or at least doing something unethical. Your local paper, the Columbus Dispatch, wrote it could not endorse the Republican Senate candidate because of the "abject failure," this is a quote- "of Republicans in Congress to stop visible corruption and abuse of power by the Trump administration." You referred to Republicans as almost entirely spineless. How do you counter those perceptions? Do you feel you need to?
REP. TURNER: No, first off, that- Columbus is not my local- local paper, and- and the--
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're Dayton, but--
REP. TURNER: Right, yes, I'm- I'm- I'm Dayton--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --but it is still talking about the Senate race and talking about the perception that Congress has not pushed back on the president.

REP. TURNER: Right. Well, I think- I think Congress has pushed back, and certainly I have pushed back. And in- in my community, I'm seen as part of the integral economic development team- the local economic development team of my community. And the- the aspect of what people are doing or are not doing with respect to this administration is, I think an individual candidate's issue, and people vote for individual candidates. They don't vote for a team. They don't vote for- for a slate, and- and I think that's why individual candidates are talking about their individual records as- as I do. People look in my community, they see me as a job creator. They see me as someone- if- Margaret, if you came into my community and we took a drive along my community, and I showed you my accomplishments, you'd see things at, you know, my local base where we've doubled the jobs both inside and outside the fence, the VA where we've created senior housing, and like- my opponent wouldn't be able to get out of the driveway of her house. Those are the kind of things that people look to for the individual candidates.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But the president is central here. The president is telling people, vote like he is on the ballot.
REP. TURNER: Well, that's- that's- that's the president. That's not the individual candidates.
MARGARET BRENNAN: He thinks he's doing candidates like you, some- some good when he says things like that and comes out and rallies in Ohio.

REP. TURNER: Well, he came to a rally in my community, as the- as he said in the community when he was there campaigning for the top of the ticket. When he came to my community, he actually came when he was speaking of my record that he was committing to sign legislation to restore the Delphi salary pensioners who had their pensions taken away under the Obama administration.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah, that hasn't happened yet.

REP. TURNER: He committed to sign that legislation to restore those pensions that I had been working on for over a decade. That makes over 5,000 people in my community restore their pensions. I've been working on paychecks and pensions, and that's the type of thing that makes a difference in my community.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well- well, let's talk about some of those things, which, because that hasn't passed yet, some of those things could get gunked up in the lame-duck because of what I'm about to ask you about and that is--
[CROSSTALK]
REP. TURNER: --that the president has committed to sign.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, if it can get to his desk. I want to ask you about Elon Musk's SpaceX technology, Starlink. Ukraine uses it for communication, they use it to control their drones. Secretary Rubio said no one at the White House ordered it to be slowed down this week so that drones couldn't use it. But effectively, that was the outcome. Here is how Secretary Rubio explained it last night.
[START SOUND ON TAPE]

SEC. MARCO RUBIO: We had nothing to do with it. I don't- I don't- the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened. But my understanding is it's been restored.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Is "it sort of happened" sufficient explanation for you and others on the Armed Services Committee?

REP. TURNER: Absolutely not. I mean, this is something where there needs to be an investigation. There needs to be a congressional investigation. I mean, this is one of those things where- where we see that- that policies occur where sometimes there's- there's breaks in- in weapon systems that are supposed to be sent to Ukraine that doesn't happen, where monies are- are- don't arrive, where intelligence gets broken, where then later that we have- find, you know, unnamed people in the Pentagon perhaps break it. There needs to be an investigation. We need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things. And even today, you know, the Institute for the Study of War reports today--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
REP. TURNER: --and Zelenskyy reports that, you know, perhaps it's spotty. There are areas where that it's restored--
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's been straddled back.
REP. TURNER: --and there are areas where perhaps it is not. People's lives are at risk, and this- this is within Ukraine. This is areas where they're trying to defend themselves.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
REP. TURNER: This is essential to the United States support of Ukraine in defending real aggressive attacks by Russia within Ukraine, and this needs to be restored.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But Elon Musk, who owns this company, and Starlink is a commercial enterprise. Elon Musk publicly opposes President Zelenskyy. He posted on social media he doesn't want Starlink used for offensive military action. I know Secretary Rubio said it had been restored, but--
REP. TURNER: But this is within Ukraine. This is defending Ukraine against aggression within Ukraine.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Exactly, but it is just- they're all pointing at each other, saying no, DOD is in charge. No, Elon Musk's in charge. I don't know, it just sort of happened.
REP. TURNER: But the policy decision has been made that- that Starshield will be utilized for the purposes of Ukraine defending itself against Russian aggression--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Starshield.
REP. TURNER: Starshield.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Which is the U.S. military contract.

REP. TURNER: Within its territory, and it has, by everybody's reports, been broken in- in its ability to be able to be accessed. And there should be an investigation as to why, and it should be completely restored.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The president- there were a series of actions, not just the diesel waivers. These actions in regard to Ukraine's ability to defend itself, and then you saw him waive or at least pause for a period of time the sanctions that you voted should be in place under the Lindsey Graham bill. They were supposed to punish buyers of Russian oil. He said, "Don't implement them."
REP. TURNER: Well, there's- there's two--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Will you encourage him to reverse course?
REP. TURNER: Okay, there's two separate things here. The- the sanctions under the Lindsey Graham bill this weekend there was a deadline for the president--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Today.

REP. TURNER: --to either waive or to impose sanctions upon- there are three categories: the individuals in the Russian government, Russia itself, and individuals doing business, governments doing business with Russia.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

REP. TURNER: The president had those three categories- impose them, or waive them, or waive them in part. I would encourage the president to do so. That bill being in place is- and the president has signed it- is important. It's a legacy of Lindsey Graham. It's important that's in place. The president now has that authority. He has waived it. He has in that waiver that he signed, a continuing opportunity to now- and the- Secretary Rubio has confirmed, to continue daily--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
REP. TURNER: --the opportunity to waive in part or not waive in part. In other words, to- to institute those sanctions, I would encourage him to do so.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Does that mean you would withhold your vote for some of his agenda items in the lame-duck, as we've had other representatives, Don Bacon, Brian Fitzpatrick, Mike McCaul suggest they would do?

REP. TURNER: Well, I think it depends as we go through the- this- this process of discussion as to what this- I don't- I don't think there's any, you know, brinksmanship that needs to have to occur on this. I think there are discussions need to occur on these- these waivers. Some of those waivers should not be absolute because, for example, you know, the- the biggest offender of this, and Zelenskyy needs to come to the table loudly. The EU is the fourth largest offender of purchasing--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REP. TURNER: --energy from Russia, and the- France is one of them. A quarter of a billion dollars, they purchased of energy from--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REP. TURNER: --Russia, just in August.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, we have to leave it there. Congressman, thank you.
REP. TURNER: Thank you.
MARGARET BRENNAN:  We'll be right back, one minute. Stay with us.

summary: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso join Margaret Brennan.
story: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, moderated by Margaret Brennan:

Anthony Salvanto, CBS News executive director of elections and surveys Rep. Mike Turner, Republican of Ohio Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, Democratic candidate for Senate Sen. Kevin Cramer, Republican of North Dakota Anthony Salvanto, CBS News executive director of elections and surveys, Caitlin Huey Burns, CBS News political correspondent and Ed O'Keefe, CBS News senior White House and political correspondent
Anthony Salvanto, CBS News executive director of elections and surveys
Rep. Mike Turner, Republican of Ohio
Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, Democratic candidate for Senate
Sen. Kevin Cramer, Republican of North Dakota
Anthony Salvanto, CBS News executive director of elections and surveys, Caitlin Huey Burns, CBS News political correspondent and Ed O'Keefe, CBS News senior White House and political correspondent
Click here to browse full transcripts from 2026 of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm Margaret Brennan in Washington.
And this week on Face the Nation: Midterm elections campaigning enters the homestretch, and President Trump's latest move to ease pressure on Vladimir Putin sparks fury among some Republicans.
From East to West and far North to Deep South, it's down to the sweet 16 for the 2026 candidates, even for the politician whose name won't actually appear on any ballot this year.
(Begin VT)
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): What an honor. I love doing this stuff, you know? This is worth the eight hours in a plane.
(LAUGHTER)
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: And don't forget, I got eight hours going back too.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: The president says his quest for a red state romp is working.
(Begin VT)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: So I think these rallies have changed everything. I think a lot of people that maybe were having trouble won't have so much trouble. But I feel I owe it to the Republican Party.
(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: But will the rallies be enough to reverse those hurricane-force headwinds the president's party is facing? We have brand- new polling on that Texas race. It's one of the tightest toss-ups in the country.
Democrats face their own tough challenges, like getting a fractured party to go out and vote, if not for them, then against Trump's Republican candidate.
(Begin VT)
STATE REP. ANGIE NIXON (D-Florida) (Senatorial Candidate): Are you ready to put an end to corruption that's driving up our prices and ruining our democracy?
(CHEERING)
STATE REP. ANGIE NIXON: Well, I'm ready too.
(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will also look at the president's latest move to make it easier for Vladimir Putin to sell oil, an executive order freezing the just-passed Lindsey Graham law intended to cut off funding for Putin's war chest.
Ohio Republican Congressman Mike Turner and North Dakota Senator Kevin Cramer will weigh in on that. And we will talk with Florida Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon.
It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.
Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.

With just two weeks and two days until November 3, there is no better way to begin the broadcast today than with our executive director of elections and surveys, Anthony Salvanto, with our brand-new Texas poll.
Anthony, good morning.
CBS estimates Democrats have the edge to take the House. They need four seats to take the Senate. How can they do it?
ANTHONY SALVANTO: Well, you set the scene.

Through the fall, the Democrats have put a lot of Senate races in play in a lot of red Republican-leaning states. Texas is a really good example of that. So, let me take you there. What you have got here in the matchup between Talarico and Paxton, our new poll shows this really as tight as can be, Margaret, at 51-49.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Wow.
ANTHONY SALVANTO: But the story in there is a common theme that we see running through a lot of these races. One is, can the Republican base consolidate behind their candidates?

Here in Texas, you see, at least because they're the party's nominee is one reason that folks are backing Paxton. But at the same time, you also see a big thing here, where you have got these party breaks, Talarico doing better with independents and also better with people who say that they're hurting financially because of prices.

That's a common theme. And I'm going to take you back to the map now and show you the rest of these places that we're really watching, for one thing, Ohio. That's another state that the president won fairly easily. That, we see as a toss-up. I can take you out to Alaska. This is another toss-up, again, a Republican-leaning state.

And there are a couple of others too. To just remind folks, Iowa, it's leaning red right now in this race, but certainly competitive. Even Kansas is another spot that we're going to be watching closely on election night in that one. And, again, to remind folks, this is a place the president won easily, but is in play now.

So that's the Democrats' challenge that comes along with that expanded map. One other point, though, because it's really important as we go. You have got to watch for the Democrats to hold on to places that they already have.

So, Michigan, this is a toss-up. They'd have to hold up. And then another one, I'm going to show you, Maine, because this one's interesting, Susan Collins running for reelection in a state that Kamala Harris won. This race is neck-and-neck too, and that's a toss-up, probably also one the Democrats would have to have.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, the last time you were here, you told us Democratic voters were telling you they're more likely to show up at the polls than Republicans were. Is that still the case?
ANTHONY SALVANTO: It is. And I'm going to show you a slide that kind of tells the tale here.

This is from our House estimates. And you see this gap between the Democrats who say they're definitely going to vote and the Republicans who say they're definitely going to vote. This is driving a lot of the gaps you see in the polling, and it's also driving the political narrative, the president hitting the campaign trail, trying to boost that Republican turnout.
Because Republicans, especially if they say inflation has hit them hard, they're not going to vote for Democrats, but they might stay home.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And that's everything, turnout.
Anthony Salvanto, thank you.
ANTHONY SALVANTO: Thanks.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're joined now by Ohio Republican Congressman Mike Turner.
Good morning, and thanks for being here in person.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER (R-Ohio): Thank you.
(CROSSTALK)
MARGARET BRENNAN: A lot to get to with you, but let's start on politics.

Ohio has been reliably Republican, but you've got a competitive gubernatorial race and Senate race. In Minnesota, in Iowa, in Michigan, and in Maine, Republicans have been positioning themselves as independent of the president on some issues. Take a listen.
(Begin VT)
MICHELE TAFOYA (R-Minnesota Senatorial Candidate): When Trump is right, I will work with him. When he's wrong, I will stand up for Minnesota.

REPRESENTATIVE ASHLEY HINSON (R-Iowa) (Senatorial Candidate): We need to lower gas prices in this country. We need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it.
MIKE ROGERS (R-Michigan Senatorial Candidate): Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now.
SENATOR SUSAN COLLINS (R-Maine): I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: I know you've been endorsed by President Trump. You did appear at a rally with him, but do you feel it would help to create some distance, like they did?

REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, as you know, I don't run with the president. I don't run from the president. It's one of the reasons why you have me on this show, because of the fact that – that I have my – my own agenda.

And I think what's important, as your pollster has – has indicated, he's in – he's talking of – of trends. What's most important, as he ended his presentation, as Anthony said, this is about who gets out to vote, and everybody needs to get out and vote.

You know, Margaret, my very first race, I won by 244 votes out of 44,000. It's really, really important as to who gets out and votes. So, my message would be to everyone is to get out and vote. And also, when they go to the polls, they need to make certain that they vote in every race.
It's amazing the number of drop-offs…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: … that people have. As they go down the ballot, people need to vote in every race, and they need to get out and vote.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But, clearly, those candidates felt they needed to say that.

FOX had a poll this week showing six in 10 respondents were extremely concerned about government corruption. AP had one that said six in 10 adults believe Trump is illegally profiting from the presidency or at least doing something unethical.

Your local paper, "The Columbus Dispatch," wrote it could not endorse the Republican Senate candidate because of the "abject failure" – this is a quote – "of Republicans in Congress to stop visible corruption and abuse of power by the Trump administration." They referred to Republicans as almost entirely spineless.
How do you counter those perceptions? Do you feel you need to?
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: No, first off, that – Columbus is not my local – local paper. And – and the…
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're Dayton.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Right, yes. I'm – I'm – I'm Dayton…
MARGARET BRENNAN: But it is still talking about the Senate race and talking about the perception that Congress has not pushed back on the president.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Right.

Well, I think – I think Congress has pushed back, and, certainly, I have pushed back. And in – in my community, I'm seen as part of the integral economic development team, the local economic development team of my community.

And the – the aspect of what people are doing or are not doing with respect to this administration is, I think, an individual candidate's issue. And people vote for individual candidates. They don't vote for a team. They don't vote for – for a slate.

And – and I think that's why individual candidates are talking about their individual records, as – as I do. People look in my community. They see me as a job creator. They see me as someone, if – Margaret, if you came into my community and we took a drive along my community, and I showed you my accomplishments, you'd see things at, you know, my local base, where we've doubled the jobs both inside and outside the fence, the VA, where we've created senior housing.
And, like, my opponent wouldn't be able to get out of the driveway of her house. Those are the kind of things that people look to for the individual candidates.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But the president is central here. The president is telling people, vote like he is on the ballot.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, that's – that's – that's the president. That's not the individual candidates.
MARGARET BRENNAN: He thinks he's doing candidates like you some – some good when he says things like that and comes out and rallies in Ohio.

REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, he came to a rally in my community, as the – as he said in the community when he was there, campaigning for the top of the ticket. When he came to my community, he actually came, when he was speaking of my record, that he was committing to sign legislation to restore the Delphi salaried pension who had their pensions taken away under the Obama administration.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. That hasn't happened yet.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: He committed to sign that legislation to restore those pensions that I had been working on for over a decade.
That makes over 5,000 people in my community restore their pensions.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: I have been working on paychecks and pensions, and that's the type of thing that makes a difference in my community.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well – well, let's talk about some of those things, which – because that hasn't passed yet, some of those things could get gunked up in the lame-duck because of what I'm about to ask you about. And that is…
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: It's…
(CROSSTALK)
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: … that the president has committed to sign.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK, if it can get to his desk.

I want to ask you about Elon Musk's SpaceX technology. Starlink, Ukraine uses it for communication. They use it to control their drones. Secretary Rubio said no one at the White House ordered it to be slowed down this week so that drones couldn't use it. But, effectively, that was the outcome.
Here is how Secretary Rubio explained it last night.
(Begin VT)

MARCO RUBIO (U.S. Secretary of State): We had nothing to do with that. I don't – I don't – the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened. But I – my understanding is, it's been restored.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Is "It sort of happened" sufficient explanation for you and others on the Armed Services Committee?
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Absolutely not.

I mean, this is something where there needs to be an investigation. There needs to be a congressional investigation. I mean, this is one of those things where – where we see that – that policies occur where sometimes there's – there's breaks in – in weapon systems that are supposed to be sent to Ukraine that doesn't happen, where monies are – are – don't arrive, where intelligence gets broken, where then later that we have – find, you know, unnamed people in the Pentagon perhaps break it.

There needs to be an investigation. We need to find out who these people are, because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things. And, even today, you know, the Institute for the Study of War reports today…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: … and Zelenskyy reports that, you know, perhaps it's spotty. There are areas where – that it's restored.
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's been straddled back.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: And there are areas where perhaps it is not. People's lives are at risk. And these – this is within Ukraine. This is areas where they're trying to defend themselves.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: This is essential to the United States' support of Ukraine in defending real aggressive attacks by Russia within Ukraine. And this needs to be restored.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But Elon Musk, who owns this company – and Starlink is a commercial enterprise. Elon Musk publicly opposes President Zelenskyy.
He posted on social media he doesn't want Starlink used for offensive military action. I know Secretary Rubio said it had been restored, but…
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: But this is within Ukraine. This is defending Ukraine against aggression within Ukraine.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Exactly, but it is just – they're all pointing at each other, saying, no, DOD is in charge. No, Elon Musk's in charge. I don't know. It just sort of happened.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: But the policy decision has been made that – that Starshield will be utilized for the purposes of Ukraine defending itself against Russian aggression.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Starshield…
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Starshield.
MARGARET BRENNAN: … which is the U.S. military contract.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Within its territory.
And it has, by everybody's reports, been broken in – in its ability to be able to be accessed. And there should be an investigation as to why, and it should be completely restored.
MARGARET BRENNAN: the president, there were a series of actions, not just the diesel waivers, these actions in regard to Ukraine's ability to defend itself.

And then you saw him waive or at least pause for a period of time the sanctions that you voted should be in place under the Lindsey Graham bill. They were supposed to punish buyers of Russian oil. He said, don't implement them.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, there's – there's two – two…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Will you encourage him to reverse course?
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: OK, there's two separate things here.
The – the sanctions under the Lindsey Graham bill, this weekend, there was a deadline for the president…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Today.

REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: … to either waive or to impose sanctions upon, there are three categories, the individuals in the Russian government, Russia itself, and individuals doing business, governments doing business with Russia.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: The president had those three categories, impose them, or waive them, or waive them in part.

I would encourage the president to do so. That bill being in place is – and the president has signed it – is important. It's a legacy of Lindsey Graham. It's important that's in place. The president now has that authority. He has waived it.
He has, in that waiver that he signed, a continuing opportunity to now – and the – Secretary Rubio has confirmed – to continue daily…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: … the opportunity to waive in part or not waive in part, in other words, to – to institute those sanctions. I would encourage him to do so.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Does that mean you would withhold your vote for some of his agenda items in the lame-duck, as we've had other representatives, Don Bacon, Brian Fitzpatrick, Mike McCaul, suggest they would do?

REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, I think it depends as we go through the – this – this process of discussion as to what this – I don't – I don't think there's any, you know, brinksmanship that needs to have to occur on this.

I think there are discussions need to occur on these – these waivers. Some of those waivers should not be absolute, because, for example, you know, the – the biggest offender of this – and Zelenskyy needs to come to the table loudly. The E.U. is the fourth largest offender of purchasing…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
(CROSSTALK)
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: … energy from Russia. And France is one of them, a quarter-of-a-billion dollars they purchased of energy from…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: … Russia just in August.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.
We have to leave it there. Congressman, thank you.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Thank you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll be right back, one minute. Stay with us.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Florida State Representative Angie Nixon. She is the Democratic Party's nominee for Senate, and she joins us from Gainesville.
Good morning to you.
STATE REP. ANGIE NIXON (D-Florida) (Senatorial Candidate): Good morning. Happy to be here with you…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it's good to talk you.
STATE REP. ANGIE NIXON: … in Gator Nation.
(LAUGHTER)
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's good to talk to you.

You identify as a progressive, but I know this past June you joined the Democratic Socialists of America during your primary bid. Our CBS polling shows 42 percent of Americans have a somewhat or very negative view of socialism.
I'm wondering, what elements of the Democratic Socialist platform drew you to it? How do you define your vision here?

STATE REP. ANGIE NIXON: For sure. So, first of all, thank you for having me on the show today, and I think it's really important for me to lay the groundwork, because a lot of people, this is my first introduction to them.

I am someone who is a lifelong Floridian, having worked in the state of Florida as a community organizer and a union organizer, and our campaign is on fire. We actually had over 4,000 people show up yesterday at rallies, and some in deep red counties, and we are on fire.
We were able to out-fund-raise our opponent by over $2 million in this past quarter. And I know, in regards to my joining that organization…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

STATE REP. ANGIE NIXON: … it's not about letters, but it is actually about the fact that we are fighting to ensure that there's access to quality health care for everyone, and access to fully funded public schools, in addition to ensuring people have a roof over their head.

My opponent, Ashley Moody, actually voted to end health care for over 440,000 people here in the state of Florida, which also jacked up premiums for private – people's private insurance. And so I just want to make sure that people don't go bankrupt simply because they're trying to live or go to the doctor.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: Well, Margaret, on this topic and a whole bunch of others, I think capitulating to a bully generally means you're going to make more demands going forward. That's the problem with, you know, taking sort of a business negotiation approach to the – to negotiating with a thug, which is what Vladimir Putin is.

So, I share those colleagues' positions on it. However, I also have to, you know, acknowledge that we are a few weeks or a couple of weeks from an election. One of the important topics of the election is the cost of diesel fuel. It's really an important issue here in North Dakota.

As Representative Turner pointed out, and I was cheering him on, our allies throughout Europe have been buying energy from Vladimir Putin and funding his war machine for decades. And they should stop right now.

Having said all of that, I expect this will be a short-term pause. And I certainly hope so. Because I – one of the things that President Zelenskyy asked of us when I was with him on – last Thursday, I think it was, Thursday or Friday, was that the president would fully enforce the Lindsey Graham sanctions bill. MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. Yes.

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: Well, I certainly hope that he does, Margaret. Again, speaking of thugs who will never, you know, never agree to terms, or at least not continue to agree to terms that would be negotiated –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: And Xi Jinping is another one. I think we have to start approaching our geopolitical negotiations the way that we ought to, and not the way that you do in a boardroom.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: You know, it – this is not a finality outcome to a dictator. The outcome of a negotiation with a dictator is more – you know, asking for more demands. And we have to start, you know, playing nice with our friends and treating our adversaries like they are adversaries.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You just met with President Zelenskyy. As you know, President Trump publicly blasted him again this week and said Ukraine needs another new president. Let me ask you something specific about how they defend themselves and conduct this war.

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: So, that – you're right, that was a proposal we brought to President Zelenskyy. Senator Wicker, Roger Wicker, the chairman of the Armed Services Committee, came up with that idea. President Zelenskyy was enthusiastic about it. He said, I can do that tomorrow. I would absolutely stop attacking Russia's energy facilities if I could have access to targeting capabilities, which is what Starshield would provide them, to go deep into Russia and attack their attackers. In other words, their launch facilities. And, you know, kill the archer, not the arrows.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: So, his requests were three, they were simple, and I agree with all three of them. So, I would hope we can get to that point where remembering that what President Zelenskyy's protecting are civilians. Russia has chosen to go after civilian populations –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: While President Zelenskyy has simply gone after, you know, the launchers and, more importantly, these – you know, the war machine's funding source, which is energy.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right, bringing us back to where we started here.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: Including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. I think – I – but I worry, Margaret, that there's a disconnect. Once again, I go back to my earlier illustration. MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: And so I worry about that.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, is Senator Wicker presenting this deal to the White House? Like, what are you doing with what you negotiated?

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: Yes. Yes. Oh, yes. Yes. Yes, for sure. I mean we had talked to people in the White House, at the Department of War, and to the State Department, even prior to meeting with President Zelenskyy.

So, I do support some sort of an investigation.
Certainly Congress itself could and should investigate. I think the letter that Senator Shaheen and Senator Tillis are talking about would be an inspector general investigation perhaps.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: But, sure, we want to get to the bottom of it. In the meantime, what's more important is that that power is put back on full scale and that we actually enhance Ukraine's ability to hit these launch facilities inside of Russia, deeper inside to like 300 kilometers I think is what President Zelenskyy was asking for.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. President Zelenskyy said today that it has been restored, but has been throttled back. And in terms of that Starshield expansion, as you say, no deal yet.

Let me ask you about something closer to home. You said this summer that you "hate" – that was the word you used, "President Trump's decision to import foreign beef tariff free because it's not America first, wrong- headed, and threatens the future of U.S. food production."

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: Well, first of all, Margaret, it won't have any affect in North Dakota on the – in the election cycle. We don't have a governor up. The president's, obviously, not up. We don't even have a senator up. So – and we're going to have an overwhelming Republican victory here.

Having said that, it's very discouraging to our ranchers. Again, I think there's a misunderstanding of commodity cycles, the commodity economic cycles. Ranchers rebuild their herds when prices are high. Their herds are, obviously, made much smaller when prices are low. That's why – that's why the countercyclical effect of commodity prices are well known to us, and why it's discouraging when we – when we reduce or eliminate the barriers to importing somebody else's beef, which is not nearly as safe or as high quality, at the cost of – at – to – at the cost of our local ranchers. They rely on these higher prices.
And by the way, I don't – I doubt that bringing in a bunch of Argentine beef is going to bring the price at the grocery store down any, you know.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, it hasn't.
SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: It has not. But it – but it will hurt the market price of the cattle themselves.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: So, they're going up against a lot of things.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: But their input costs are also higher. They don't come down because the price of a cow goes down.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: But, yes, so I still strongly oppose it and I think it was wrongheaded.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

And what is really especially jarring is, they don't – they haven't released who – or talked about who may be behind this. Federal law enforcement is investigating. But the uptick that we've seen and threats against lawmakers and their families has risen in the past year over 50 percent.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. Yes, it's something we are tracking very much in our public life these days.
Thank you all for this panel.
ED O'KEEFE: Good to see you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Get ready, it's going to be a fun two weeks.
CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Buckle up.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll be back in a moment.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's it for us today. We'll see you next week.

title: Ukraine, Sudan immigrants to retain deportation protections for now
summary: The TPS protections of tens of thousands of Ukrainians and hundreds of Sudanese immigrants were officially slated to terminate on Monday.
story: Immigrants from Ukraine and Sudan enrolled in the Temporary Protected Status policy will be able to live and work in the U.S. without fear of deportation for the time being, even though their protections were set to expire soon, the Department of Homeland Security told CBS News on Sunday.
The TPS protections of tens of thousands of Ukrainians and hundreds of Sudanese immigrants were officially slated to terminate on Monday.
But in statements on Sunday, DHS said final decisions on the fate of the humanitarian immigration programs will "be made at the appropriate time."
Until such decisions are announced, DHS added, nationals of Ukraine and Sudan enrolled in the TPS program will "retain protection."
The decisions to keep the deportation protections in place, albeit not final, stand in sharp contrast to the Trump administration's broader posture toward TPS programs.

Trump administration officials have routinely denounced TPS as a de facto amnesty policy abused by the Biden administration that encourages illegal immigration and that has been extended too often, despite its temporary nature.

Over the past year and a half, the Trump administration, as part of its aggressive immigration crackdown, has revoked the TPS protections of more than 1 million immigrants from over a dozen countries, including Afghanistan, Haiti and Venezuela.

The programs for Ukrainian and Sudanese nationals are among a handful of TPS policies that have remained in place nearly two years into President Trump's second term, alongside the protections for tens of thousands of immigrants from El Salvador. Their TPS program was also set to lapse last month, but DHS retained their protections, pending a final announcement.

Created in 1990 by Congress, TPS allows the U.S. government to offer a temporary deportation reprieve and work permits to immigrants, illegal and legal alike, who hail from countries facing armed conflict, an environmental disaster or another crisis that makes their return there unsafe.

The TPS policy for Ukrainians was first announced by the Biden administration in the spring of 2022, soon after Russia launched its full-blown invasion of Ukraine. As of March 2025, there were more than 100,000 Ukrainians enrolled in TPS, including those allowed into the U.S. under a Biden-era sponsorship policy.

The TPS program for Sudan has been around since the late 1990s, with different administrations extending the policy due to the armed conflict and political turmoil that has plagued the African nation. As of March 2025, roughly 1,800 Sudanese nationals had TPS.

title: Trump says D.C. golf course construction will start next month
summary: President Trump said Sunday that construction at the historic East Potomac Golf Links course will begin Nov. 15.
story: President Trump said Sunday that construction on a historic Washington, D.C., golf course will begin next month, despite an ongoing court challenge to his long-sought renovation of the East Potomac Golf Links course.

"I am pleased to announce that the Department of the Interior, under the auspices of Secretary Doug Burgum, and in conjunction with famed Golf Course Architect, Tom Fazio, has developed a plan to build a World Class Championship Golf Course on the site of the current East Potomac Golf Links, located in Washington, D.C.," Mr. Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

The president, who did not acknowledge the court challenge in his post, said that while the new golf course would remain open to the public, it would also be designed to host tournaments like the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup and the Presidents Cup. He also billed it as a "tremendously positive" economic opportunity for D.C. that would "create many jobs."

Mr. Trump described the current course as an "old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect ... with falling, dangerous, and disease infested trees, and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall." He said the site "was famous for no trees" originally but has since become "overgrown, dysfunctional, and unsafe."
Mr. Trump said construction will begin Nov. 15 on the course, which will be closed for about 15 months until the new one opens.

His announcement Sunday came less than a week after a federal judge barred the Trump administration from removing trees at the current golf course through Oct. 16, after hundreds of trees were cut down the weekend prior.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said in the order that until that date, the administration may not make "any irreparable modification" to the East Potomac course without first providing three business days' notice of such plans to the court, as well as to the plaintiffs in a lawsuit seeking to stop Mr. Trump's planned overhaul of the site.

"The administration has time and again tried to avoid the law in their mad rush toward converting a public recreation space to a high-end golf course and today's order will stop them from doing further irreparable harm to a precious public resource," said attorneys for the plaintiffs, the D.C. Preservation League and two local golfers, in response to the judge's order. "We are pleased that the court intervened and will prevent additional work while we seek more lasting relief."

title: In Michigan, consumer sentiment is pessimistic before midterms
summary: Due to high fuel and housing costs, and wages that aren't keeping pace with inflation, consumer sentiment is lower than at almost any other time in modern history. CBS News spoke with Michiganders to find out how the economy is playing on the minds of voters.
story: In most of the country, autumn is campaign season. But in Michigan it is also cider season. The Franklin Cider Mill is an institution in suburban Detroit that churns out hot donuts and ice-cold cider slushies. Between bites, we asked visitors to assess the state of their wallets three weeks before Election Day.
"I would say most are struggling, if I'm being honest," one woman said. Another man offered, "I don't feel great about the economy right now."
Jeffrey Robinson, a high school principal, put it succinctly: "It sucks," he said. "We have parents that carpool that are finding it hard to keep gas in the car."

If it seems like people are feeling especially gloomy about the economy, Joanne Hsu has the proof. She runs the nation's longest-running consumer sentiment survey at the University of Michigan. It dates back to 1946. She says that, since the start of the Iran conflict, "We've been seeing quite a bit of decline in consumer sentiment across the board, across all walks of life."

In fact, Hsu says, consumer sentiment is lower than almost any other time in modern history – including the stagflation era in the mid-1970s; the financial crisis in 2008; and the post-COVID price spikes under the Biden administration.
"Democrats, Independents and Republicans, all three groups, feel worse about the economy in this administration than they did in the first Trump administration," said Hsu.

And, she said, people are feeling bad about the economy despite the stock market doing well and rising wages. "The wages not keeping up with inflation is the key point there," Hsu said. "So, people don't feel like they're able to get ahead. The share of consumers who are expecting their wages to grow faster than inflation fell from 18% just a year-and-a-half ago, to only 11% in September. That's a huge drop."

Hsu says consumer sentiment initially went up when Mr. Trump was reelected two years ago. But the president has failed to deliver on one of his key campaign promises, one he made right here in Michigan just a few weeks before Election Day. "One of my top priorities will be to quickly defeat inflation and make America affordable again," Mr. Trump said in 2024. "It'll all happen very quickly. This will rapidly drive prices down, lower interest rates, and put more money into the pockets of American consumers. It'll also bring your grocery bill way down."

Instead, grocery prices rose by more than four percent in the past two years, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics; gas prices are up 35 percent, according to AAA; and 30-year fixed mortgage rates are projected to stay above seven percent through next year, according to Freddie Mac.
"The average public is paying a price"
Real estate agent Michael Perna told us, "It would not surprise me if we saw a rate that starts with an 8 before we see a rate that starts with a 6."

In Northville, Mich., a house that normally would have been on the market for just a week has been for sale for more than a month. Perna says the house is priced a little over what buyers can afford right now: "Originally the mortgage rates were about 6.5 percent, and now they're at 7.5 percent, and buyers can afford $50,000 less, [so] we're a little over."

He says, even for homebuyers with a stable income, every rate hike means they have to settle for less – which makes for a pretty bad attitude about this economy. "Absolutely, a lot of people, myself included, have a bad attitude about this economy!" Perna said.

So, will sour consumers make for angry voters? Back at the Franklin Cider Mill, some are optimistic, but not all. One woman criticized President Trump's tariffs ("It raises all of our prices, so it's hard"), but thinks in the long term they are needed to bring more manufacturing jobs to the U.S.
One man said this economy is not what he expected under Mr. Trump in his second term: "He promised us, and I don't think he kept his promise."

High school principal Jeffrey Robinson said, "The average public is paying a price. I'm not looking for my $5,000 check, because I know that's not coming. But I don't know how long the economy and the average person is going to be able to sustain what we're going through right now."
Story produced by Mark Hudspeth. Editor: Jason Schmidt.
