title: OpenAI employee accused of planting recording device in office
summary: A Saudi national who worked at OpenAI as an engineer is suspected of planting a recording device in one of the company's conference rooms.
story: An OpenAI employee suspected of secretly planting a recording device in one of the company's conference rooms has been arrested on criminal charges, the Justice Department said Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and made his initial appearance in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on Tuesday. Alfozan was charged with trying to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
Prosecutors said that Alfozan had worked at OpenAI as an engineer since July 2025.

On Sept. 30, the company's employees discovered the audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television inside an executive conference room. The company later determined that the recording device had been concealed in toilet paper and installed about two days before it was discovered.

The meeting room where it was hidden was often used by OpenAI's employees to discuss highly confidential and proprietary matters, including research, product plans and business development, the Justice Department said.
In a statement, OpenAI said that after discovering the device, it contacted the FBI and has terminated the employee accused of planting it.

"The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work. At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the company said.

"We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a post on X that the FBI and its partners had carried out the arrest and that the investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan's attorney, William Pernik, noted to CBS News that his client is presumed innocent, and cautioned against "jumping to conclusions at this very early stage of the case when very little information is known," or seeking to "politicize" a prosecution based on factors like nationality.

The criminal complaint, made public on Tuesday, alleged that Alfozan used a productivity tool to make inquiries about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, and locations of "leadership and exec" and external partner meetings.

Other evidence gathered in the investigation, meanwhile, showed that a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse had also submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30, related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating and remote accessing a continuous audio recording device.
A photograph included in the complaint also shows that Alfozan entered the conference room where the device was hidden on Oct. 5 and looked behind the television.

That same day, the complaint says Alfozan left his bag unattended in another room, and the company's security personnel opened it and found his ID, wallet and another recording device similar to the one planted in the conference room.
Alfozan is due to appear in federal court again on Oct. 19 for a detention hearing.

title: Character.ai declares bankruptcy, citing legal and business woes
summary: AI company has faced multiple lawsuits from families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using its platform.
story: Character.ai said it has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, with its chief executive attributing the chatbot provider's financial problems to "significant legal, regulatory and operational headwinds."

The company said it will continue operating as it seeks to sell its business, and added that The Walt Disney Co. has agreed to pay $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to Character.ai's intellectual property.

Character.ai's financial struggles follow scrutiny and litigation over its technology, which uses artificial intelligence to create custom bots consumers can chat with. In early 2026, Character.ai and Google, which had a licensing deal with the AI company, agreed to settle several lawsuits filed by families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using Character.ai's platform.

The company settled a wrongful death lawsuit earlier in 2026 — the first filed in the U.S. against an AI company — with a Florida family who said their teen son died after conducting an emotional and sexual relationship with a chatbot known as "Dany." The family said in their lawsuit that Character.ai had no mechanisms in place to protect their son or notify an adult when teens were spending too much time interacting with Chatbots.
The company added several safety features designed with teens in mind after several lawsuits alleged its chatbots inappropriately interacted with underage users.

Several states have also sued Character.ai over its technology, with Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman alleging in January that its chatbots "preyed on children and led them into self-harm." In May, Pennsylvania sued Character.ai after one of its chatbots allegedly claimed to be a licensed psychiatrist in the state and provided a "fake Pennsylvania license number."
In a statement issued late Monday, Character.ai said it believes the company will be sold by late November or early December.

"After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders," Character.ai CEO Colin Adams said in the statement. "As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging user experience for our Character.ai community remains a top priority."
Is Character.ai shutting down?
The company said on Monday that its services continue to operate and that subscriptions remain active.
"If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance," Character.ai said.

In a blog post, the company said customer data "continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy." That policy states that data Character.ai collects from users — including chat transcripts, voice recordings, and images and videos — could be disclosed in connection with a sale or a negotiation to sell the company or its assets.
"As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website," the company said.

title: Anthropic warns "AI worms" could soon infect smart home devices
summary: Small AI models could clone themselves and infect internet-connected devices such as smart TVs and appliances, the researchers warned.
story: Anthropic is sounding the alarm about a new risk posed by artificial intelligence: Self-replicating "AI worms" could soon infest your "smart" home devices.

In a report released on Monday, Anthropic safety researchers said small AI models may be only "months away" from gaining the ability to clone themselves and spread across internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens, TVs and vacuum cleaners. The ability to reproduce themselves without human control would make it hard to control such agents because there's "no centralized point to shut off," said Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot.
Stronger AI models are already capable of what the researchers called "end-to-end replication," a threshold they say smaller models could reach by year-end, according to Anthropic.
AI worms, a type of AI-powered malware, can quickly spread across networks and devices while evading detection, according to cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks.

Smart devices in people's homes, as well as internet-connected devices such as security cameras, are vulnerable given that internet-enabled devices tend to have weaker security protections, the Anthropic researchers said. In what they described as a worst-case scenario, a swarm of AI agents — bots that work together to accomplish a shared goal — could propagate across computer hardware using "replication schemes."

The researchers said they are unsure of what form these attacks could take, noting that the AI models could be distributed as "digital slime mold" or as more powerful models capable of hacking into data centers.

"We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay," the Anthropic researchers wrote in the report.

title: As AI dominates conversations, here are key terms to know
summary: Artificial intelligence and the conversations around it are rapidly evolving. These terms can help to understand the developments.
story: As artificial intelligence — and the conversation surrounding it — rapidly evolves, keeping up with the language being used to describe it has become essential to understanding its impacts.
Here are some key terms to know:
Abliteration

Abliteration (a portmanteau of the words ablation, meaning to remove a part of something, and obliteration) is a process where an AI model's safety guardrails and refusal mechanisms are removed. Once an AI model is abliterated, it will not refuse requests, including harmful ones.

The patterns that a model learns during safety training to identify harmful requests can be found in a model's weights, or the billions of numerical parameters that represent its knowledge. Models that are open-weight, meaning the weights are public and can be modified, are vulnerable to abliteration.
AI agent

An AI agent can carry out tasks with some degree of autonomy on a user's behalf. Users can interact with an AI agent like they would a chatbot, but as Meta — which recently released its AI agent, "Muse" — puts it: Unlike a traditional chatbot, AI agents can complete multiple steps of a task without requiring input at each stage.
AI agents use external tools such as web browsers and apps so that they can perform tasks, including sending an email, booking a reservation or managing a user's calendar.
AI agents have been popular in Silicon Valley for years and are now bursting into the mainstream with consumer-friendly AI agents like Meta's "Muse" and OpenAI's "Dots."

Since AI agents are tasked with completing the goals assigned to them by the user, there have been rogue incidents where agents, in pursuit of a goal, behave in unexpected ways in order to achieve it. A recent report from nonprofit research lab Transluce identifies cases where AI agents targeted U.S. government websites using "aggressive techniques to access publicly available data."
Alignment

When an AI model is described as aligned, it behaves in line with human goals and values. As a model undergoes safety training, it is fine-tuned to follow instructions and generate responsible outputs. OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki defines alignment as "getting the AI to 'try to do the right thing by human standards'" and wrote that it is "the core problem in AI research."

When AI is misaligned, it might behave unexpectedly. In September, OpenAI released a framework for reporting misalignment and said that identifying and sharing these cases can help show where safeguards need strengthening. Anthropic says its alignment team trains models to remain "helpful, honest and harmless" and shares its findings with the public.
There is debate among researchers about how to ensure alignment, or if it is even possible to do so.
Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
Some researchers believe that when an AI system has reached the same level of learning, reasoning and cognitive performance as a human, it will have achieved artificial general intelligence.
Stanford University calls the term "controversial," pointing to the fact that "human-level intelligence" can mean different things to different people and is a subject of debate by AI experts.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is among those who believe AGI is here already, saying on a podcast, "I think we've achieved AGI." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told CNBC's "Squawk Box" in 2025 that AGI is "not a super useful term," echoing experts who believe it only serves to confuse.
Artificial superintelligence (ASI)

If AI systems surpass even the most advanced humans in every cognitive domain, they will be considered artificial superintelligence. This hypothetical scenario has sparked debate among researchers, AI experts and politicians.

Some industry leaders and researchers have warned about the existential risks of the pursuit of superintelligence, with the concern that an AI that powerful could evolve beyond human control. The CEO of Microsoft AI Mustafa Suleyman called superintelligence an "anti-goal" because it "doesn't feel like a positive vision of the future."

Other technology leaders, such as Mark Zuckerberg, are generally in favor of the notion of superintelligent AI. Zuckerberg argued that developing superintelligence and distributing it widely could lead to "a new era of personal empowerment where individuals can use this powerful new capability to reach their full potential, pursue their interests, and improve their lives and the world more than ever before."
Distillation
Distillation is a process where a smaller AI model is trained, usually, on a larger, stronger one so that it behaves similarly.

In an announcement on detecting and preventing distillation attacks, Anthropic said that while distillation is a legitimate method used by frontier labs, which distill their own models to create smaller, more cost-effective versions, it can also be used to snatch capabilities from competing labs whose models are more powerful. Companies might do this because it is faster and cheaper than developing their own.

The NSA and FBI warned in September that China-based AI companies "are engaging in aggressive, industrial-scale distillation activities" to extract restricted functionalities from U.S. frontier models.
Gradual disempowerment

Gradual disempowerment is a phrase coined by AI safety researchers that describes a path where AI displaces all, or most, of human labor and decision-making. In this scenario, AI agents or AI-enabled robots are superior to humans at nearly all tasks and human creativity, cognition and agency erode away.
Jailbreak
Jailbreaking is an attempt to bypass or "trick" an AI model's guardrails typically through prompting. Researchers jailbreak systems to identify vulnerabilities.

Jailbreaks can vary in terms of their severity, according to Anthropic. "Sometimes they only unblock minor undesirable behaviors, and sometimes they unblock a wide range of harmful outputs, making a model much more dangerous," the company wrote in July.
When a model is jailbroken, it may answer questions that could cause harm, such as designing a chemical weapon or creating illegal images.
Open models
When a model is "open," some of its internal mechanics are publicly available.

A model can be "open weight," meaning that its weights, which represent a model's knowledge, are public and can be copied or modified by anyone. Some examples of open-weight models include Beijing-based Moonshot's Kimi model series and Meta's Llama models.

While the ability to tamper with a model's weights can lead to the weakening of its safety or ethical guardrails, it can also be beneficial. Researchers are able to examine the weights, fine-tune them and identify vulnerabilities that can lead to strengthening. They are also less restricted when it comes to, perhaps, using the model for hard science or cyberattack defense.

A model can also be "open source," which is when its code is publicly available. That can be in addition to its weights being open. When a model is open source, anyone can see how it was built and can go in and change it.

Open models tend to be cheaper, or even free to use, and can be hosted on the users' own hardware. They've been embraced in China, which some researchers say is closing the AI capability gap between China and the U.S. The open-weight marketplace also appears to be expanding in the U.S. with Meta and Apple announcing in October a rare collaboration to bring open-weight models to Apple desktops.

Some open models are mere months behind proprietary, or closed, ones in terms of capability, though there is some evidence that the reason they remain close behind is because they are trained using American proprietary models. According to MIT, open models achieve about 90% of the performance of closed models upon release.
Proprietary models
The AI models American consumers commonly interact with, such as Anthropic's Claude Opus, OpenAI's GPT-5 and Google's Gemini 2.5, are closed, proprietary models.
When a model is "closed," its provider keeps elements of a model's inner workings — such as its weights, source code and underlying infrastructure — private.
These models tend to be more expensive to use than ones that have open weights.
Recursive self-improvement (RSI)
Recursive self-improvement describes when an AI model can improve itself or build its successor.

Anthropic says this has not yet been achieved, but that it could "come sooner than most institutions are prepared for," and OpenAI last month shared a detailed report on progress toward RSI, saying the company aims to build an automated AI researcher that, under human supervision, can "further progress on deep learning and alignment, enabling iterative improvements."

At a recent hearing on AI safety, held by the New York City Council, all three AI whistleblowers who appeared spoke about RSI. Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who publicly resigned from Anthropic over the summer, said that automatic AI research has become the primary goal of AI companies. Daniel Kokotajlo, who resigned from OpenAI two years ago, said that AI companies should not be allowed to pursue RSI, but that if they do, the process should be slowed. Alex Turner, a former researcher at Google DeepMind, said RSI could "quickly yield AIs that are intelligent beyond our comprehension," calling it an "extremely dangerous thing."
Red team

Red teaming is a cybersecurity method where a team is tasked with simulating an adversarial attack in order to test a system's defenses and see how it will respond. Red teaming of AI models is also used to test how well a model is aligned, or behaving in line with human goals and values.
Sandbox
A sandbox is a controlled, secure environment where AI tools can be tested. It's a place to learn how an AI agent or model might behave before releasing it to consumers.

OpenAI has documented cases where its AI agents have escaped their sandbox during testing and hacked into the servers of Hugging Face. The models, OpenAI said, were so "hyperfocused on finding a solution" to a cybersecurity challenge that they went to extreme lengths to achieve it.
Anthropic has also disclosed sandbox escapes where Claude models broke out in order to complete a task.

title: Should you trust personal AI agents? What security experts say.
summary: The more access you give personal AI agents, the more capable they can be. But should you trust them?
story: Cybersecurity expert Hed Kovetz would love to have a personal AI agent handle some of his administrative tasks and lighten his workload. But he doesn't trust any of the commercially available agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots, with access to his email accounts, banking details, health records and other sensitive information.

"It's tempting to use a personal AI assistant. They access your email, order stuff and pay your bills. I would love to get that kind of help," he told CBS News. "But they could be taken advantage of or decide to go beyond the scope of what they are told to do."

While Kovetz sees tremendous commercial value in such products, he believes leading technology firms rushed them to market without sufficient security measures. For that reason, he advises consumers to be discreet about what they share with personal AI agents. Yet other AI security experts advise that consumers can use the tools as long as they rely on safeguards and are aware of the risks of providing personal data to an AI agent.

"I would be careful about giving full access to some of these commercial AI agents," Kovetz said. "I am aware of the fact that their security and privacy are far from being ready. Some consumers say, 'I don't care, I don't have anything to hide.' But that's not true; they still have medical records, bank accounts."

Such agents are already tremendously popular among consumers. When Meta's Muse first became available last month, it quickly became the most downloaded product in Apple's App Store. But while AI agents promise to save consumers time and even money by reading private correspondence and spending money on a user's behalf, they could also take actions that a user never explicitly authorized, leaving the user with limited recourse.

For example, it may be hard to know whether your AI agent is working for you or a retailer, Lindsay Owens, a consumer protection expert, told CBS News. She noted that Walmart's shopping agent, named Sparky, boosted average consumer basket sizes by almost 40% compared to shoppers who browse normally. Such data suggests that some AI agents could be trying to upcharge their users, she said.
Here's what security experts say they would and wouldn't let an AI agent do for them.
Should you let an AI agent shop for you?

Lynette Owens, a consumer education expert at TrendLife, an organization formed to protect households in the age of artificial intelligence by informing them about its capabilities and risks, also warned consumers against entrusting personal AI agents with too much access and information about them.
When it comes to online shopping, she believes AI agents can be extremely useful for researching products and comparing deals, but she cautions against letting them spend money.

"If you want to offload something like comparing deals, that's OK, but I'm not ready to hand off agency around a purchase, especially a high-ticket one. I wouldn't let it use my credentials like a credit card," she said.

One reason why she doesn't trust any commercially available AI agent to roam the internet with her credit card in hand is that criminals could trick it. Using what's called a "prompt injection," cybercriminals can trick an AI agent into ignoring its original instructions, such as "Don't spend more than $25."

Unlike traditional cyberattacks, prompt injection doesn't necessarily require hackers to break into an account or install malicious software. Instead, an attacker can plant instructions in a webpage, email or document that an AI agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.
If the agent mistakes those instructions for commands it should follow, it could be manipulated into revealing private information or taking actions its user never intended.

"We've seen an increase in incidents of prompt injections, and criminals are getting more clever about how they're hiding malicious code on websites," Owens said. "We're so excited about these new capabilities, but with any new technology, the security piece always lags."
Media and technology attorney Douglas J. Wood said consumers are liable if they authorize an AI bot to shop on their behalf, and it misinterprets instructions or overspends.

"If you give an AI agent, e.g., Muse, credit card information, you are making the bot an authorized user with the power to act on it," he told CBS News. "If it exceeds your instructions and spends your money, the card issuer will argue you authorized the purchasing tool."
Under federal law, such an individual would not be entitled to loss protection, Wood explained.
"Since you can't pursue the AI bot for improper use (it is not an entity that can be sued), your only remedy is to cut it off," he said, adding that by then the harm will have already been done.
His advice to consumers is: "Don't be lazy."
"Shop the old-fashioned way with the card in your hands. Authorizing an AI agent to use your card is like giving a bank robber the vault combination and telling him to steal only $100," he said.
How much data are you sharing?

New York-based entrepreneur Chris Franco, founder of marketing firm Woodridge Growth, has taken the opposite tack. He said tech companies have been collecting consumers' personal data for decades for various uses, such as selling it to advertisers, who use it to better market their goods and services.

"We've been giving out personal data to ad platforms for the last 20 years, and all we got back was better ad targeting," he told CBS News. "With these agents, you're sharing information, but the benefits are greater. It's a trade-off, but it's a much better deal."

To be sure, he wouldn't feel comfortable giving a Muse, Dots or Instinct AI agent full rein over his life, and believes it necessary to give it strict instructions while also monitoring its behavior and activity.

He likened giving an AI agent his credit card details to a parent handing off an exclusive credit card for high-net-worth individuals to a teenager without parameters. Both would be unwise, according to Franco.

Franco also allows his personal AI agents, including Muse and Grok Bot, to comb through his Gmail inbox. He's tasked them with organizing his receipts into a spreadsheet so that he can manage — and cancel — subscriptions.
It's a task he'd estimate would take him hours to do manually, if he ever got around to it at all.
"In 10 minutes, it had found a few I wasn't using. I would have canceled them anyway, but this did it way sooner," Franco said.

He acknowledges that it has insight into his personal life, including sensitive family matters, but at the end of the day, believes that the benefits of giving AI agents great access to his life outweigh the risks.

"The upside and pros of giving it context, in my view, are so much greater than whatever sci-fi-like scenarios there are of it going rogue," he said. "I am comfortable with it having that knowledge about me, because it can help me meet my goals faster."
Ask how it works

Matt Fredrikson, a computer engineering expert at Carnegie Mellon and founder of Gray Swan AI, an AI security company, said he gives his AI agents a fair bit of autonomy but also closely monitors their activity, using tools his company builds.
"The consumer-facing agents meant for normal people aren't immediately transparent about what they're doing with your data," he said. "But you can ask for that info if you probe them."
Simply ask your agent for a plain-language summary of how it went about completing the tasks it handled for you.
He also likened outsourcing administrative tasks to an AI agent to hiring a human personal assistant, which comes with a similar set of risks.

"If you have a human assistant, you've built a relationship with them, and there's a reason why you hired them in the first place. You trust them with a certain level of authority and autonomy," he said.

Simultaneously, when working with a human personal assistant, you're engaging in conversation with them and asking them to explain their thought processes. "You have to do that with these agents as well," he said.
Columbia Business School psychology and computer science expert Sandra Matz also drew parallels between working with a human assistant and an AI agent.
"If you wouldn't trust another person to deal with your personal information and process it safely, I wouldn't trust an agent," she said.
She highlighted one distinct difference between AI and humans, though.

"What prevents humans from sharing things they know about you is that they might feel guilty or ashamed, or have a negative emotional response to breaking the trust you've built with them," she said. "You can train an agent not to violate your trust, but they may violate it because they don't have guilt."

title: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be hardest to stop
summary: The time to prepare for "gradual disempowerment" is now, according to researchers. One calls it "a civilization-scale problem."
story: It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless.

But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers."
It's not just a threat to jobs. They warn that allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.

One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way.
And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts.
"I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities.
Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks, which could be accelerated by capable AI.
"It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."
What is "gradual disempowerment" and how could AI cause it?
The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.
At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems, doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture.

We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.

It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job.

To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.

But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all.

But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them.

Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead.
Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.

The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?
With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them.

"If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world.
"What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"
A risk to democratic governance

It's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military, for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable.

If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle, its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge.

"The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group.
States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future?
"If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit.

Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit.
If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.

"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve.
"Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."
How does humanity avoid gradual disempowerment?
Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here.

Gradual disempowerment "does not need to emerge from a deliberate scheme or powergrab by AI systems," wrote Kulveit and his colleagues. "In the short-term, it is being incentivized by the perceived value that AI systems can bring to economic, cultural and state functions."
"We can't be in the situation where we are competing with the machines," said Kulveit. "Because if we are just competing with the machines, we will probably lose."

The gradual disempowerment authors believe stopping our disempowerment may be a heavy lift for humanity, since it involves complex systems that feed into each other — government, culture, and the economy.
"This may be a bigger challenge than merely preventing AI systems from pursuing overtly harmful goals," they write.

One first step in slowing disempowerment is keeping indicators of how much work is being ceded to AI, and of what kind of specific jobs AI systems are capable of handling. If thousands of workers are being displaced by AI in, say, call center jobs, it helps to know that in granular detail.

But measurement isn't enough without action, Mitchell said. She argues that removing humans from the loop in AI processes both worsens oversight and degrades the skills of the human overseer. Therefore, companies and leadership in all fields must take proactive steps to keep humans engaged.

"This general practice within tech is we want our systems to be frictionless," said Mitchell, referring to the idea that everything should move fast and without obstacles. "There's this sense that the less friction the better, but there's been a push within the more ethical AI community that strategic friction can be good because it can draw people's attention to critical issues that otherwise they might overlook."

Mitchell argues that strategic friction — keeping humans in the work loop at predetermined steps — can be done both by developers of AI, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic and Google, and by companies and organizations that deploy AI. Thoughtful and purposeful design of AI can benefit society as a whole, and the individuals who use it.
Kulveit agrees that AI should be thoughtfully designed to add value to humans, not necessarily replace our every task.

"You want to carve out places where we agree that we will not allow competitive pressures to remove humans from the loop," he said. "It would be nice if the companies train the AIs to be more complementary to humans. Currently, the AIs are implicitly trained to be a replacement for humans. But you can imagine training the AIs so they are better at explaining to us what's happening."

Kulveit is describing AI that doesn't just spew out the answers to whatever question you ask it, at the very least in sectors where it is critical to include human expertise and decision-making, like war. Quick and easy answers can be helpful, but they can also make you dependent and credulous, believing anything the chatbot tells you, whether right or wrong.

But AI can be more than that. It can help you not just by doing the work for you, but by educating you along the way. That way the human worker continues to learn while using AI as a partner, not a substitute.

"There has been such a singular focus on capability or functionality of these systems to the detriment of people, to the detriment of users," said Mitchell. "If your only goal is to get a high score on a benchmark, then you are not going to be taking into account cognitive support design. But if your goal is to make a system that works really well for people — like if the race is for a utility as opposed to benchmark score — then you end up designing fundamentally different systems."

If gradual disempowerment really is a large-scale risk, compared to more talked-about doom scenarios — like AI helping to design bioweapons or chemical weapons — it may suffer from a relative lack of vividness.

"We know what it means for a robot to take over the world. We know what it means for countries to nuke each other," said Chooi. "AI taking over the world is very legible in the human consciousness. But gradual disempowerment? No one has made a movie about gradual disempowerment."
But to Chooi, gradual disempowerment is very easy to picture.
"All the organizations have the incentives to adopt it and phase out humans," he said. "This is a very logical conclusion. It's not very hard to see it."

title: Elon Musk pledges to give a SpaceX share to every U.S. child
summary: The SpaceX CEO wrote on social media on Monday that the gift "will be the first of many."
story: Elon Musk said in a social media post on Monday that he plans to give one of his SpaceX shares to each child in the U.S., writing that the gift "will be the first of many."

Musk didn't specify how the shares would be distributed or other details of how the pledge might be fulfilled. The offer arrived a day after artificial intelligence company Anthropic announced that it will commit 5% of its shares to a new "public benefit" fund.
Anthropic said it will contribute an additional 2% of shares at its board's discretion for every 50% increase in the company's value, above a set threshold.
Shares of SpaceX, which will report quarterly earnings on Tuesday, rose $3.46, or 2.7%, to $149.49 in Monday morning trading.

The SpaceX CEO is the company's largest shareholder with a 10.5% stake, according to financial data firm FactSet. His stake included 4.8 billion shares of SpaceX when the company went public earlier this year, an event that briefly made Musk the world's first trillionaire.
There are about 73 million children in the U.S., according to Census Bureau data.
Musk, the world's richest person, is currently worth about $904 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Anthropic made its pledge to commit a portion of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which it described as "a new entity," at a time when AI researchers from leading labs are warning of doomsday scenarios with potentially catastrophic outcomes that extend far beyond job losses.

Anthropic said the company has a two-pronged mission, with its research providing both a public benefit component and for-profit value. The new fund will give it more flexibility to make large donations to nonprofits or gifts to specific populations, the company added.

Anthropic also called out AI's impact on workers, acknowledging that tech advances could "cause instability" for many employees, and noted that it has already committed $200 million to analyzing and addressing AI's effects on parts of the labor force.
"Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good," Anthropic said.

Musk could conceivably use the recently created Trump Accounts program to gift SpaceX shares to U.S. children. The accounts, under new rules laid out by the Treasury, allow donors to deliver stock to the accounts without paying capital-gains taxes.

Michael Piwowar, executive director of Georgetown McDonough's Psaros Center for Financial Markets and Policy, called Trump Accounts the "perfect vehicle" through which Musk could deliver SpaceX shares to recipients.
"One of their great features, in addition to $1,000 seed money, is the ability of philanthropists to make philanthropic donations to a class of individuals," he said.
The Treasury Department is automatically enrolling up to 60 million children in the Trump Accounts program.
Piwowar added that with Musk's donation, "American children will immediately be invested in the American dream."

The tax-deferred accounts, created under Mr. Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill tax and spending bill for U.S. citizens born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a $1,000 seed donation from the government.

title: California billionaire tax could backfire, Stanford study says
summary: A new analysis from Stanford economists cautions that enacting a billionaire tax could have unintended consequences.
story: California voters next month will decide on whether to tax billionaire wealth, a proposal designed to generate billions of dollars to shore up the state's healthcare system. But Stanford economists are now cautioning that the tax could backfire, leaving the state with less in tax revenue than before.

Seven billionaires have already publicly moved out of California, removing about $540 billion, or 30%, of the state's total billionaire wealth from potential taxation, according to Stanford University economists Benjamin Jaros and Joshua Rauh in a new working paper published by the National Bureau of Economic Research. The billionaires who have left the state include venture capitalist Peter Thiel and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin.

Because additional billionaires have likely quietly moved since the tax proposal was announced, the measure may ultimately generate only about $30 billion, far less than the $100 billion estimated by its proponents, the economists said. If enacted, the tax would apply a one-time 5% state tax on billionaire wealth.
To be sure, $30 billion is still a sizable amount of new tax revenue. But future income tax losses from those billionaire departures could more than offset that windfall, the economists calculated.

California could lose roughly $1 billion to $3.5 billion a year in income tax revenue due to its shrinking billionaire population, the paper's authors estimated. If those losses persist permanently, their value in today's dollars would exceed the wealth tax proceeds by about $39 billion, the economists said.

"These findings suggest that the Billionaire Tax Act will not fulfill the primary functions for which it was designed," Jaros and Rauh wrote. "Although the Act was designed to raise revenue, behavioral response prior to voting has eroded most of the projected tax base."

The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), a healthcare worker union that introduced the ballot measure, didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the new research.

Other economists have come to different conclusions about the tax. Economists including Daron Acemoglu of MIT and Joseph Stiglitz of Columbia University, both Nobel Prize winners, have signed their support for the measure, pointing out that California has attracted more venture funding since the wealth tax was announced.

"What will allow California to thrive in the future is not letting a handful of billionaires live tax free: it is adequate public spending on health, education and public infrastructure, key engines of economic growth to which it is only fair to ask the ultra-wealthy to contribute," they wrote in a September letter of support for the tax.

Ahead of the vote on the ballot measure, called Proposition 40, voters in California are apparently divided on the tax. About 46% of likely voters say they favor Proposition 40, while 43% are opposed, according to a new poll from Citrin-Politico.
Dave Regan, the leader of the union that introduced the measure, told CBS News' Jo Ling Kent that he's "pretty confident" the tax will pass.
"There's never been a proposal like this anywhere in the world, so it's a novel idea," Regan said. "We are facing an emergency."

title: Ex-OpenAI worker who allegedly planted bug contacted Saudi royal
summary: The wife and infant son of the ex-OpenAI engineer left the U.S. for Saudi Arabia in October with business-class tickets purchased by a Saudi military official, prosecutors allege.
story: A former OpenAI engineer who allegedly installed a sophisticated listening device in an executive conference room was in close contact with a member of the Saudi royal family and was planning to leave the U.S. for Riyadh when authorities arrested him, federal prosecutors said Sunday in a court memorandum.

Abdulrahman Alfozan is accused of tapping artificial intelligence tools to help him develop encrypted recording devices and identify meeting rooms used by OpenAI executives, government officials and business partners.
The Saudi national earned an annual paycheck of $385,000 at OpenAI and received a $2.2 million equity grant when he first joined the company in July 2025.

In an 11-page filing, prosecutors wrote that investigators recovered evidence suggesting Alfozan may have planned to place even more devices inside OpenAI offices. Prosecutors also revealed that the suspect engaged in WhatsApp messages with an unidentified Saudi royal who repeatedly encouraged him to return to the kingdom and join a Saudi AI initiative.

The filing also shows photographs of other potential surveillance locations, internal searches concerning meetings between OpenAI and Saudi government officials, and notes suggesting he planned to take back the devices before leaving the company.

Investigators allege that on Sept. 28 Alfozan installed a "surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days."
Prosecutors allege that he "modified the device to prevent data transfer between it and the television into which it was inserted" and "had also encrypted the content stored on the device's microSD."

In the days before the device was installed, investigators claim that Alfozan used an AI chatbot account belonging to his wife to research how to customize the recording device, including how to: "build a continuous audio recorder," "captur[e] microphone audio and save compressed WAV recordings to an SD card," "improve audio and live listening," "develop … speech-triggered recording," "add browser access and controls" including "live listening," and "encrypt the SD card" and "decrypt and recover recordings from the removed card."

Meetings in that executive conference room, according to prosecutors, "frequently involve discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships."

According to the filing, investigators determined that in the "days surrounding the time period that the device was installed, OpenAI executives met with government officials in that very room," alleging the "defendant's conduct could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."
Prosecutors also disclosed that his cellphone contained photographs of at least one other concealed recorder as well as electronic equipment in other OpenAI meeting rooms.
Prosecutors allege that throughout 2025 and 2026, Alfozan "was in frequent communication via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family, including as recently as October 5, 2026."
The Saudi royal, according to prosecutors, told Alfozan that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and enticed him to join it.
"Saudi needs you more than [sic] the US!" the member wrote, part of a campaign to recruit the defendant. Alfozan agreed but said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested.
The suspect was arrested Oct. 9, three days before he was scheduled to depart San Francisco with his wife and infant son on a one-way flight to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Instead, his wife and 3-month-old son left the country the following day on business-class tickets purchased by a Saudi military official, prosecutors allege. Before his arrest, the defendant had been scheduled to take two months of parental leave beginning in October 2026.

Alfozan, who has no prior criminal record, according to the filing, became a U.S. permanent resident in September 2020 and applied for citizenship thereafter. OpenAI fired him after his arrest. A detention hearing was scheduled for Monday, before U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex Tse.

The government has argued that Alfozan should be detained pending his trial, alleging that his wealth, connections and apparent assistance from Saudi government officials put him at risk of fleeing the country.

title: New evidence points to alleged O.J. Simpson accomplice in 1994 murders
summary: A new investigation offers a different account of what might have happened the night O.J. Simpson's ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman were stabbed to death.
story: More than three decades after the O.J. Simpson murder trial, a new investigation offers a different account of what might have happened the night his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman were stabbed to death in 1994.

After O.J. Simpson was acquitted in the deaths in 1995, Los Angeles prosecutors received new information from Simpson's friend about the murder weapon's disposal, according to newly unsealed court documents obtained by the New York Times.
"You would think that there could not possibly be anything new, and now, for the public, there certainly is," said legal analyst Rikki Klieman, who covered the case at the time for Court TV.

According to court records, a letter from an assistant U.S. attorney to a federal judge requested a lenient sentence for Joey Ippolito on a prison escape charge because the convicted drug trafficker had become a federal informant.

The letter described Ippolito as a valuable source who "had become privy to many facts relevant to the [O.J. Simpson] case," including Simpson's "disposal of the murder weapon," which was never found.
Ippolito allegedly met Simpson through Al Cowlings, the man behind the wheel during Simpson's infamous Bronco chase.

Ippolito died in 2006, but his brother, Sam, told the Times that Joey left the night of the killings to help a friend, only to return with what appeared to be blood on his hands and a bag containing a heavy object. He then allegedly told Sam to dispose of it while he showered. Sam said he tossed the bag in a dumpster at a nearby construction site.

"What gets complicated here is that you're not only dealing with the original informant, Joey Ippolito, but you're dealing now with the embellishment by his brother, and there's no real reason to trust the word of the brother," Klieman said.

Others close to the case are also skeptical. Former prosecutor Marcia Clark told the Times she had no knowledge of Ippolito and because of that he must have "had no credible or relevant evidence to provide."

The Times, meanwhile, reports that Ippolito's brother Sam insisted he was 100% certain his brother was at the crime scene. But after the paper turned down his request for compensation for providing them this story, he attempted to retract those statements.
Still, the account bears striking similarities to Simpson's book "If I Did It," in which he gave a "hypothetical" account of an accomplice who helps him dispose of the weapon.
"The authorities, that is, police and the current district attorney of Los Angeles County, cannot simply discount it. They have got to look at it, or continue to look at it," Klieman said.
Simpson was found liable for the murders in a civil trial in 1997 and ordered to pay $33.5 million to Brown and Goldman's family. Goldman's family declined to comment on the Times investigation.

In a statement to CBS News, the executor of Simpson's estate, Malcolm LaVergne, said the only three people whose firsthand accounts of that night matter the most are now deceased, referring to Brown, Goldman and Simpson, who died in 2024.

"None of those three people can speak for themselves today," LaVergne said. "And I certainly cannot speak for them about what happened that night. At some point, I believe we must recognize that the continued production of theories, allegations, and sensational accounts may do little to bring meaningful resolution to those who have already suffered so much."

title: Trump signs executive order on women's health
summary: "Who the hell wouldn't have a women's health division?" President Trump said Monday.
story: Washington — President Trump on Monday signed an executive order creating a women's health division within the National Institutes of Health and a White House Women's Health Task Force.
First lady Melania Trump joined him for a signing ceremony in the Rose Garden and said the executive order will make progress on five objectives:

Directing research funding to find cures that disproportionately affect women.Using artificial intelligence to speed up medical discoveries.Accelerating new therapeutics for women.Delivering medical breakthroughs for women at an affordable price.Making conversations about women's health less taboo.
Directing research funding to find cures that disproportionately affect women.
Using artificial intelligence to speed up medical discoveries.
Accelerating new therapeutics for women.
Delivering medical breakthroughs for women at an affordable price.
Making conversations about women's health less taboo.

"This is a transformative moment for women in America," the first lady said. "Beginning today, we will change the reality of women's health. Previous generations fought for women's rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest."

Mr. Trump credited the first lady with conceiving the idea for a women's health division within NIH. The first lady added her signature to the executive order after the president did, although her signature has no legal weight.
"Think of it, a women's health division," Mr. Trump said. "Who the hell wouldn't have a women's health division? Melania said, 'They don't have it.'"

The president said Americans will soon hear about "incredible things that we're doing" to get women the care they need, although he didn't offer specifics. It's not yet clear how much funding will be directed toward research funding, accelerating therapeutics, or making medical breakthroughs more affordable for women.

The women's health announcement comes on the heels of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles' battle with breast cancer. She continued in the job after her March diagnosis, and in September announced she is cancer-free.
Mr. Trump gave a shout-out to Wiles during Monday's announcement, calling her "fantastic."

"I don't know if Susie wants this brought up, but as many of you know, Susie recently won her battle against a very tough opponent, breast cancer," the president said. "It wasn't easy. We went through it, we got her through it, and she got through it, and she's tough. But she's a tremendous fighter and much like our first lady, she cares deeply about improving the health of American women."

White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the White House task force "will work to close critical research gaps and strengthen care for women across all stages of life, targeting some of the most widespread health conditions affecting them."

title: Fighter jets intercept plane violating airspace over Cincinnati
summary: Military fighter jets intercepted a plane flying through restricted airspace over Cincinnati, Ohio, while President Trump was speaking at a nearby rally in Kentucky.
story: Fighter jets intercepted a plane flying through restricted airspace over Cincinnati, Ohio, on Saturday, U.S. military officials said.

The incident took place as President Trump spoke at a rally at the Northern Kentucky University campus, just south of Cincinnati. Although the military didn't explicitly say why a temporary flight restriction had been effected in the area, the Federal Aviation Administration issues them around high-profile events, especially those attended by politicians.

F-16 fighter aircraft intercepted what was described as a general aviation plane violating airspace restrictions over Cincinnati at around 3 p.m. CT on Saturday, according to the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD.

The command said military jets safely escorted the plane from the area. It also noted that pilots who violate temporary flight restrictions may "be met by federal authorities upon landing and subject to interview or further enforcement action."

In light of the interception over Cincinnati, Air Force officials reminded pilots on Sunday to be aware of airspace restrictions while planning a flight and before taking off. The FAA shares information about airspace limitations with pilots through Notices to Airmen, or NOTAMs, which are released and updated regularly.

It isn't uncommon for military jets to intercept civilian planes transiting areas under temporary restrictions. At the end of September, F-16s were scrambled to intercept a group of 15 planes that violated restrictions put in place over the Chicago area, while Mr. Trump was visiting, CBS Chicago reported.

In August, fighter jets also intercepted a civilian plane that had entered restricted air over Geneva, Ohio, where Mr. Trump was attending the 2026 Patriot Games, a teen athletic tournament that was heavily backed by the White House and the president's supporters, according to NORAD. Jets were also scrambled around that same time over Bedminster, New Jersey, where one of Mr. Trump's golf courses is located, the military command said.
Earlier, in July, a similar interception incident took place over East Rutherford, New Jersey, when NORAD said planes violated flight restrictions in place for the World Cup final.
Military officials said planes were safely escorted from restricted areas in each of those instances.

title: Theranos whistleblower calls Holmes "almost unrecognizable" in film
summary: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz said he "was pretty shocked" by the version of Elizabeth Holmes he saw onscreen in the new documentary "You Can See Everything."
story: Tyler Shultz, a former Theranos employee and one of the whistleblowers credited with exposing Elizabeth Holmes' now-infamous biotech company as a fraud, said he "was pretty shocked" by the version of Holmes he saw onscreen in the new documentary "You Can See Everything."

"The Elizabeth that I knew completely commanded a room, even if that room was full of secretaries of state, secretaries of defense, generals, senators. She would own a room," Shultz said Monday on "CBS Mornings." "She had so much confidence, and the woman that I saw onscreen looked, frankly, like a, a broken woman."
"It was almost unrecognizable," he added.

Shultz also said he believes Holmes misled Nathan Fielder, who directed the documentary alongside Lance Oppenheim, when at one point in the film she pulled out what she claimed was Theranos' blood-testing device.

"She brings out the Theranos device, and she lays it across the table and all of its components, so you know you can see everything," said Shultz. "But my problem was: that was not the device that I worked with 12 hours a day. That was not the device that we hid from regulators. That was not the device that failed quality controls. That was not the device that we used to knowingly give patients incorrect medical information, and she completely misled [Fielder] down this completely different rabbit hole."

Holmes never admitted wrongdoing in the wake of the Theranos scandal, a stance on which she held firm in the documentary which brings viewers inside Holmes' San Diego rental property in 2023 just weeks before the start of her 11-year prison sentence. At the time, she was living with her partner, Billy Evans, who is also featured prominently in the documentary, and their two children.

Holmes was convicted in 2022 of multiple counts of defrauding Theranos' investors, who, like the public, were led to believe that the company could conduct thorough clinical analyses on tiny blood samples pricked from a fingertip rather than drawn the traditional way. The technology was billed as revelatory for the field of diagnostics, increasing access to and costs of crucial, even life-saving, testing.

But Theranos turned out to be a sham — the technology couldn't do what it claimed. And Holmes, who had become a symbol of Silicon Valley's visionary potential, became the subject of widespread scrutiny as people wondered how she managed to deceive so many, and why she had gone to such great lengths to try to build a business on a false promise.

"She knows that she did something wrong," Shultz said on Monday. "She knows that she was lying, because she created this whole web of lies that you would not have needed to create if you actually believed the lies."

Shultz was hired in 2013 as an intern at Theranos, where his grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State George Shultz, served as a board member. Tyler left the company the following year and went on serve as an informant for investigations into its dubious practices by The Wall Street Journal and various government regulatory agencies. He later participated in the 2016 HBO documentary "The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley," which covered Theranos' downfall.
"You Can See Everything" premiered on Friday and earned $15 million at the box office in its opening weekend, the second-most profitable opening weekend ever for a documentary.
This story published first on CBS News at 10:50 a.m. on Oct. 19, 2026.

title: Supreme Court turns away appeal from alleged 9/11 mastermind
summary: The Supreme Court rebuffed an effort by alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to revive a plea deal reached with military prosecutors and revoked by the Biden administration.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday rebuffed a bid from accused Sept. 11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices to revive plea agreements that they reached with military prosecutors before being revoked by the Biden administration.

In an unsigned order, the high court turned away the appeals from Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash of a lower court decision that prevented a military judge from enforcing pretrial agreements they reached with military prosecutors in 2024, which were withdrawn by then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.
In rejecting their case, the government's withdrawal of the plea deals remains in place. Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not participate in the court's consideration of the appeal.

Mohammed, Hawsawi and bin 'Atash, were captured in 2003 and charged before a military commission with several crimes for their alleged roles in crafting and perpetrating the Sept. 11 attacks, five of which carry the death penalty. In August, the judge overseeing their cases set a trial date of June 2028, which depends on the parties meeting certain deadlines and milestones on time.

The prosecutions have been mired in lengthy legal delays over whether evidence extracted during their interrogations could be used in court. The defendants were held at secret CIA prisons, where they were subjected to "enhanced interrogation techniques," or torture, before they were moved to Guantanamo Bay in 2006. They were formally charged in 2008.

In 2023, following the appointment of retired Brigadier General Susan Escallier as the Convening Authority for military commissions, military lawyers began discussing plea deals with the defendants. Agreements were subsequently reached in 2024 and approved by Escallier, who oversees the military court at Guantanamo Bay.

Under the terms of the deals, the defendants would plead guilty to all charges arising from their alleged roles in the 9/11 terror attacks and serve life sentences, avoiding the death penalty. But shortly after the agreements were announced, Austin said he was revoking them.

But a military judge ruled in November 2024 that Austin's nullification of the deals was unlawful, rendering the agreements valid and enforceable. A military appeals court then said Austin couldn't rescind the plea deals because the defendants had begun to perform one of the terms.

The Justice Department then asked the D.C. Circuit to step in and find that Austin validly withdrew from the pretrial agreements. The D.C. Circuit sided with the government in a decision last year and ruled that the defense secretary "indisputably" had the authority to withdraw from the plea deals.
"The Secretary acted within the bounds of his legal authority, and we decline to second-guess his judgment," the D.C. Circuit panel found.

title: Expedition to find Amelia Earhart's missing plane comes up empty
summary: The researchers said what they had hoped was the plane was "likely a collection of large trees" that had washed away, leaving a "single Y-shaped segment."
story: A mysterious object discovered near a remote Pacific island is not the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's missing plane, researchers said after an expedition to the site, dealing another setback to efforts to solve one of aviation's greatest mysteries nearly 90 years after the pilot disappeared.

"Evidence gathered at the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro confirmed that the visual anomaly first seen in satellite imagery in 2020 was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit," the researchers said. "By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment," which they said is what they had initially hoped was the plane.

The researchers said the reflective surface of the anomaly, which had led them to believe it could be metal, was the result of a carbonate veneer, noting other items found nearby were "similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand."

On Oct. 14, a 17-member expedition team led by Purdue University's Steve Schultz and the Archaeological Legacy Institute's Richard Pettigrew launched an expedition to investigate a mysterious object that in aerial photos appeared to resemble possible wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E plane.

Severe weather kept the research team aboard their ship for three of the five days allotted for the search, while limited fuel and supplies prevented them from extending the expedition. The search area was so remote, it took the team five days at sea to reach it.

The expedition focused on a lagoon off Nikumaroro, where researchers examined the Taraia Object, an anomaly spotted by a Navy veteran in satellite imagery during the COVID pandemic. Although visible in aerial photos dating back to 1938, the object went unnoticed until 2020. Pettigrew said before reaching it that they believed it could be metal rather than a tree, but further investigation was needed to confirm its identity.

"Amelia Earhart's spirit of courage and curiosity drove every step of the search," Pettigrew said Sunday. "We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we're deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible. Our team remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished."

The team had developed plans to photograph and film the lagoon and Taraia Object before using magnetometers and sonar equipment to survey the area. Researchers then planned to retrieve the object for identification. The Archaeology Channel documented the expedition through short video updates on its Heritage Broadcasting Service streaming platform.
The research team previously said in a news release that there was "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.

Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared on July 2, 1937, roughly 22,000 miles into their trip. Earhart was attempting to become the first female pilot to circle the world, and the first pilot to do so around the equator, Earth's widest point.
Recently, President Trump ordered the declassification of records related to Earhart.

Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island lies about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were headed when they disappeared during their attempted flight around the world.

Pettigrew believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumaroro and survived there for some time. He points to relics dating to the 1930s and to human remains discovered on the island, which were later lost as possible evidence. However, several competing theories about the aviator's disappearance have emerged over the decades, many of which lack conclusive evidence.

Researchers have spent decades searching for Earhart's plane, hoping its discovery could shed light on her disappearance. In 2024, an expedition team captured a sonar image of what appeared to be an aircraft on the ocean floor, but the object was later identified as a rock formation.
