MEDICAL IDENTITY THEFT FOLLOWS YOU INTO THE DOCTOR'S OFFICE
Oracle Health's legacy Cerner systems were targeted in a cyberattack that reportedly exposed the personal and medical information of nearly 20 million patients. (iStock)
Oracle Health breach reportedly affects nearly 20 million people

The Oracle Health data breach appears to be much larger than earlier patient notifications suggested. According to figures reported in filings with the Texas Attorney General, the personal and medical information of approximately 19.9 million people was compromised in a cyberattack involving legacy Cerner systems. The Texas Attorney General's official data breach portal published Cerner's entry on October 2, 2026. It lists 2,992,244 affected Texas residents. The nationwide figure reported in connection with the filing is 19,929,149 people.

Oracle has not separately confirmed the nationwide total in a public statement. Still, the reported scale would place this incident among the largest healthcare data breaches in U.S. history. The attack involved older systems belonging to Cerner, an electronic health records company Oracle acquired in June 2022 for approximately $28.3 billion. The business now operates as Oracle Health. Cerner's technology helps hospitals and healthcare providers manage patient information. As a result, unauthorized access to those systems can expose records belonging to patients across multiple healthcare organizations.
How hackers broke into Oracle Health's older systems

The trouble began in early 2025. Oracle started notifying affected healthcare customers in March after discovering unauthorized access involving older Cerner systems. According to Oracle's customer communications, the company became aware of the incident around February 20, 2025. Investigators found evidence suggesting that an attacker used stolen customer credentials to access a legacy server sometime after January 22. The attacker then copied information to a remote server.

The server had not yet been migrated to Oracle Cloud. However, investigators have not publicly established that the server's age caused the breach. The precise way the attacker obtained the stolen credentials also remains unclear. This raises an uncomfortable question. How much sensitive patient information remains on older healthcare systems, even after a major technology company takes ownership?
Hackers reportedly demanded millions to keep medical records private

The attacker allegedly tried to turn the stolen information into a multimillion-dollar payday. According to earlier BleepingComputer reporting, an individual using the name "Andrew" contacted affected hospitals and demanded cryptocurrency payments. The attacker reportedly threatened to leak or sell stolen patient information unless the victims paid.

The individual also allegedly created public websites about the breach to increase pressure on healthcare organizations. At the time, researchers had not established a connection between the attacker and a known ransomware or extortion group. For hospitals, that creates a difficult situation. Even if an organization pays, there is no guarantee the criminal will delete the stolen records or refrain from selling copies. Meanwhile, patients may have no idea their information is being used as leverage.
What personal and medical information was stolen?
A sample breach notification filed with California regulators provides a closer look at the information potentially exposed.
Depending on the patient, the compromised records may have included:
Full names and Social Security numbersMedical record numbersDoctors and diagnosesPrescription medicationsMedical test resultsMedical imagesTreatment and care information
Full names and Social Security numbers
Medical record numbers
Doctors and diagnoses
Prescription medications
Medical test results
Medical images
Treatment and care information

The exact information exposed can vary from person to person. However, the combination of personal identifiers and medical details makes this incident particularly troubling. Unlike a stolen credit card, you cannot simply cancel your medical history and request a replacement. Your diagnoses, treatment records and past prescriptions can remain sensitive for years.

Criminals could potentially use that information to create convincing medical scams, impersonate patients or commit identity theft. They may also combine medical details with other stolen information to make fraudulent calls and emails appear more credible.
FAKE PATIENT PORTAL SCAM CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN AND INFECT YOUR PC

Stolen patient records may include Social Security numbers, medical diagnoses, prescription information and test results, raising concerns about identity theft and medical fraud. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Millions of patients affected across multiple states

State breach filings offer a clearer view of the attack's scale. The Texas attorney general's October 2, 2026, filing lists 2,992,244 affected residents in Texas alone. Other state notifications show how widely the incident spread. Oregon reported 1,978,661 affected residents, while South Carolina identified 283,903. Washington also reported 69,238 people whose information was compromised.

These figures represent portions of the overall incident and should not be added to the nationwide total of nearly 20 million. Meanwhile, filings with Oregon regulators identify January 22 through April 1, 2025, as the reported breach period, with February 20 listed as the discovery date. These disclosures show how complicated healthcare breach reporting can become. Patients in different states may receive notifications at different times, while the full impact can take months or longer to emerge.
How the Oracle Health breach compares with other healthcare attacks

Unfortunately, healthcare organizations have become attractive targets for cybercriminals. Medical records contain information that can support identity theft and fraud long after an initial attack. One of the biggest examples came in 2024, when attackers targeted Change Healthcare, a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group. That breach ultimately affected approximately 192.7 million people.

The Oracle Health incident appears smaller by comparison. Still, a reported 20 million affected individuals represents an enormous amount of sensitive information. The incident also raises questions about how healthcare organizations protect records stored on older systems. Those systems can remain essential to daily operations, even as companies upgrade their technology. In this case, investigators identified stolen credentials as the reported access method, rather than a publicly confirmed vulnerability in the legacy server. We reached out to Oracle Health for comment, but did not hear back before our deadline.
How to protect yourself after the Oracle Health data breach

You may have never heard of Cerner, even if your hospital uses its technology. That makes it harder to know whether your records were involved. However, there are practical steps you can take now to reduce the risk of identity theft and medical fraud.

Check your mail for notices from Cerner, Oracle Health or a healthcare provider you have visited. The notification should explain what information may have been exposed and whether any protective services are available. You can also contact your hospital's privacy office directly. Avoid clicking links in unexpected messages claiming you need to verify your medical records.

A credit freeze can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts using your identity. You can request one for free through Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You'll need to contact all three bureaus separately. A freeze will not prevent every form of identity theft, but it can block an important route criminals use.

Review your health insurance explanation of benefits statements for appointments, treatments or prescriptions you do not recognize. Also, look for unfamiliar providers or incorrect information in your medical records. Contact your insurer and healthcare provider if something looks suspicious. Medical identity theft can lead to fraudulent bills and inaccurate patient records, so catching problems early is important.

A healthcare breach can create opportunities for phishing emails and malicious attachments. Strong antivirus software can help detect malware, suspicious downloads and some dangerous links before they cause harm. Keep your devices updated and avoid downloading files from unexpected healthcare messages. Antivirus protection cannot undo the Oracle Health breach, but it can help defend against attacks that follow it. THE SCAMMER AT YOUR DOCTOR'S OFFICE MAY ALREADY KNOW WHO YOU ARE
Oracle acquired Cerner in 2022 for approximately $28.3 billion, inheriting electronic health record systems used by hospitals and healthcare providers nationwide. (iStock)

Someone who knows your doctor's name or recent treatment details may sound legitimate over the phone. Criminals could use stolen information to impersonate healthcare workers, demand payments or ask you to confirm your Social Security number. Hang up and call the provider using a number from its official website or your insurance card. Never assume a caller is legitimate simply because they know something about your medical history.

Use unique passwords for healthcare portals and enable two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever available. A password manager can help you create and store strong passwords without reusing them. If you suspect your account credentials were compromised, change the affected password immediately. Remember, changing a password will not retrieve stolen medical records, but it can help protect your accounts from additional unauthorized access.

If your Social Security number was exposed, an identity theft protection service may help you monitor for suspicious activity involving your personal information. Some services also offer alerts and assistance with recovery. Review any free monitoring offered through your breach notification before purchasing a separate plan. Keep in mind that monitoring services cannot guarantee prevention of identity theft or detect every form of medical fraud. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most about the Oracle Health breach is how little control patients have over where their medical information ends up. You can be extremely careful with your passwords and avoid suspicious links, yet your most sensitive records may still sit on a server you never knew existed. The fact that this attack involved a legacy server makes the situation even more frustrating. Investigators have identified stolen credentials as the reported access method, but we still don't know exactly how those credentials were compromised. When a company acquires a healthcare technology provider, protecting the information already stored in those systems should be a priority. Patients deserve to know that their records remain secure throughout technology upgrades. And consider the timing. The attack dates back to early 2025, yet its potential scale is becoming clearer in October 2026. That's a long time for people to remain uncertain about what happened to their information. Healthcare organizations need to do a better job protecting patient records and communicating clearly when something goes wrong.

title: Tesla Roadster flies, flips and hits 60 mph in a flash
summary: The new Tesla Roadster drove upside down and launched into the air at SpaceX's Texas facility, but a 2028 production target remains unconfirmed.
story: Chasing Horsepower founder Mike Caudill joins ‘America Reports’ to analyze the engineering behind Tesla’s new Roadster prototype. Caudill highlights its rocket-powered thrusters and ability to accelerate from zero to 60 mph in less than one second.

I've watched plenty of car unveilings over the years, but Tesla's latest Roadster demonstration had me doing a double take. A sleek white sports car climbed a towering curved ramp until it was completely upside down. Then it launched into the air, flipped over and landed safely back on the pavement. And that was only part of the show. Tesla also demonstrated acceleration from zero to 60 mph in a claimed 0.81 seconds. After nearly nine years of waiting, Elon Musk finally showed the world what his redesigned Roadster can do. Now comes the bigger question. Will Tesla actually deliver it?

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. No technical experience is needed.

FLYING SPORTS CAR HIDES ITS WINGS AS PRODUCTION GETS CLOSER
Tesla's redesigned Roadster features a sleek, low-profile design with dramatic upward-opening doors. (Tesla)
Tesla Roadster takes flight in dramatic Texas unveiling

On Oct. 15, 2026, Tesla unveiled its redesigned Roadster at SpaceX's rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas. The event brought together engineers from both companies to demonstrate technology more commonly associated with spacecraft. During the demonstration, a Roadster prototype accelerated up a massive curved ramp. A powerful suction system helped keep the vehicle attached as it climbed upside down. Once it reached the top, compressed-gas thrusters propelled it into the air. The vehicle then rotated in midair and landed back on its wheels.

Tesla followed that stunt with another impressive maneuver. The Roadster lifted off the ground and flew over a lineup of Tesla vehicles, including a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y and Model 3. Nobody was inside the Roadster during these high-risk demonstrations. Musk said Tesla used automated controls to avoid putting anyone in danger. Tesla shared footage of the event on its official X account. You can also watch the full Tesla Roadster unveiling on YouTube.
How the Tesla Roadster uses SpaceX technology to fly

Here's where the engineering gets especially interesting. Tesla worked with SpaceX to develop a system that uses highly compressed gas to generate thrust. Unlike conventional rocket engines, these cold-gas thrusters don't burn fuel. Instead, they release pressurized gas through nozzles to push the vehicle in a particular direction. The Roadster also uses four powerful electric fans positioned near the rear of the car. They pull air from underneath the vehicle to create suction. That increases the force pressing the tires against the surface, helping the car maintain grip even while upside down. Tesla also uses a ground-sealing system to help maintain suction underneath the vehicle.

Meanwhile, the thrusters handle a very different job. Four rear-mounted nozzles provide extra forward acceleration. The most advanced Rocket configuration adds six more thrusters positioned around the vehicle to help control movement in the air. According to Tesla engineering executive Lars Moravy, the standard thruster setup uses a 200-liter high-pressure storage vessel behind the seats. The Rocket configuration adds another 400 liters of storage capacity, bringing the total to approximately 600 liters. That additional equipment takes up the passenger seat area.

There's also a practical limitation that gets lost in the excitement. According to Tesla engineering executive Lars Moravy, refilling the Rocket prototype's entire 600-liter high-pressure gas storage system currently takes approximately six to seven hours. Tesla hopes to cut that time significantly. So while the demonstration was extraordinary, the Roadster's brief airborne maneuvers are a long way from sustained flight like an airplane. Inside, Tesla has taken a different approach to the driving experience. The Roadster features a steer-by-wire yoke that electronically transmits steering inputs. Tesla also uses lightweight materials, including magnesium and carbon fiber, along with a fixed seat base to reduce weight. Meanwhile, Track Mode lowers the suspension so drivers can adjust the car for more aggressive handling.
The Tesla Roadster climbs a towering curved ramp during a demonstration of its extreme driving capabilities. (Tesla)
How fast is the new Tesla Roadster?

Tesla has made some extraordinary performance claims about the Roadster, and its latest unveiling added another. During the event, Tesla showed a thruster-assisted acceleration run that it said took the prototype from zero to 60 mph in approximately 0.81 seconds. That's remarkably quick, even compared with some of the fastest electric supercars.

However, the result came from Tesla's own demonstration. Independent testing has yet to verify that acceleration figure on a production vehicle. Tesla also claims the Roadster's more powerful configurations can exceed 230 mph. Musk went even further during the unveiling, suggesting engineers eventually want to reach half the speed of sound. That would be roughly 380 mph, depending on atmospheric conditions. For now, that more ambitious target remains an aspiration rather than a demonstrated capability. Tesla also projects more than 300 miles of driving range on a charge. That's a substantial reduction from the approximately 620 miles promised when the second-generation Roadster was first introduced in 2017. At the time, Tesla also envisioned a four-seat sports car.
FLYING TAXIS ARE TAKING OFF IN TEXAS. IS YOUR CITY NEXT?
Tesla plans three versions of the new Roadster

Here's something worth knowing before getting too excited about the flying demonstration. Tesla offers a road-focused Performance configuration, along with two more extreme options called Thrust and Rocket. Each adds capabilities that take the Roadster further beyond a conventional electric sports car.

The Performance version is designed for conventional road driving. It seats two people and features active aerodynamics along with the advanced suction system. Tesla claims it can accelerate from zero to 60 mph in under 1.6 seconds without the rocket-style thrusters.

The Thrust configuration takes acceleration considerably further. It adds four rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters to the two-seat design. Tesla claims this version can reach 60 mph in under 0.9 seconds. The company describes it as race-ready and plans a limited release.
Cold-gas thrusters propel the Tesla Roadster into the air during a controlled demonstration of its flying capabilities. (Tesla)

The Rocket version is the one that really pushes the technology. It uses 10 thrusters to provide forward acceleration, upward movement and airborne maneuvering. Tesla claims this configuration could reach 60 mph in under 0.59 seconds. However, all that additional equipment requires a compromise. The Rocket version seats only one person and will be available by invitation. Tesla also explicitly warns that it has not received approval for public road use.

Musk acknowledged that safety wasn't necessarily the top priority when developing the Roadster's most extreme capabilities. He also expressed uncertainty about where those features would be legal to use. For now, Tesla has only demonstrated the airborne maneuvers under controlled conditions. Keep in mind that these acceleration figures are Tesla's projected specifications. They have yet to be independently confirmed on production vehicles.
How much will the Tesla Roadster cost?

This is where potential buyers should pay close attention. When Tesla originally announced the second-generation Roadster in 2017, it discussed a starting price of approximately $200,000. However, Tesla did not announce a new final purchase price at its October 2026 unveiling. Instead, the company reopened reservations with substantial upfront payments. For the Performance version, Tesla requires an initial $5,000 payment followed by another $45,000 within 10 days. That brings the total reservation payment to $50,000.

The limited-release Thrust version requires the same initial $5,000 payment. However, buyers must then provide another $245,000 within 10 days. That's a total reservation payment of $250,000, even though the vehicle's final purchase price remains unknown. Tesla has not disclosed pricing for the invitation-only Rocket configuration.

According to Tesla's official Roadster Reservation Agreement, a reservation secures an approximate place in line rather than a completed vehicle order. Tesla says customers can cancel their reservations and receive a full refund until they complete their vehicle configuration after Tesla invites them to do so. However, the money won't be held separately in escrow or earn interest.

There's another important detail. Tesla explicitly states that the Roadster remains under development and that it cannot guarantee when a vehicle will be delivered, or whether it will be delivered at all. And Tesla has already missed its original deadline by several years. The company initially expected deliveries to begin in 2020. Musk now says production should begin in 2028, although that remains a target rather than a guaranteed date.
Why Tesla calls the Roadster one of its last human-driven cars

Here's something else that caught my attention. Musk suggested the Roadster could be among Tesla's last cars designed for human drivers. Think about that for a moment. Tesla is spending billions developing cars that drive themselves, yet its most exciting new vehicle is designed for people who actually love being behind the wheel. I find that pretty ironic, especially coming from the man who wants to make autonomous driving the norm.

Just look at Tesla's Cybercab. It doesn't even have a steering wheel or traditional driving controls. We've already seen how Tesla's Cybercab is carrying riders in Austin, although questions about safety and operating restrictions remain. Meanwhile, the Roadster is all about the thrill of driving. There's something to be said for feeling the car respond when you hit the accelerator or take a sharp turn. Of course, Musk hasn't confirmed that Tesla will eliminate manual driving from its other vehicles. But if that's where the company is headed, I wonder how many drivers will be willing to give up the steering wheel.
JCB HYDROMAX SHATTERS A WORLD RECORD WITH ‘EXTRAORDINARY’ SPEEDS TOPPING 400 MPH IN HYDROGEN-POWERED CAR
The Roadster flies above a lineup of Tesla vehicles, showcasing technology developed in collaboration with SpaceX. (Tesla)
What this means to you

You probably aren't planning to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on a Tesla Roadster. Still, this project raises some interesting questions about where automotive technology could be headed. For starters, the Roadster's advanced suction system demonstrates how electric fans can dramatically increase traction. Similar technology already exists in specialized high-performance vehicles. Further development could eventually influence other types of performance cars.

However, the cold-gas thrusters introduce challenges that may limit their usefulness outside controlled environments. The hardware occupies valuable space, while the pressurized gas supply requires replenishment after use. There's also the gap between demonstrating a prototype and delivering a finished vehicle. Tesla still needs to prove the Roadster can be manufactured reliably and meet applicable regulations.

For anyone considering a reservation, I would take a close look at Tesla's current Roadster information and reservation terms before paying. The company's specifications are still subject to change, and the Roadster shown at the unveiling remains a prototype.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to give Tesla credit for getting my attention with this one. Watching a sports car drive upside down and then launch itself into the air was pretty incredible. And knowing that engineers from Tesla and SpaceX worked together to pull it off makes the technology even more interesting. But here's what I'm watching. Tesla first showed us the next-generation Roadster back in 2017, and customers are still waiting. Now we're hearing 2028. I'd love to see this car actually make it into production because there's something refreshing about an electric sports car designed for people who still love to drive. But asking customers to put down as much as $250,000 without a final price or guaranteed delivery date is a lot to swallow. As much as I'd love to take one for a spin, I think I'll leave those midair flips to the engineers until Tesla can prove this technology belongs outside a controlled demonstration.

title: Here's some tips on how to organize photos with keywords on your phone
summary: Apple's iOS 27 lets you add keywords to iPhone photos, while Samsung Gallery tags and Google Photos search offer similar organization tools.
story: ‘The Five’ debates Instagram's feature that lets users blur their partners' faces in photos.

Your phone probably holds thousands of pictures. Some are important family memories, while others are screenshots you saved because you thought you might need them later. Then comes the frustrating part. You remember taking a particular photo, but finding it feels like searching for a needle in a digital haystack.

Apple's iOS 27 offers a way to make that search easier by letting you add keywords to individual photos. Instead of scrolling through months of pictures, you can search for a word you've assigned to a photo and pull it up again.
Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel users have similar ways to organize their pictures, although the tools work differently. Here's how to take advantage of them and spend less time hunting for photos.

YOUR PHONE CAN FIX BADLY FRAMED PHOTOS AFTER YOU TAKE THEM
Samsung Galaxy users can organize photos with custom tags in the Gallery app, while Google Pixel users can search images using Google Photos. (Photographer: SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How to add keywords to photos on iPhone

Apple's Photos app can already recognize people, pets, places and objects. However, automatic searches don't always understand why a particular photo is important to you. That's where manually assigned keywords can help.

For example, you might photograph a parking spot at an airport or save a picture of a particular appliance model number. Adding a keyword you will remember later can make the photo much easier to find.
These instructions are based on an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 27.

Open the Photos app on your iPhone.Find and open the photo you want to organize.Tap the Info (ⓘ) icon or swipe up on the photo.Tap Add Keywords.Enter the keyword or keywords you want to associate with the picture.Tap the checkmark icon to save your changes.If you want to edit or add more keywords later, you can tap Edit .
Open the Photos app on your iPhone.
Find and open the photo you want to organize.
Tap the Info (ⓘ) icon or swipe up on the photo.
Tap Add Keywords.
Enter the keyword or keywords you want to associate with the picture.
Tap the checkmark icon to save your changes.
If you want to edit or add more keywords later, you can tap Edit .

Choose words that make sense to you. For example, a picture of your car's license plate might get a keyword such as "license plate." You could also tag pictures from a family vacation with a memorable trip name.
Once you've added keywords, searching for those pictures takes only a few seconds.

Open the Photos app.Tap the Search icon, which looks like a magnifying glass.Type one of the keywords you previously added.Look for a suggested search result with the Aa symbol.Tap that result to see photos and videos associated with the keyword.
Open the Photos app.
Tap the Search icon, which looks like a magnifying glass.
Type one of the keywords you previously added.
Look for a suggested search result with the Aa symbol.
Tap that result to see photos and videos associated with the keyword.

You can also manage your keywords by opening Photos > Collections > your profile icon > Manage Keywords. From there, you can rename keywords, delete them or add frequently used keywords to your favorites.

Pro tip: Start with photos you actually struggle to find. Important documents, appliance labels and travel information are useful candidates. There's no need to spend an entire weekend tagging your photo library.
How to organize photos on Samsung Galaxy

Samsung Galaxy phones also let you add tags to pictures using the built-in Gallery app. That means you can assign your own keywords and search for them later, much like you can on an iPhone. Depending on your Galaxy model and Gallery version, the exact location of the tagging controls may vary. However, Samsung supports manual photo tagging on compatible devices.
Here's how to tag a picture using Samsung Gallery.

Once you've tagged a photo, you can use the Gallery's search feature to find it again.

For example, you could tag pictures of your home appliances with their model names. Later, when you need a serial number or replacement part, you can search for the tag instead of scrolling through your entire camera roll.
Albums offer another way to keep related pictures together, especially when you want to organize several photos from the same event or project.

For example, you could create an album for home repairs and keep pictures of paint colors, appliance labels and receipts in one place.
Pro tip: If you regularly photograph product labels or serial numbers, keep them together in an album called "Home information." You'll appreciate having those pictures handy when something breaks.
HOW TO SAVE A VIDEO FRAME AS A PHOTO ON YOUR PHONE
Google Photos can automatically recognize objects, places and documents, helping Pixel users find pictures without manually tagging each image. (Photo by Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
How to organize photos on Google Pixel

Google Pixel phones take a different approach. Instead of relying on manually assigned keywords, Google Photos uses automatic recognition to help you find pictures based on what's in them. For example, you can search for "dog," "beach" or "receipt" and Google Photos may find relevant pictures without requiring you to tag them first. You can also create albums to organize pictures you want to keep together.
Google Photos can recognize many objects, places and other details in your pictures. Here's how to use its built-in search feature.
Open the Google Photos app.Tap Search at the bottom of the screen.Enter a word describing what you're looking for , such as receipt , dog or beach .Browse the matching pictures.

Google Photos can often identify objects and locations without requiring you to manually label every picture. However, results depend on what the app can recognize, so you may need to try a different search term if your first attempt doesn't find the right photo.
If you prefer organizing pictures yourself, albums offer a straightforward way to group related photos.

You can create albums for vacations, family events or important household information. That way, pictures you frequently need are grouped together instead of scattered throughout your photo library.

Google Photos also offers a useful feature for organizing certain documents automatically. On supported versions, backed-up pictures of receipts and other paperwork may appear in a dedicated Documents collection.
To check, open Google Photos > Collections > Documents. If Google Photos recognizes documents in your backed-up pictures, you may find them organized into categories.
This can be particularly helpful when you're trying to locate a receipt or another document you photographed months ago.
Pro tip: Try searching Google Photos before creating dozens of albums. You may discover that it already recognizes much of what you're looking for.
Smart ways to organize photos without wasting hours
You don't need a complicated system to keep your pictures under control. In fact, a few consistent habits can make a bigger difference than spending hours organizing every image you've ever taken.
Start with photos you know you'll need again. Travel confirmations and warranty information are good candidates. Then choose simple names that you'll remember when searching.

Avoid overly specific labels that might be difficult to recall months later. For example, "kitchen repair" will probably be easier to remember than the exact date you photographed a broken dishwasher.

Also, remember that photo organization doesn't replace a backup. Important pictures should be protected through a trusted cloud backup service or another reliable backup method. And if you're photographing sensitive information, think carefully about whether you want those pictures stored in a cloud account.
STOP LOSING PHOTO QUALITY WHEN YOU SHARE PICTURES
Apple's iOS 27 lets iPhone users add keywords to photos, making it easier to find important pictures without scrolling through their camera rolls. (Photo by Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I've lost count of how many times I've taken a photo specifically so I wouldn't forget something, only to spend several minutes trying to find it later. A simple keyword or well-named album can solve a surprisingly annoying problem. What I like about Apple's approach is the ability to assign a word that means something to you. Your phone might recognize a picture of a car, but it doesn't necessarily know that you took it because you needed to remember where you parked. Samsung Galaxy users can take advantage of manual tags, too, while Google Pixel owners have powerful automatic search tools built into Google Photos. My advice is to start small. Organize the pictures you'll actually need again, and let your phone's built-in search handle the rest.

title: Hackers hide dangerous fake AI downloads behind Google ads
summary: A fake Claude AI download scam uses Google ads, and Bing redirects to trick Mac users into pasting a hidden malicious command in their Terminal.
story: 'America Reports' co-anchors John Roberts and Sandra Smith discuss President Donald Trump hosting top tech leaders to discuss the future of artificial intelligence.
You search Google for Claude, the popular AI assistant, and spot a sponsored result. The link points to Bing, Microsoft's search engine. Nothing immediately screams scam.
However, that click could send you through several websites before landing on a convincing fake Claude download page designed to trick you into running a dangerous command on your Mac.

Security researchers at Push Security uncovered a clever attack that uses legitimate search engine links to hide a malicious installer. The technique, which researchers jokingly call "Adception," takes advantage of how Google ads and Bing redirects work.
Even more concerning, the fake installer shows one command on the screen while secretly copying another. Here's how the scam works and what you should know before downloading AI software.
ANTI-SCAM SETTINGS ON IPHONE, PIXEL AND GALAXY YOU SHOULD CHECK

Cybersecurity researchers uncovered a fake Claude AI download page that tricks Mac users into running a potentially dangerous terminal command. (Phil Barker/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
How a fake AI download scam starts with Google

The attack begins with a Google search for "Claude Mac." According to Push Security, researchers discovered a sponsored search result that displayed bing.com as its destination. That address might seem reassuring because Bing belongs to Microsoft.

However, clicking the advertisement sends users through a series of redirects. First, Google's advertising system processes the click. Next, Bing's legitimate click-tracking service forwards the browser to a compromised WordPress website belonging to a South American retailer. Finally, that website sends the visitor to a fake Claude download page.

The final website, claude-desk-code[.]com, imitates the real Claude download experience. It presents what appears to be a legitimate macOS installation option. By the time someone reaches the page, they may have little reason to suspect the journey began with a malicious advertisement.

Researchers say the attackers deliberately used a real Bing search result for a compromised website. This allowed the attackers to display Bing's legitimate domain in the Google advertisement while using Bing's click-tracking redirect to send visitors toward the malicious destination.
Why the fake Claude installer is difficult to spot

The scammers added another layer of deception to make their operation harder to detect. The compromised retailer's website checks whether visitors arrived through Bing and whether their browsers send certain information. Meanwhile, the fake Claude website checks whether visitors came from Google or Bing.

Someone who visits the malicious website directly may see a 404 error page instead of the fake installer. That behavior can make it harder for security scanners to investigate the attack because they may never encounter the page that victims actually see.

Push Security calls this technique cloaking. Attackers use it to control who reaches their malicious content while showing something harmless to other visitors. In this case, the researchers observed two separate checks designed to protect the attack from unwanted attention. The result is a carefully constructed path that makes a dangerous destination appear more trustworthy than it really is.
The fake Claude download button hides a dangerous command

Here's where the attack gets particularly sneaky. The fake Claude page displays an installation command that appears to come directly from Anthropic, the company behind Claude. The command references Claude's legitimate website and looks like something a technically confident Mac user might recognize. However, the page's Copy button places a completely different command on the clipboard.

According to Push Security, the substituted command uses Base64 encoding to conceal an attacker-controlled website. When someone runs the pasted command in Mac Terminal, it first displays a reassuring message claiming that Claude is being downloaded from its official website.

Behind the scenes, the command decodes the hidden address, downloads a remote script and sends it directly to the Mac's Z shell for execution. That means the person running the command sees references to Claude's legitimate website even though the Mac is executing code from an unrelated server.

This attack follows a technique known as InstallFix, a variation of ClickFix. These scams convince people to execute malicious commands themselves, often by disguising the instructions as a software installation or troubleshooting step.

Push Security identified several additional websites associated with the same malicious toolkit, which it tracks internally as AcSig. The researchers found matching installation commands and similar fake installer interfaces across those sites.
What happens if someone runs the fake Claude installer?

The research confirms that the malicious command is designed to download a remote script from an attacker-controlled server and pass it directly to the Mac's Z shell for execution. However, Push Security's published findings do not identify the final payload or establish what the downloaded script does after execution.

That uncertainty is important. Running an untrusted Terminal command can give malicious code an opportunity to operate with the permissions of the person executing it. Depending on the script, an attacker could potentially steal information, modify files or install additional software. The researchers have not confirmed those specific outcomes in this campaign.

The bigger concern is how easily the attack can persuade someone to bypass their own caution. The user voluntarily pastes the command, believing it came from a legitimate software provider. Meanwhile, the actual destination stays hidden inside encoded text.

Push Security reports that four out of five ClickFix attacks it detects reach victims through search engines. That figure comes from the company's own detection data rather than a measurement of all attacks worldwide. Still, it shows why malicious search advertisements deserve attention.
Google suspends accounts behind malicious ads
Google confirms it has taken action against the advertiser accounts associated with the reported campaign.

"We've suspended the advertiser accounts running the reported campaign. Using ads to distribute malware is an egregious violation of our policies, and we consistently update our detection systems to stay ahead of bad actors' evolving tactics," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy.

Google also says attackers use cloaking to show its advertising review systems different content from what people actually see. The company says it continues monitoring attempts to evade its protections and updating its detection systems.
Microsoft responds to malicious AI download campaign
Microsoft also responded to CyberGuy's request for comment, confirming that its security protections identify the malicious indicators described in the research.
"We take reports of malicious online activity seriously and continuously work to help protect customers from evolving threats," a Microsoft spokesperson told CyberGuy.
"Microsoft Defender protections detect and block the malicious indicators identified in the report."
We also reached out to Anthropic for comment on the findings but did not hear back before our deadline.
Scammers are using Google search ads and legitimate Bing redirects to steer Mac users toward a fraudulent Claude AI installer. (Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How to protect your Mac from fake AI downloads
You don't need to understand every line of computer code to avoid this scam. A few precautions can help you recognize suspicious downloads before they put your Mac at risk.

Instead of searching for a download and clicking the first sponsored result, go directly to Claude's official download page. Anthropic provides a macOS download there, so you can install the desktop application without relying on an unfamiliar website. You can also access Claude through your browser at claude.ai.

Be especially careful when a website tells you to copy a command into your Mac's Terminal. Terminal commands can download software, change system settings and execute scripts. Even legitimate-looking instructions can become dangerous when they come from an untrusted source. For the regular Claude desktop app, Anthropic provides a downloadable installer. You don't need to paste a command from a search advertisement to get started.

A website's Copy button can place different text on your clipboard than what appears on the page. Before running an unfamiliar command, paste it into a plain-text editor and compare it with the instructions. Watch for unexplained web addresses, encoded strings or commands that download and immediately execute remote scripts. However, even a command that looks harmless may contain hidden risks. When in doubt, stop and verify the instructions with the software developer.

Install macOS security updates and keep your browser current. Additionally, use strong antivirus software that offers real-time protection against malicious downloads and suspicious activity. Security software may help detect harmful scripts or their effects, although no antivirus product can guarantee protection against every attack. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

A sponsored placement means someone paid to promote a link. It does not guarantee that the destination is safe. Before clicking, check the advertiser by selecting the three dots next to a Google search ad. You can review who paid for it and check the advertiser's verification status.

Google's Ads Transparency Center at adstransparency.google.com offers another way to research advertisers. Always confirm you're visiting the software developer's official website before downloading anything. If an ad looks suspicious, use its three-dot menu to select "Report this ad."
What to do if you already ran the fake Claude command

If you pasted an installation command from a suspicious Claude website into Terminal and pressed Return, treat your Mac as potentially compromised. The researchers have not established what the final payload does, so don't assume everything is safe simply because nothing unusual appears on your screen.

Disconnect your Mac from the internet. Turn off Wi-Fi and unplug any Ethernet connection to help prevent potential communication with an attacker.Run a security scan. Use strong antivirus software to check for malicious files or suspicious activity. Keep in mind that a clean scan cannot guarantee your Mac is safe.Change important passwords. From another trusted device, use a password manager to create strong, unique passwords for sensitive accounts, especially those you accessed after running the command. Prioritize your email and financial accounts, and change your password manager's master password if you suspect it was exposed. Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever possible.Check for suspicious apps and permissions. Look for unfamiliar applications in your Applications folder and review System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions for unexpected items. Also check System Settings > Privacy & Security for unfamiliar apps with sensitive permissions.Consider professional help. If your Mac contains sensitive personal or financial information, have a qualified technician or security professional examine it before reconnecting to the internet.Contact your IT department. If you use a work computer, notify your IT or security team immediately. They can investigate what the command executed and determine whether additional steps are necessary.
Disconnect your Mac from the internet. Turn off Wi-Fi and unplug any Ethernet connection to help prevent potential communication with an attacker.
Run a security scan. Use strong antivirus software to check for malicious files or suspicious activity. Keep in mind that a clean scan cannot guarantee your Mac is safe.

Change important passwords. From another trusted device, use a password manager to create strong, unique passwords for sensitive accounts, especially those you accessed after running the command. Prioritize your email and financial accounts, and change your password manager's master password if you suspect it was exposed. Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever possible.

Check for suspicious apps and permissions. Look for unfamiliar applications in your Applications folder and review System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions for unexpected items. Also check System Settings > Privacy & Security for unfamiliar apps with sensitive permissions.
Consider professional help. If your Mac contains sensitive personal or financial information, have a qualified technician or security professional examine it before reconnecting to the internet.

Contact your IT department. If you use a work computer, notify your IT or security team immediately. They can investigate what the command executed and determine whether additional steps are necessary.
WHY VERIFIED SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS CAN STILL LEAD YOU INTO A SCAM

A fake Claude download website displays a legitimate-looking installation command while secretly copying a different command designed to execute a remote script. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most about this attack is how much effort the scammers put into making everything look familiar. You start with Google, pass through a legitimate Microsoft service and eventually arrive at a page that looks like it belongs to a popular AI company. Then, with one click of a Copy button, the website quietly substitutes a command that could put your Mac at risk. I've always encouraged people to pay attention to website addresses before downloading software.

That's still important, but this case shows why checking the address alone may not be enough. The attackers used trusted services to disguise where their link was taking people. My advice is to go straight to the software developer's official website, especially when installing AI tools.

And whenever a download page asks you to run something in Terminal, make sure you understand exactly what you're authorizing. A few extra seconds of caution could save you from a much bigger headache.

Would you trust a software download if it appeared in a Google ad and showed a familiar Microsoft link, or has this kind of scam made you question whether search results can be trusted at all? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Major US grocery chains hit by cybersecurity incident
summary: Ahold Delhaize's cybersecurity incident knocked online ordering and digital coupons offline at Stop & Shop, Food Lion, Hannaford and Giant Food stores.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You pull out your phone to check your grocery store's digital coupons or place an order for dinner. Suddenly, the app won't open. The website is unavailable, and the groceries you were counting on for tonight may never arrive. For anyone who depends on online grocery shopping, that's a frustrating problem.

That's the situation shoppers encountered this week at several major U.S. supermarket chains. A cybersecurity incident at grocery giant Ahold Delhaize forced the company to take some systems offline. The disruption affected Stop & Shop, Food Lion, Hannaford and the Giant supermarket chains. The company says its physical stores have remained open, although customers have experienced interruptions to online services.

There's another reason this story deserves attention. The same company suffered a major data breach in 2024 that exposed personal information belonging to more than 2.2 million people. So, as investigators work to understand the latest incident, shoppers have a reasonable question: Could their personal information be at risk again?
CHICK-FIL-A DATA BREACH EXPOSES CUSTOMER ACCOUNTS

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE
Stop & Shop is among five major U.S. supermarket chains that experienced online service disruptions following a cybersecurity incident at parent company Ahold Delhaize. (Ahold Delhaize)
Major grocery cybersecurity incident affects five US supermarket chains

On Oct. 12, Ahold Delhaize confirmed a cybersecurity issue within its network. The Netherlands-based company owns some of America's best-known regional supermarket chains and operates more than 9,400 stores worldwide. The company took certain systems offline to protect its operations while security teams investigated the problem. In its official statement, Ahold Delhaize said: "Our teams are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue. This includes taking some systems offline to help protect them."

The company serves approximately 60 million customers each week across its international businesses. Consequently, a problem involving its technology can affect grocery shopping far beyond a single store.
Which US grocery stores are affected?
The cybersecurity incident has disrupted online services for five major U.S. supermarket chains:

Stop & Shop: Serves customers across the Northeast, including Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts and Rhode Island.Food Lion: Operates supermarkets throughout the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic.Hannaford: Serves communities in Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts and New York.Giant Food: Operates stores in Maryland, Virginia, Delaware and the Washington, D.C. area.The Giant Company: Operates Giant and Martin's stores primarily in Pennsylvania and neighboring states.
Stop & Shop: Serves customers across the Northeast, including Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts and Rhode Island.
Food Lion: Operates supermarkets throughout the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic.
Hannaford: Serves communities in Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts and New York.
Giant Food: Operates stores in Maryland, Virginia, Delaware and the Washington, D.C. area.
The Giant Company: Operates Giant and Martin's stores primarily in Pennsylvania and neighboring states.

According to Grocery Dive, websites and mobile apps for all five chains were still unavailable on the morning of Wednesday, Oct. 14. That marked at least the third consecutive day of online disruptions. Customers have encountered problems accessing online ordering and digital coupons. Some app-based loyalty features have also been unavailable. In its Oct. 13 update, Ahold Delhaize said it was beginning a controlled relaunch of certain systems. However, as of Oct. 14, the company had not announced a firm timetable for restoring all affected services.
Are Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Hannaford stores still open?

Yes. In its Oct. 13 statement, Ahold Delhaize confirmed that its supermarkets across Europe and the United States remained open and were serving customers. Notices from the affected U.S. chains also indicated that pharmacies were operating during their normal business hours. However, online shopping has experienced significant disruptions. Customers have faced interruptions to grocery pickup and delivery services. Meanwhile, shoppers who rely on digital coupons have encountered problems accessing their usual discounts.

As of Oct. 14, Food Lion, Giant Food and The Giant Company also directed customers to third-party delivery services, including Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats, where available. For customers who depend on grocery delivery because of mobility challenges or limited transportation, these disruptions can create a serious inconvenience.
Food Lion stores remain open despite cybersecurity-related disruptions affecting the supermarket chain's website, mobile app and online ordering services. (Food Lion)
What happens to online grocery orders and refunds?

If you placed an online grocery order that was never fulfilled, the affected supermarket chains said customers would receive refunds for those orders. However, it's worth checking your credit card or bank account to make sure the refund actually arrives.

Keep your original order confirmation and any emails related to the purchase. If the refund doesn't appear within the retailer's stated processing period, contact customer service through a verified channel. If your grocery app remains unavailable, shopping inside a physical store may be your most dependable option. Still, consider calling ahead if you need a specific service or want to confirm that a prescription is ready.
Grocery giant moves toward restoring systems after security incident

On Oct. 13, Ahold Delhaize issued a statement, updated Oct. 14, saying it was in the process of starting a controlled relaunch of certain systems. The company said it was working with external cybersecurity experts and appropriate authorities to investigate the incident. In a direct response to CyberGuy, an Ahold Delhaize USA spokesperson provided an update on efforts to restore affected services. "Please know our teams are working as quickly as possible to restore systems safely that we took offline as a precautionary measure, including our websites," the spokesperson told CyberGuy.

The spokesperson also confirmed that stores remain open and apologized for the disruption to customers. However, Ahold Delhaize has not publicly identified who caused the problem or explained how its network was compromised. It has also not confirmed whether ransomware played a role. That leaves several important questions unanswered, including how the incident began and when all affected services will be restored. The company has not provided a firm timetable for full restoration.
Was customer data stolen in the grocery cybersecurity incident?

This may be the biggest concern for shoppers who have online grocery accounts. In its statement, Ahold Delhaize said investigators had found no evidence at that point that customer, employee or partner data was taken during the incident. That's encouraging for shoppers who have provided personal information to these supermarket chains. However, investigators were still examining the incident as of that update. The company's preliminary findings do not definitively rule out data theft. As of Oct. 14, Ahold Delhaize had not confirmed that personal information was stolen during this latest incident. That means shoppers should remain alert without assuming their personal information has been compromised.
Ahold Delhaize suffered a major data breach in 2024

Unfortunately, this isn't the first major cybersecurity incident involving Ahold Delhaize. In November 2024, hackers gained unauthorized access to internal U.S. business systems operated by Ahold Delhaize USA Services. The attackers obtained files containing sensitive personal information. The company eventually disclosed that more than 2.2 million people were affected. According to a filing with the Maine Attorney General, the breach involved approximately 2.24 million individuals. In a June 2025 breach notification, the company explained that the stolen information varied by person.
Exposed records could include:
Names and contact informationSocial Security numbersDriver's license and passport numbersFinancial account informationHealth information contained in employment records
Names and contact information
Social Security numbers
Driver's license and passport numbers
Financial account information
Health information contained in employment records

The vast majority of those affected were current or former employees, along with their dependents and beneficiaries. The company said it had no indication that customer payment or pharmacy systems were compromised during the 2024 attack. The ransomware group INC Ransom claimed responsibility for the earlier incident. However, Ahold Delhaize did not publicly confirm the group's involvement. There is currently no confirmed connection between that attack and the October 2026 cybersecurity incident.
Why repeated cybersecurity incidents raise concerns

For many of us, grocery shopping now involves much more than walking into a store with a shopping list. We create accounts, save payment details and use loyalty programs to access discounts. Some families depend on online ordering every week. When a supermarket chain experiences a cybersecurity incident, those conveniences can suddenly disappear. For Ahold Delhaize, the challenge now extends beyond restoring its apps. The company also faces questions about the security of its systems after experiencing two major incidents in less than two years. Customers deserve to understand what happened once investigators have reliable answers.
Grocery shoppers increasingly rely on mobile apps for digital coupons and online orders, making cybersecurity-related outages especially frustrating. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
7 ways to protect yourself after a grocery store cybersecurity incident

Even without confirmed customer data theft, a widely reported cybersecurity incident can give scammers opportunities to target shoppers. These seven precautions can help you protect your information and avoid additional headaches.

Scammers may send emails or text messages claiming that you need to verify your payment information to receive a grocery refund. Those messages can seem especially convincing if you've recently had an order canceled. Avoid clicking unexpected refund links. Instead, review your original payment account or contact the retailer using a verified phone number. Never provide your banking password or pay a processing fee to receive a refund.

If you placed an order around the time of the outage, check whether the store charged you for groceries you never received. Save your confirmation emails and keep any receipts. Then, review your account for a refund. If the money doesn't appear within the retailer's stated processing period, contact customer service or your payment provider.

If you reuse your grocery account password on other websites, replace it with a unique one. A password manager can generate and store strong passwords without forcing you to remember each one. Also, enable two-factor authentication (2FA) if your grocery account supports it. That gives your account another layer of protection against unauthorized access.

A real cybersecurity incident gives scammers an opportunity to send convincing fake breach notifications. You might receive a message claiming that your grocery account has been compromised and that you must immediately verify your identity. Before entering personal information, confirm the alert through the retailer's official communications.

Although Ahold Delhaize reported no evidence of data theft in its Oct. 14 update, regularly checking your financial accounts remains a smart precaution. Enable transaction alerts through your bank or credit card provider. Pay attention to unfamiliar charges or unexpected account activity.

If you normally use your grocery store's app to access digital coupons or loyalty rewards, check your receipt carefully. Some discounts may be unavailable while the retailer's online services are down. Before checking out, ask a store employee whether there's another way to receive an advertised discount. Keep your receipt if you believe you were overcharged so you can request an adjustment when customer service becomes available.

If you clicked a suspicious grocery refund or security alert link, your next steps depend on what information you shared. If you entered your password, change it immediately through the retailer's official website once it's available. Update any other accounts using that password. If you provided credit card or banking information, contact your financial institution and ask about securing your account. You can also report suspected fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov. If you downloaded a suspicious attachment, run a security scan using strong antivirus software on your device. Kurt's key takeaways

I find it troubling that a company responsible for feeding millions of American families is dealing with another major cybersecurity incident so soon after its last one. We depend on grocery stores for something as basic as putting dinner on the table. Increasingly, those stores also want us to use their apps to access the best prices and place orders. What concerns me is how quickly those everyday conveniences can disappear when something goes wrong with a retailer's technology. And after the 2024 breach exposed personal information belonging to more than 2.2 million people, I think Ahold Delhaize has some serious questions to answer. I'd like to know what caused this latest incident and whether the company addressed weaknesses identified after the previous attack. Those answers could go a long way toward restoring customer confidence. As of the company's October 14 update, investigators had found no evidence that customer, employee or partner data was taken in the latest incident. That's reassuring, although the investigation continues. In the meantime, you should remain cautious about unexpected refund messages or suspicious security alerts.

title: Amazon About You may know you a little too well
summary: Amazon's About You feature includes personality details from your shopping history, and some shoppers are finding hilariously awkward results.
story: Amazon's 'About You' page sparks concern as the 'Outnumbered' panel reacts to the retail giant's data tracking. Kayleigh McEnany, Kat Timpf, Adam Carolla, Harris Faulkner and Kennedy discuss a viral post regarding the discovery.

Amazon knows what you buy, what you search for and even what you tell its shopping assistant. Now, the company is giving you a look at the personality profile it has built from all that information. When I checked my own Amazon About You profile, I found 81 results, including a reference to my mother that caught me off guard. The feature brings together details about your shopping habits and preferences. Some are helpful. Others might make you wonder how Amazon reached those conclusions in the first place.

Shoppers are now sharing screenshots of descriptions that range from funny to completely inaccurate. Amazon says the feature helps improve shopping recommendations. However, it also raises an interesting privacy question. How much should a retailer know about you, and how much control do you really have over that information?
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE
Amazon's About You feature reveals the personal preferences and shopping habits the company uses to recommend products. (Amazon)

Amazon introduced About You in May 2026, although the feature has recently attracted widespread attention as shoppers share their profiles on social media. Amazon has personalized shopping recommendations for years. If you bought a coffee maker, you probably noticed suggestions for filters or other accessories soon afterward. That kind of recommendation has become familiar to anyone who shops online. Now, Amazon is taking personalization further with About You, a section that shows shoppers what the company believes about their interests and preferences.

According to Amazon's announcement, the feature draws on information from several sources, including your purchase history, product reviews and items saved to Lists. Searches and conversations with Alexa for Shopping can also influence what Amazon learns.

For example, someone who regularly buys dairy-free milk might receive recommendations for other dairy-free products. A shopper researching gardening supplies could start seeing suggestions for fertilizer or companion plants. That sounds useful enough. However, Amazon can also develop assumptions about your personal preferences from individual purchases or short-lived interests. That's where things can get awkward.
Amazon's About You feature is already amusing shoppers

Some shoppers have started sharing screenshots of their Amazon profiles on social media. The results range from remarkably accurate to unintentionally hilarious. One Threads user discovered that Amazon had included the description "flat buttocks" in her profile. "I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I'm literally speechless," she wrote.

She even acknowledged that the assessment wasn't entirely wrong. Still, it's hard to imagine anyone asking an online retailer for that particular evaluation. Meanwhile, another shopper shared a profile describing an obsession with minimalist, one-bag travel and a preference for Anker charging products. The shopper confirmed that Amazon had accurately identified those interests. A different user discovered that Amazon had recorded a "one-time specialty cheese exploration." The response was simple: "guilty."

Other shoppers have shared descriptions such as "has no friends" and "cannot keep real plants alive." One woman even reported that Amazon had described her as a "fifty-year-old man." These are the kinds of assumptions that can leave you wondering whether Amazon knows you at all.

My own profile included some remarkably specific observations. Amazon said I "do not like scary movies," "value professional grade audio equipment," "prefer dark chocolate treats" and "enjoy swimming." It even noted my regular fresh flower purchases. But one entry really surprised me. Amazon claimed my mother had stayed at a hotel with another person, whom it identified by name, and had a negative experience. I certainly didn't expect to find that kind of information about a family member in my shopping profile.

These examples show how an algorithm can turn shopping activity into surprisingly specific personal descriptions. Of course, Amazon's conclusions may be incomplete or inaccurate. Buying something for a friend, for example, doesn't necessarily mean you have any personal interest in that product.
YOUR PHONE MAY REVEAL DOCTOR, CHURCH AND PHARMACY VISITS
Amazon organizes what it knows about shoppers into categories, including diet, hobbies and family, which users can review and update. (Megan Montgomery/Threads)
Why Amazon knows so much about your shopping habits

Every time you interact with Amazon, you potentially give the company another clue about your preferences. A product search can suggest an interest, while a purchase provides a stronger signal about something you wanted at that moment. Amazon also uses information from its AI shopping assistant. If you tell Alexa for Shopping that your cat prefers a particular flavor of food, Amazon can use that detail to recommend similar products later.

According to the company, these interactions help make recommendations more relevant. However, a single purchase might reflect a temporary need rather than a lasting preference. Think about buying an unusual gift for a relative. You might suddenly find Amazon treating that purchase as evidence of a personal hobby. That raises another concern. Some purchases can indicate sensitive interests involving health, relationships or other aspects of your private life. Even when Amazon draws an incorrect conclusion, you may still want to remove it from your shopping profile.
How to see what Amazon knows about you
Amazon makes About You available through its Shopping app, mobile website and desktop website. You can review the information the company has associated with your profile and make changes.

How to remove personal information from Amazon About You

Here's where I would spend a few minutes if you use Amazon regularly. The company says About You lets you correct preferences, provide feedback and remove information you don't want used for personalization.

You don't need to provide a reason.Repeat these steps for other unwanted entries.

If you want to correct a detail instead of removing it, open the entry and look for an edit or feedback option. Make your changes and follow the prompts to save them. Amazon hasn't established that every account will show identical editing controls. The available options may depend on the information displayed. Removing a detail from About You changes how Amazon uses that preference for personalization. It does not necessarily erase the original purchase, search or conversation from every Amazon system.
How to reduce what Amazon uses for recommendations
Editing your About You profile is a useful starting point. However, you should also review the activity that influences Amazon's suggestions.
Amazon provides browsing history controls that can help reduce recommendations based on products you've viewed.

Removing a product from the browsing history display should not be treated as confirmation that Amazon has deleted every record of the interaction.
Amazon also provides controls for managing recommendations associated with past purchases.

Sign in to your Amazon account.Visit Amazon's recommendation preferences help page.Follow the available links to your recommendation settings.Review purchases or other activity that may influence your recommendations.Exclude eligible items from recommendations when Amazon provides that option.

Review purchases or other activity that may influence your recommendations.
Exclude eligible items from recommendations when Amazon provides that option.
This can be particularly helpful when you've purchased gifts or products that have nothing to do with your interests.
Review Alexa shopping interactions

If you regularly use Alexa for Shopping, consider what you share during those conversations. Amazon says the assistant can remember details you provide and use them to improve future shopping experiences. Ask "What do you know about me?" to review the preferences Alexa can describe. Then use About You to correct or remove unwanted details. For additional privacy controls, review your Alexa privacy settings and voice history in the Alexa app or your Amazon account. Deleting voice recordings and removing shopping preferences are separate actions, so check both.
Can you completely delete your Amazon shopping profile?

Amazon provides ways to edit preferences and manage certain recommendation signals. However, the company hasn't established that removing everything displayed in About You permanently deletes all underlying information. Your purchase history, for example, can remain associated with your account even after you exclude an item from recommendations. Amazon may retain certain transaction records for operational or legal reasons. Also, About You is only one part of Amazon's broader personalization system. Correcting an assumption doesn't necessarily stop Amazon from generating new recommendations based on future shopping activity. If privacy is your priority, review your browsing history, recommendation settings and Alexa privacy controls rather than relying exclusively on the new profile page.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've always found Amazon's recommendations fascinating, but seeing 81 personal details in my own profile was an eye-opener. Some were surprisingly accurate. Others, including information about my mother, left me wondering how Amazon reached those conclusions. I appreciate being able to review and remove these details, but I'd like more transparency about what happens to that information afterward. My advice? Take a few minutes to check your own Amazon About You profile. You might be surprised by what the company thinks it knows about you.

Would you be comfortable with Amazon building a personality profile from everything you buy and search for, or has online shopping personalization gone too far? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Was your identity stolen? What to do in the first 24 hours
summary: Identity theft recovery starts with securing bank accounts, freezing credit and enabling two-factor authentication within the first 24 hours.
story: Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion. Knutsson hosts a free live class to teach families how to protect their money and secure accounts.

Discovering that your identity has been stolen can leave you feeling angry, frightened and unsure where to begin. Maybe someone drained your bank account, opened a credit card in your name or filed a fraudulent tax return using your Social Security number. Whatever happened, your next steps can help limit the damage.

The first 24 hours are especially important because identity thieves may continue using your information until you secure your accounts. Fortunately, you can take several steps right away to protect yourself and begin recovering.

IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT
Reviewing your credit reports and documenting suspicious activity are important steps toward recovering from identity theft. (Sara Diggins/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)
Why the first day is so important

Identity theft can quickly spread beyond the account where you first discovered the problem. Someone who gains access to your email, for example, might use it to reset passwords for your banking, shopping or other accounts. That's why acting quickly can make a difference.

However, you don't have to solve everything in one day. Identity theft recovery can take weeks or even months, depending on the circumstances. Your immediate goal is to stop additional fraud, protect your information and create a record of what happened.
What to do in the first 24 hours after identity theft
The following checklist breaks the process into manageable steps. The time frames are guidelines, so prioritize active fraud and compromised accounts rather than waiting for a particular hour.
Start with the accounts most likely to expose your money or personal information.

Contact your bank or credit card company. If someone accessed your account or made unauthorized transactions, call the number on your card or the institution's official website. Report the fraud and ask whether the account should be locked, frozen or replaced. Also ask about disputing unauthorized transactions.Change compromised passwords. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Protect your email, financial accounts and other important services. Use an authenticator app or passkey when supported.
Check for unauthorized account changes. Review recovery email addresses, phone numbers, forwarding rules and active sessions. Sign out of unfamiliar devices.
Important: If money has been stolen, report it to your financial institution immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary by account and transaction type.
Next, make it harder for criminals to open additional accounts using your personal information.

Place a fraud alert on your credit file. Contact Equifax, Experian or TransUnion. The bureau you contact must notify the other two. An initial fraud alert is free and generally lasts one year.Freeze your credit with all three bureaus. Hours 16 to 24: Document everything
Once you've addressed the most urgent threats, organize your recovery efforts.

Common identity theft recovery mistakes to avoid
Even when you're moving quickly, certain mistakes can create additional problems.

Keep records of who you contacted, what they said and any deadlines they provided.Stopping after securing one account. Review other accounts that may share passwords or recovery information.

Helping a family member organize financial records and contact the right institutions can make identity theft recovery less overwhelming. (John Carl D'Annibale /Albany Times Union via Getty Images)
What can wait beyond the first day

Some recovery tasks will continue beyond the first day, including disputing fraudulent accounts, correcting credit reports and following up with creditors. However, report unauthorized financial transactions immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary depending on the type of account and transaction. Your initial priority is to stop additional fraud and secure your information.
How identity theft protection can add another layer of security

Recovering from identity theft often involves contacting multiple financial institutions, disputing fraudulent charges and keeping track of important paperwork. An identity theft protection service may help simplify the process by offering recovery assistance, ongoing monitoring and guidance when suspicious activity appears.
