title: Former OJ Simpson attorney, longtime friend both support possibility of accomplice in 1994 murders
summary: A mob-linked drug trafficker who knew OJ Simpson claimed knowledge of the missing murder weapon and efforts to dispose of evidence, a report reveals.
story: Unsealed court documents reveal new details in the O.J. Simpson murder case, suggesting a dead mobster may have acted as an accomplice. Simpson 'Dream Team' member Alan Dershowitz joins Sandra Smith and John Roberts to discuss the legal implications of these decades-old revelations.

A mob-linked drug trafficker with ties to OJ Simpson secretly became a jailhouse snitch and claimed to have information about efforts to dispose of evidence, potentially including a murder weapon that was never recovered, according to a new report.

A former member of Simpson's "Dream Team" defense during one of the most scrutinized murder trials in American history says the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman are still an "open case" and that the claims should be further investigated.
"It seems plausible and perhaps credible," former Simpson defense attorney Alan Dershowitz said on Fox News' "America Reports" Monday.
BROTHER OF POSSIBLE OJ SIMPSON ACCOMPLICE CLAIMS HE RETURNED WITH BLOODY HANDS ON NIGHT OF MURDERS: REPORT
O.J. Simpson sits in Superior Court in Los Angeles in 1994 during an open court session. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
He said he believes there are "unresolved" questions that deserve to be looked into.

Those questions were raised in a New York Times report Sunday about Joseph Ippolito, a former cigarette boat racer, drug trafficker and restaurateur who knew Simpson and had become close with Al Cowlings, the former NFL star who drove the white Ford Bronco ahead of Simpson's arrest in Los Angeles.
NICOLE BROWN SIMPSON TOLD FORMER LOVER SHE'D 'RATHER DIE' THAN RETURN TO O.J. SIMPSON BEFORE HER MURDER
Ippolito told federal prosecutors he had information on the murder weapon. One has never been recovered.

Further, Ippolito's brother Sam told the Times that his brother returned home on the night of the murders with a heavy bag and apparent blood on his hands. He claimed to have ditched the bag in a dumpster on Los Angeles' Doheny Drive without asking questions. He later asked for payment for his story and recanted, according to the report.
Nicole Brown Simpson was killed along with restaurant waiter Ronald Goldman on June 12, 1994. (FILES/AFP via Getty Images)
But the claims are worth a look, Dershowitz said.

"I think we ought to start from scratch and look at this evidence anew and see if there is credible evidence of a second person," he told Fox News. "I've often, right from the beginning, thought that this was very difficult for one person to have brought off and not only killed two people, but then disposed of the evidence and done all the things that we know occurred in this case."

Charlie Ehrlich, a friend of Ippolito since 1971 and eventually a close pal of Simpson's, said it's possible that a second person was involved — while vehemently denying unproven online speculation that it could've been him.
"In my mind, there is a secondary guy," he told Fox News Digital Monday. "Who? I have no clue. But I believe, in my mind, there is."
A family photo of Ronald Goldman, who was murdered with O.J. Simpson's ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson on June 12, 1994, at a private residence in Agoura Hills, California. (WireImage)

The white Ford Bronco, driven by Al Cowlings and carrying O.J. Simpson, is seen during a 90-minute slow-speed car chase on June 17, 1994, on the 405 freeway in Los Angeles. (Sygma via Getty Images)

"Do I think he did it? I don’t know," he said. "If he did it, or if he did not do it, I never saw him get angry — and I was with him a lot the last 10-12 years here of his life here in Florida. We were together every weekend."
He has not been charged in connection with the Brown Simpson and Goldman case — nor was Ippolito or any of Simpson's other associates.

title: Convicted serial rapist originally sentenced to 124 years walks free after 20, sparking outrage
summary: Andrew Luster, convicted of 86 felony counts for drugging and assaulting women, is reportedly living in Glendora after serving only 20 years in prison.
story: California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton reacts to rising crime rates under Governor Gavin Newsom. Hilton criticizes the state's leadership and discusses the urgent need for policy changes to address rampant crime affecting local communities.

A California man convicted of drugging and raping three women and originally sentenced to 124 years in prison has been released after serving approximately 20 years, sparking outrage from local officials who have raised public safety concerns.
Andrew Luster, the great-grandson of cosmetics mogul Max Factor, was released from state prison earlier this month and is reportedly residing in Glendora, California, according to KTLA.
Glendora Mayor David Fredendall condemned the release in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital, calling it unacceptable that a convicted serial rapist is now reportedly living in the community.
NEWSOM-BACKED LAW LETS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHILD RAPIST SEEK EARLY RELEASE AGAIN AS DA URGES 'STOP THE MADNESS'

"The City of Glendora is beyond disappointed. We are outraged," Fredendall said. "Andrew Luster was convicted of 86 felony counts stemming from the drugging and sexual assault of unconscious women. He was originally sentenced to 124 years in prison. He has now been released from State prison and is reportedly residing in our community. This is unacceptable."

Max Factor cosmetics heir Andrew Luster is led to a car by a law enforcement officer on June 19, 2003, after arriving at the Los Angeles International Airport. Luster, who has been on the run since January 3, was arrested in Mexico and returned to the United States to serve a 124-year jail term for his self-video-taped rape of three women after he drugged them unconscious. (Getty Images)
Luster was convicted in 2003 of 86 felony counts stemming from the drugging and sexual assault of three women at his beachfront home in Ventura County.
Prosecutors said he used the drug GHB to render the women unconscious before sexually assaulting them.

Luster fled to Mexico in January 2003 while free on $1 million bail during his trial. He was convicted in his absence and later captured by celebrity bounty hunter Duane "Dog" Chapman in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico.

The Max Factor heir was originally sentenced to 124 years in prison, but a California judge set aside the sentence in March 2013 after finding that the trial court failed to adequately explain its reasons for imposing consecutive sentences, as Fox News Digital previously reported.
Ventura County Superior Court Judge Kathryne Ann Stoltz rejected Luster's attempt to overturn his convictions but granted him a new sentencing hearing.
CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

Max Factor heir Andrew Luster stands during break in trial in Ventura County Superior Court in Ventura, Calif., Dec 17, 2002. Luster, an heir to the Max Factor cosmetics fortune, is charged with raping three women after rendering them unconscious with the date-rape drug gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB). (Anacleto Rapping/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
In April 2013, Stoltz resentenced Luster to 50 years in prison, The Associated Press reported.
Prosecutors opposed the reduced sentence, describing Luster's crimes as "cruel, vicious and callous."
NEWSOM BLASTED BY SHERIFF IN HIS OWN BACKYARD OVER CALIFORNIA CRIME AS VICTIMS CRY FOUL

His release has renewed criticism of California's criminal justice system, particularly Proposition 57, a voter-approved measure passed in 2016 that expanded parole consideration for certain offenders.

KTLA reported that Luster was denied parole in 2022 before being granted parole in 2024. Ventura County prosecutors successfully challenged that decision, and Luster was denied parole again in April 2025.
CHARLES MANSON FOLLOWER TIED TO SHARON TATE MURDERS GETS RECOMMENDED FOR PAROLE AFTER 55 YEARS IN PRISON
He was subsequently expected to remain incarcerated until October 2026, when his calculated prison term would end, the outlet reported.
Fredendall argued that the outcome undermines promises made to California voters when Proposition 57 was approved.
CALIFORNIA DEMS TRIGGER OUTRAGE AFTER SIDING WITH CONVICTED CHILD SEX OFFENDERS IN SHOCKING VOTE
"When California voters approved Proposition 57 in 2016, they were assured by Governor Jerry Brown and his administration that dangerous offenders would remain behind bars," Fredendall said.

"The State may argue that this was not technically an early release. It can point to sentencing credits, legal calculations, and administrative requirements," the mayor continued. "However, those technical explanations do not address the larger concern: how an individual originally sentenced to 124 years in prison for heinous crimes is able to walk out of a secured facility after only 20 years."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
California Assemblywoman Blanca E. Rubio also criticized the release in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.

This handout photo showing Andrew Luster, heir to the Max Factor cosmetics fortune, was released by the Ventura County Sheriff's Department on January 8, 2003, in Ventura, California. (Ventura County Sheriff's Department/Getty Images)

"I am outraged and deeply disturbed by the decision to grant parole to convicted serial rapist Andrew Luster," Rubio said. "It is incomprehensible that an individual originally sentenced to 124 years in prison for such horrific crimes could be granted parole after serving approximately 20 years."
Rubio, who represents California's 48th Assembly District, said the decision raises questions about the state's parole system and whether it adequately protects victims and communities.

"Our justice system is supposed to protect the innocent, hold violent criminals accountable, and provide victims with a sense of justice," she said. "Decisions like this undermine public confidence in that system and send a devastating message to survivors of sexual assault."

Rubio said she is working with local officials and law enforcement to learn more about the circumstances surrounding Luster's release, including the conditions of his supervision.

Fredendall also expressed concern about Luster reportedly living near schools, parks, playgrounds and other community spaces.

"Our Police Department will work with State parole authorities to ensure every applicable law and condition of supervision is followed," Fredendall said. "We will do everything within our lawful authority to protect our residents. But local governments should not be forced to shoulder the public-safety consequences of decisions made in Sacramento without adequate transparency and accountability."

The mayor said the city is demanding additional information from state officials about the release and measures being taken to protect residents.

"The victims deserve better. The people of Glendora deserve better. California must do better," Fredendall said.

story: A private investigator analyzes the harrowing details surrounding the double murder of a husband and his son that happened at a popular mountain resort. Metallica Harrison, 27, is facing homicide charges relating to the killings.
The mother who police say killed her husband and their 3-year-old son at Great Wolf Lodge could face the death penalty, according to a private investigator.

Metallica Rose Harrison, 27, is currently behind bars in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, after prosecutors say she used kitchen knives — which she allegedly brought from home — to stab and kill Charles "Chaz" Harrison, 36, and their son, Tristan.
She's due in court next month.
GREAT WOLF LODGE FAMILY MASSACRE BLEW UP DURING ‘UNCOMMON’ THREE-WEEK STAY AT PRICEY RESORT, OFFICIALS SAY

Metallica Harrison, 27, faces murder charges after prosecutors say she stabbed and killed her husband and the couple's 3-year-old son at the Great Wolf Lodge in the Poconos in Pennsylvania. (Pocono Township Police Department; Great Wolf Lodge; Facebook/Meta: Chaz Harrison)
Private investigator Rod Devine, who is based in the Lehigh Valley area, said it's possible Harrison could face the death penalty.

story: A massive four-alarm fire tore through a vacant Staten Island warehouse, injuring a firefighter but sparing a historic church featured in the 1972 classic "The Godfather." (via FDNY)
Firefighters saved a historic New York City church, notable for its appearance in "The Godfather," as a four-alarm fire tore through a nearby vacant warehouse.

More than 200 firefighters and EMS personnel rushed to Mount Loretto in Staten Island after the blaze began to spread inside an empty warehouse at around 5:45 p.m. on Saturday, FDNY Chief of Operations Kevin Woods said at a press conference that evening.
"There is heavy, heavy damage to this structure, the roof did collapse, and right now we’re maintaining a collapse zone around that structure," Woods said.

"Upon arrival, units encountered heavy fire throughout the building and immediately went into a defensive operation," Woods said. "We set up multiple large-caliber stream tower ladders and handlines."

The warehouse at 6581 Hylan Boulevard has been vacant for five years, but it is located near several other structures on the Mount Loretto grounds, including two schools and the historic Old Church of St. Joachim and St. Anne, which was famously featured in exterior shots of the baptism scene of the 1972 film "The Godfather."

The warehouse has been vacant for five years, but it is located near several other structures on the Mount Loretto grounds. (FDNY)
The ornate Catholic Church was largely destroyed by a fire in 1973, though its façade survived, and it was rebuilt three years later.

title: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro
summary: A no-bond Florida arrest warrant charges Raúl Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in the 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown.
story: Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., discusses the indictment of former Cuban President Raúl Castro on murder and conspiracy charges tied to the 1996 shoot-down of two civilian aircraft that killed four American pilots on ‘Sunday Night in America.’

Florida has obtained a state arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro on a no-bond charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder stemming from the 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown, according to a warrant obtained by Fox News Digital.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, whose office reopened the state's investigation into Castro after he took office, secured the new arrest warrant. Gov. Ron DeSantis is expected to address the development at a press conference Monday morning.The no-bond warrant, issued in Miami-Dade County, directs law enforcement to immediately arrest Castro and says a judge found probable cause to believe he conspired to commit first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of four men aboard the unarmed civilian aircraft.The warrant marks a new front in efforts to hold Castro accountable for the Feb. 24, 1996, attack, which has long reverberated through South Florida's Cuban-American community. Castro already faces a separate federal prosecution over the shootdown.
HAVANA REGIME IN SUSPENSE AFTER CASTRO INDICTMENT WITH TRUMP PRESSURE ON, SAYS CUBAN-BORN GOP REP.
Florida has obtained a state arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro on a no-bond charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. (AP Photo/Ramon Espinosa)

"The investigation revealed evidence of a conspiracy to kill persons aboard BTTR aircraft. The deaths of Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña, and Armando Alejandre Jr. were the object of that conspiracy," the warrant reads.

According to the warrant, investigators allege that in 1996, the Castro regime's foreign intelligence service's plan to shoot down Brothers to the Rescue aircraft and kill their occupants traveled through the chain of command, with Raúl Castro and his brother, former Cuban leader Fidel Castro, as the final decision-makers.
Raúl and Fidel Castro attend a parade Dec. 2, 1996, in Havana, Cuba. (Sven Creutzmann/Mambo Photography/Getty Images)

"They have violated the airspace, the waters of the Republic. I made it clear that this had to be decentralized if we wanted it to do its job, and five generals were given the authority. I used to say: Try to shoot them down over our territory. But they would come into Havana and leave," Raúl Castro, now 95, said in a recorded statement months after the incident, recounting orders he gave to senior military leaders before the shootdown, according to the warrant.

"Of course, with a missile shot like that, plane against plane, what comes down is a ball of fire, and it is going to fall on top of the city. So I said: Fine, shoot them down at sea when they show up, and those who have the authority are not to consult anyone," he added in his statement.
RAÚL CASTRO MAKES FIRST PUBLIC APPEARANCE SINCE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION CHARGED HIM WITH MURDER

The Attorney General’s Office of Statewide Prosecution will assume jurisdiction over the multi-circuit criminal conspiracy case against Raúl Castro. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

Brothers to the Rescue is a Miami-based organization that flew unarmed civilian aircraft to search for Cuban migrants stranded or lost at sea. By the mid-1990s, the group had also become involved in anti-Castro political activity, including dropping pro-democracy leaflets over Cuba.
The Cuban government has rejected the U.S. prosecution of Castro, maintaining that Brothers to the Rescue repeatedly violated Cuban airspace and that Cuba acted in defense of its sovereignty.

The warrant indicates that Florida authorities are seeking full extradition of Raúl Castro if he is arrested outside the Sunshine State, authorizing authorities to pursue his return to Florida to face the felony charge if he is arrested in another U.S. jurisdiction.
The attorney general’s Office of Statewide Prosecution will assume jurisdiction over the multi-circuit criminal conspiracy case against Castro.

title: Arizona man accused of plotting mass casualty attack on religious site with 'cookbook' tied to OKC bombing

"Again, the FBI served a search warrant, got all of his electronic devices. He gave them access, gave him his passwords to those devices. They went through all of those electronic devices. They didn't see anything about terrorism. And FBI cut him loose," he continued.

Schell also argued that the three seized guns were lawfully possessed, adding that Bjornholt's civil rights were restored after completing a previous sentence on a drug charge stemming from a closed first-degree murder case. title: Teen suspected of killing boy and stepmom was in prosecutors' sights for years — until new law let them strike
summary: A legal gap in Indiana's juvenile jurisdiction law delayed murder charges for nearly two decades in the stabbing deaths of Blake and Chynna Dickus.
story: Michael Jerome James has been charged in the July 24, 2006, killings of Blake, 10, and Chynna Dickus, 26.

Indiana investigators identified a suspect years before charging a man with the 2006 murders of 10-year-old Blake Dickus and his 26-year-old stepmother, Chynna Dickus, but prosecutors say an unusual gap in state law prevented them from bringing the case.

Johnson County Prosecutor Lance Hamner told Fox News Digital that authorities had identified Michael Jerome James as a suspect in the double murders, but spent years working to establish a legal path to prosecute him for crimes he allegedly committed at age 14.
"That's what took us so long," Hamner said. "We had a suspect identified. We weren't able to bring charges for several years because we were trying to get the jurisdictional statute in place."
Blake, 10, and Chynna Dickus, his 26-year-old stepmother, were stabbed to death in their Franklin, Indiana, home on July 24, 2006. (City of Franklin, Indiana)
KILLER UNDONE BY DECADES-OLD THREADS — GLOVE, TOWEL AND SHIRT STITCH TOGETHER COLD CASE JUSTICE
James, now 35, appeared in Johnson Circuit Court in Franklin on Thursday, Oct. 8, following a grand jury indictment in the July 24, 2006, deaths of Blake and Chynna.
James faces four counts of murder. Prosecutors accuse him of killing Blake and Chynna while burglarizing or attempting to burglarize their Franklin home.

During his court appearance, James told Johnson Circuit Court Judge Andrew Roesener that he did not have an attorney yet but planned to get one. Roesener gave James until Nov. 2 to hire an attorney and set his next status hearing for the same day.
James' age at the time of the killings is what created an unusual problem for the state, Hamner said.

Indiana law historically gave juvenile courts jurisdiction over crimes committed by minors, creating a dilemma when authorities identified an alleged juvenile offender only after that person had aged out of the system.
Since authorities did not identify or charge James while he was a juvenile, prosecutors faced the question of whether an adult court could legally hear the case.
TEEN ACCUSED OF KILLING TWO GIRLS IN ALLEGED HIT-AND-RUN WILL BE TRIED AS ADULT AFTER IDENTITY REVEALED

"That leaves a gap because this person is alleged to have committed a crime when he was 14, was not charged in juvenile court, and now that he's over the age of 18 could not be charged in adult court because of the way that law was written," Hamner said.

In 2023, state law changed. A new legal path was created for adult courts to handle certain cases involving those accused of committing serious crimes as juveniles. The law did not cover every violent crime and depended partly on whether prosecutors could have sought adult prosecution when the offender was a juvenile.
Michael Jerome James has been charged with killing 10-year-old Blake and his 26-year-old stepmother, Chynna Dickus, in Franklin, Indiana, on July 24, 2006. (Johnson County Sheriff's Office)

Hamner said another case involving child molestation allegations tested the 2023 statute. The Indiana Court of Appeals rejected its application in that case, and the Indiana Supreme Court later reached the same conclusion.
"That means that we couldn't use it either," Hamner said.
NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS

"We started back over. We went back to the legislature and, with the guidance of the decision in that 2023 statute, drafted a new law that would satisfy the concerns that the Indiana Supreme Court had."
Hamner said lawmakers passed a new statute in 2025 after considering the concerns raised by the Indiana Supreme Court. The 2025 change gave prosecutors the legal mechanism needed to charge James.
"Then we were back in business to be able to charge this individual," he said.
Hamner said he is more confident the latest statute will withstand a legal challenge.
"Nothing's ever certain, but I'm a lot more confident about this statute than we were with the other one," Hamner said.
Lance Hamner said the development in the Dickus investigation played a major role in his decision to run for prosecutor again. (Courtesy of Lance Hamner)

Criminal defense lawyer Mike Cunningham, however, told Fox 59 News that he believes Indiana law does not allow prosecutors to charge James as an adult for crimes he allegedly committed before the state changed its juvenile jurisdiction law in 2023.

"For acts that are committed after 2023, if you’re a juvenile and we don’t learn about it until after you’re 21, then you may be held accountable in adult court," he said. "But what the court has said is for anything that happened before 2023, the law does not permit that because they did not have adequate notice."
If James' eventual defense attorney challenges the court's jurisdiction, the dispute could determine whether prosecutors can pursue the murder case at all.
Blake and Chynna suffered multiple stab wounds inside the family's home on Aberdeen Drive in the otherwise peaceful Branigin Woods subdivision.
Investigators determined that Blake also had blunt-force injuries and signs of smothering.

Blake's father, Sean Dickus, returned home and discovered the bodies. Blake's mother, Christina Smith, had planned to pick up her son that day but instead arrived to find the neighborhood surrounded by police.
She later learned that Blake appeared to have fought desperately against his attacker, and had severe injuries to his hands.

"His poor little hands were so bad, like, he tried to grab the knife and like, his thumb was almost sliced off," Christina Smith told WTHR. "The knife went through his hands... I don't know how that guy could live with himself."

For years, investigators explored possible connections between the murders and a string of break-ins occurring within a half-mile of the Dickus residence. They also questioned multiple construction workers who were working in the neighborhood around the time of the murders.
"They did a very extensive and thorough investigation, but they weren't able to identify any suspects," Hamner said. "They were getting a lot of tips, but nothing was coming from it."
Hamner declined to say whether authorities uncovered evidence suggesting a juvenile committed the burglaries or whether James had any connection to them.
The Dickus murders have followed Hamner through years of his career.
Voters first elected Hamner as Johnson County prosecutor in 1991, and held the position when the 2006 murders happened.

Hamner left the prosecutor's office and became a judge in 2009 with the murders still unsolved. In 2021, he learned that investigators believed they had caught a break in the case, although he declined to reveal what initially led authorities to James.
James is in the custody of the Johnson County Sheriff's Office in Franklin, Indiana. (Google Maps)
Hamner had already considered leaving the bench and running for prosecutor again. He said the development in the Dickus investigation played a major role in his decision.
"When I found out about this, this was a huge part of my making that decision to come back and work on this case that had sadly just been languishing all those years," Hamner said.

title: Bend school district honors slain teacher, praises staff member's courage during attack: ‘Forever grateful’
summary: Bend-La Pine Schools praised educators who risked their lives during the Silver Rail Elementary School shooting that killed three students and a teacher.
story: Kaylub Giamanco, 36, is seen walking in Bend, Oregon, on Saturday, two days after he "neutralized" a shooter who killed three children and a teacher at the school. (Credit: Kevin Perkins for Fox News Digital)

BEND, Ore. — The Oregon school district that lost three young students and a teacher in a mass shooting this week expressed profound grief on Saturday, praising the courage of the educator and staff member who risked their lives during the attack.
"Our hearts are broken," the Bend-La Pine Schools district said in a social media post. "They responded to an attack on their school in a way for which we are forever grateful."
Among the victims was Megan Lambert, 25, a special education teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend.
Lambert had just joined the district this fall for her first teaching job.

Becky Drury, left, an inclusion educational assistant, was injured when a gunman opened fire inside the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., earlier in the week. Megan Lambert, right, a special education teacher, was killed in the attack. On Saturday, the district praised both for their response to the deadly shooting that took the lives of Lambert and three children. (Bend-La Pines Schools)
The district remembered her as a bright light for her "students, family, and our community," adding, "She will be missed beyond words can express."
The district also praised Becky Drury, an inclusion educational assistant who was injured during the attack and is currently recovering.

"We continue to wrap our arms around Becky Drury," the post stated. "In addition, a learning specialist responded with extraordinary courage and engaged directly with the shooter. We are so thankful for her safety and forever in her debt."
HERO DAD WHO TOOK DOWN OREGON SCHOOL SHOOTER IDENTIFIED ALONG WITH TEACHER, STUDENT BOTH KILLED IN ATTACK
Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children shot and killed at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., Thursday. (AP; Bend Police Department)
The tragic shooting has devastated the community of Bend, located about 170 miles south of Portland.

On Saturday, residents gathered near the school to mourn Lambert and the three young victims: 5-year-old Rhoam Summer, along with two other children, ages 8 and 11, whose families requested their names not be publicly disclosed.
A 7-year-old girl and Drury both sustained injuries and are recovering, according to police.
At a growing sidewalk memorial outside Silver Rail Elementary, mourners have left flowers, offered prayers, and wrote messages of support in chalk.
HERO DAD WHO TOOK DOWN OREGON SCHOOL SHOOTER IDENTIFIED ALONG WITH TEACHER, STUDENT BOTH KILLED IN ATTACK

Kaylub Giamanco, 36, a father of two daughters at Silver Rail Elementary School, had been praised as a hero for killing the gunman who killed three children and a teacher in the attack. (AP; Kevin Perkins for Fox News Digital)
Community members and authorities have also commended Kaylub Giamanco, 36, a father of two Silver Rail students, who intervened during the attack.

Giamanco was on his lunch break when he saw the teenage gunman entering the building with a shotgun. He retrieved a legally secured .40-caliber pistol from his car, pursued the shooter into the school, and fatally shot him.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz praised the rapid response of both citizens and staff, while highlighting an unnamed teacher who confronted the gunman directly by throwing a cellphone and tackling him.

title: Child among 2 killed after vehicle drives onto soccer field at Kansas sports complex
summary: A child and an adult were killed after a vehicle drove onto a soccer field at a Wichita sports complex. Police said the driver was taken into custody
story: Wichita police officials provided an update after a woman drove a pickup truck through a youth soccer game, killing a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man and leaving 11 others hospitalized (Credit:Wichita Police Department).
Two people, including a child, were killed, and several others injured Saturday when a vehicle drove onto a soccer field at a sports complex in Wichita, Kansas.
The driver, identified as a 34-year-old woman, was taken into custody following the incident at Stryker Sports Complex, Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said in a news conference.
Police said they believe the woman had a child playing soccer at the complex that day, but not on the field where the deadly crash took place.
Sedgwick County emergency dispatchers began receiving multiple calls about the incident around 3:25 p.m., Moses said.
FORMER TV ANCHOR WHO PLEADED GUILTY TO KILLING MOTHER LAST HALLOWEEN GETS LIFE SENTENCE
Capt. Aaron Moses of the Wichita Police Department in Kansas briefs the media following an incident on a soccer field Saturday. (Wichita Police Department)
Police and emergency crews responded to the complex, where two people were pronounced dead on the field and 11 others, including five children, were transported to area hospitals.
Police confirmed that a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man were pronounced dead at the scene. Both were from McPherson, Kansas, but authorities said they were not related.
Moses said ten victims suffered traumatic injuries ranging from minor bruises to extremely serious injuries. Those injuries were believed to be non-life-threatening, he added.
The injured children included two 5-year-olds, two 8-year-olds and a 9-year-old girl, according to Moses. A 61-year-old woman was also transported for a nontraumatic medical issue.
Two juveniles were inside the vehicle at the time of the incident, Moses said. The vehicle remained at the scene, and police said the driver posed no additional ongoing threat to the public.
"This is a tragedy," Moses said.

The Kansas State High School Activities Association (KSHSAA) suspended play at its inaugural girls flag football state championship following the incident, which occurred on an adjacent field at Stryker Sports Complex.

Authorities have not confirmed whether the driver acted intentionally, or whether a medical emergency, impairment or another factor caused the deadly crash.
Moses said the driver had a valid driver's license and no outstanding arrest warrants. He said the driver was cooperating with the investigation.
No charges have been announced.
Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan emphasized that investigators know what happened but have not yet established why.
"We know what happened, but now we're working very hard to find out why it happened," Sullivan said.

title: Detective suspected in girl’s murder may have killed others, former investigator fears
summary: A fingerprint on an 8-year-old's communion purse finally identified Chicago cop Thomas McInerney as Gloria Kowalewicz's killer after 65 years, police say.
story: Chicago cop Thomas F. McInerney Jr. has been identified as the man who abducted, shot and killed Gloria Kowalewicz Nov. 12, 1960.

Investigators found a bullet, Kowalewicz’s coat, her shoes and her little, white communion purse that held her prayer book. But the killer was never identified.

In Investigation Discovery’s true-crime docuseries "The Serial Killer Connection," Gower meets with Kara Robinson Chamberlain, who endured 18 hours of captivity and torture before escaping Evonitz, as they investigate whether he may be linked to other unsolved cases.
For Gower, one question has followed her since learning the truth about the man she married.
Bonnie Lou Gower has since remarried. She's now the mother of two children. (Investigation Discovery)
"When I initially learned about [his crimes] and I told people, honestly their first response is, ‘Well, obviously you knew. How could you not have known?’" Gower told Fox News Digital.

"That was my very first question to the FBI. ‘How could I not know this? How could I not know I was sleeping next to somebody for 8½ years that was doing this?’ And, of course, they assured me that there’s no way I could have known."
Looking back, Gower admitted there were things she didn’t question at the time.
Bonnie Lou Gower and Richard Evonitz in the 1990s. Gower told Fox News Digital that whenever she traveled to visit her family, Evonitz insisted on staying home. (Investigation Discovery)
Whenever she left town to visit family, Evonitz insisted on staying behind, claiming he had to work. Only later did Gower discover that he had actually taken time off while she was away.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
"One of the reasons he never came with me was because he said he was working," said Gower.
Richard Evonitz in South Carolina, circa 1988 (Investigation Discovery)

"And then, I come to find out, he had actually taken off work on the days that I was out of town. But, at the time, I wasn’t at all concerned about leaving him behind. I was just going and visiting my family. It definitely makes you look at everybody and everything now, whether you can trust someone’s words or actions."

Gower met Evonitz, who was eight years her senior, in South Carolina. He was the older brother of one of her friends and would come home whenever he was on leave from the U.S. Navy. She quickly developed a crush on him as she got to know him and, at age 16, Evonitz asked her out on a date.
They married in August 1988 when she was 17 and he was 25.
After marrying, Bonnie Lou Gower and Richard Evonitz moved from South Carolina to Maine, where Evonitz was stationed at the time. (Investigation Discovery)

"You think you know who you are when you’re 17, but I really don’t think I did," said Gower. "I don’t think I had a handle on that. And I was relatively sheltered. I was very naïve, very trusting, taking everything at face value. I think he knew that."

During the marriage, there were moments when Gower suspected Evonitz was being unfaithful. Whenever she questioned him, Evonitz told her it was all in her head. She believed him. But as the relationship progressed, Evonitz began isolating her from friends and family as they moved around the country, from Maine to San Diego to Virginia.
SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER
Bonnie Lou Gower initially believed Richard Evonitz was having an affair. He assured Gower it was all in her head. (Investigation Discovery)

"No one ever thinks that their significant other is going to be a serial killer," Chamberlain told Fox News Digital. "I think worst case, and this is something that she expressed to me, he was having an affair. No one ever thinks your spouse is out murdering someone.
"He kept that part of himself very tightly controlled and didn’t show it to the people he was closest to."
In "The Serial Killer Connection," a three-part docuseries, Bonnie Lou Gower and Kara Robinson Chamberlain retrace Richard Evonitz's past. (Investigation Discovery)

The marriage began to unravel after Evonitz left the Navy. Gower said financial pressures fueled growing tensions between the couple, while Evonitz became prone to mood swings and what she described as "rages." He also frequently criticized her weight. Behind closed doors, Gower was also uncomfortable with his interest in bondage, according to the docuseries.

In June 2002, Bonnie Lou Gower (seen here with Richard Evonitz in the '90s) discovered that her ex-husband was a murderer who had killed at least three young girls and kidnapped a fourth. The FBI showed up at her doorstep in California and informed her of her ex's secret double life. (Investigation Discovery)

Even as the marriage reached its breaking point, Gower said she still didn’t see Evonitz as someone capable of hurting her. Walking away, she said, was a decision that came after years of mounting unhappiness.
When Gower made the decision to leave the marriage, Gower said her fear was for him, not herself.
"I was concerned for his safety when he said he was going to take the gun and kill himself," Gower recalled. "I never feared for my own life."
SEND US A TIP
According to the FBI, Richard Evonitz fled to Sarasota, Fla., where he took his life after being surrounded by law enforcement. (FBI)
Even after she finally walked away, Gower said Evonitz had left her questioning whether she had any justification for doing so.
"When I left, I felt like I was leaving for no real good reason," she said. "[But] I wasn’t happy."

According to Gower's TikTok, she and Evonitz were married from August 1988 until January 1997. Multiple reports indicate that their divorce was finalized in 1998. Years later, Gower would learn just how much she hadn’t known about the man she left behind.
For 18 hours, Richard Evonitz held teenage Kara Robinson Chamberlain captive in his apartment, where he sexually assaulted her. (Investigation Discovery)

On June 24, 2002, 15-year-old Chamberlain was at a friend’s home in South Carolina when Evonitz pulled into the driveway. The stranger approached her with pamphlets and asked if her parents were home. Then, he held a gun to her neck and threatened to shoot her if she screamed. He forced Chamberlain into a dark storage container in his car.

At Evonitz’s apartment, Chamberlain was repeatedly sexually assaulted. He restrained her to a bed. After hours of torture, Chamberlain managed to free one of her hands from a pair of handcuffs with her teeth, unclip a leather leg restraint and quietly bolt out the door as Evonitz slept. As she took off, Chamberlain encountered two men who took her to a police station.
Kara Robinson Chamberlain after her medical exam. (Investigation Discovery)

Chamberlain led officers back to her captor’s apartment. But when investigators arrived, Evonitz had escaped. Police tracked Evonitz to Sarasota, Florida, but as they closed in on him, Evonitz died by suicide. He was 38.

Richard Evonitz shot and killed himself after a 100 mph car chase from Manatee County ended on Bayfront Drive across from Maria Jack in Sarasota, Fla., June 27, 2002. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)

Once investigators began digging into Evonitz’s past, Chamberlain’s abduction proved to be only part of the story. Evidence recovered from Evonitz’s South Carolina apartment, former Virginia residence and vehicle linked him to three unsolved murders.
Kara Robinson Chamberlain worked with law enforcement as a sex crime and child abuse investigator. (Investigation Discovery)

On Sept. 9, 1996, Evonitz abducted 16-year-old Sofia Silva from the front steps of her home in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, where he and Gower had been living. Her body was discovered about five weeks later in neighboring King George County.

Then, on May 1, 1997, sisters Kristin "Kristi" Lisk, 15, and Kathryn "Kati" Lisk, 12, vanished after returning home from school. Both girls had been sexually assaulted and strangled. Their bodies were discovered five days later in the South Anna River.
After her abduction, Kara Robinson Chamberlain went on to pursue a career in law enforcement. (Investigation Discovery)
Notes discovered by investigators indicated that Evonitz already had his eye on other potential victims, Fox News Digital previously reported.
It would be months after Chamberlain’s abduction that Gower learned of her ex-husband’s other victims.

"It felt like it wasn’t real at all," Gower admitted. "It felt like this was something that happens in the movies. This wasn’t real life. It was very hard to believe that he could hurt anybody. He had never hit me or physically abused me."
GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

After escaping, Kara Robinson Chamberlain went straight to law enforcement. She provided crucial information that led investigators to her captor’s apartment and helped identify him as the man responsible for at least three previously unsolved murders. (FOX Image Collection via Getty Images)
Now, Gower and Chamberlain are looking to Evonitz’s past for answers about whether there could be other victims.
Gower has helped piece together a timeline of Evonitz’s movements during their marriage, providing investigators with dates, locations and old calendars as potential cold cases are examined.
"Of course, he wasn’t always where I thought he was," said Gower.
Kara Robinson Chamberlain previously appeared in "America's Most Wanted" opposite John Walsh to raise awareness about the stories of victims. (FOX Image Collection via Getty Images)

Chamberlain, meanwhile, has been investigating whether Evonitz could be responsible for other unsolved crimes, examining cases dating back to the 1980s and tracing his movements during his years in the Navy and in the decades before her own abduction.

"I genuinely think that there is a level of escalation that we see between an indecent exposure [incident] and then three homicides in approximately nine months and then a break before me that is unexplainable to me," she said.
Today, Kara Robinson Chamberlain is a survivor advocate. (Investigation Discovery)
"Everything’s possible and nothing has been confirmed," Chamberlain stressed. "It’s a frustrating place to be, but I will not stop searching."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Kara Robinson Chamberlain is adamant that Richard Evonitz may be responsible for other crimes across the country. (Investigation Discovery)
One potential key to finding answers is DNA.

While investigating cases for the docuseries, Chamberlain said she learned that Evonitz’s DNA profile was not in CODIS, the FBI’s national DNA database. However, she said authorities in Spotsylvania County still have a blood sample that can be provided to law enforcement agencies seeking to compare his DNA with evidence from other cases.
Chamberlain said she hopes Evonitz’s DNA can ultimately be entered into CODIS, allowing for broader comparisons with evidence from unsolved crimes.

Bonnie Lou Gower, left, alongside Kara Robinson Chamberlain, is looking back at forgotten notes and old calendars to provide more information that could uncover fresh clues and leads. (Investigation Discovery)
"I genuinely believe that there’s no way he only murdered three girls and kidnapped me," she said. "I don’t think that there’s a world in which that’s true."
"The Serial Killer Connection" airs Wednesdays at 9 p.m. Episodes will be available to stream on HBO Max. (Investigation Discovery)

While making the docuseries, Gower learned that Evonitz had kept a photograph of her when she was just 11 years old — years before they began dating — hidden behind another framed picture of her. Gower said it was not a photograph she had taken with her when she left home and that she never knew Evonitz possessed it.
"It’s disturbing enough that he would have 11-year-old me in a picture behind something," she said.

Kara Robinson Chamberlain (left) was nervous about meeting Bonnie Lou Gower (right). They became fast friends. (Investi)
Decades after learning the truth about the man she married, Gower said she is still trying to make sense of it.
"I don’t think you ever make sense of it," she said. "There’s no tidy little box to put it in to make it make sense.

Bonnie Lou Gower embraces Kara Robinson Chamberlain. (Investigation Discovery)
"I’m still grappling with it. I’m still processing."

title: Alex Murdaugh's defense makes 'high-risk' move to show DNA proves he didn't kill family, prosecutor says
summary: Alex Murdaugh's defense team is betting on a Y-STR DNA test by Othram that prosecutors call "high risk" ahead of his April 2027 murder retrial.
story: Criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor Josh Ritter said Alex Murdaugh's win in court on a motion to test DNA samples from Maggie Murdaugh could potentially backfire on him.
LEXINGTON, S.C. — Alex Murdaugh’s defense team is gambling on a "high-risk" DNA test in its bid to point to another killer, a prosecutor said, citing the defense’s own expert.

Judge Debra McCaslin sided with the defense over prosecutors’ objections Friday, allowing new testing on swabs from Maggie Murdaugh’s cellphone and clippings from under her fingernails, even though the process will likely use up the last of the testable samples. McCaslin said due process requires that a defendant be given "a meaningful opportunity to present a full and complete defense."

Murdaugh was convicted in 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family's Moselle property in Colleton County. The South Carolina Supreme Court later overturned the convictions after finding that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill improperly influenced the jury.
His retrial is scheduled for April 5, 2027. Murdaugh has maintained his innocence in the killings.
MURDAUGH WANTS IDAHO MURDERS DNA DREAM TEAM BEHIND KOHBERGER CASE TO HELP REWRITE SECOND MURDER TRIAL
Alex Murdaugh at a pretrial hearing in Lexington, S.C., Oct. 16, 2026. (Tracy Glantz of The State and Henry Taylor of The Post and Courier.)

The defense team plans to employ Othram to conduct a Y-STR test, a method that isolates DNA from the Y chromosome to generate a profile of a male contributor in samples where female DNA is predominant.

Murdaugh's attorneys contend that all three samples contain unidentified male DNA and are seeking to determine whether a single man was the source. Defense attorney Phil Barber said the findings could rule out certain individuals as contributors and may provide ancestry information, although the test cannot differentiate between men who share the same paternal ancestors.
MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS NEWLY DISCLOSED RESERVE DNA SAMPLES SHOULD GO TO OTHRAM BEFORE STATE ANALYSIS
Alex Murdaugh's attorney, Dick Harpootlian, speaks at a pretrial hearing Oct. 16, 2026. (Tracy Glantz of The State and Henry Taylor of The Post and Courier)
The defense said the process will require approximately 90 days.
Creighton Waters, the lead prosecutor, said in court that the testing would be "high risk" and unlikely to generate significant evidence.
ALEX MURDAUGH'S 'WILD GOOSE CHASE' FOR MISSING MURDER GUNS TARGETS POLICE CHIEF: EXPERT

"When we talked to their expert, he said, 'Yeah, that’s pretty much a sole source sample. This would be high risk and unlikely to generate anything, and [it] appears that that’s the case, because when we got back the quantification from [Othram], it’s goose eggs on the Y chromosome," Waters said.
Barber laid out his reasoning for the new test, acknowledging the unknown male DNA could have an innocent explanation but saying the pattern is hard to ignore.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Alex Murdaugh in court Oct. 16, 2026 (Tracy Glantz of The State and Henry Taylor of The Post and Courier)

"Maybe it’s different male DNA. Maybe it’s the same. Maybe it’s red herrings. ... But as we keep progressing from one hand to two hands and now the phone, you know. It’s starting to look less and less like a red herring," Barber said.
"If you have an unknown person under both her fingernails and throwing the phone out the side of the road after she’s murdered, it’s not him, I mean, that’s extremely important to the defense."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Notably, the defense and prosecution both said once the DNA test is performed, there won't be enough samples left to test again in any post-trial proceedings, which Murdaugh was OK with.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
"To perform the test, there is enough to perform the test, but there’s not enough to perform the test and then have enough left over," Barber said.
SEND US A TIP
"My client just informed me that he will waive that," he said, referring to any post-conviction retesting.
ALEX MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS MURDER WEAPON MAY BE TIED TO SEPARATE KILLING AS JUDGE SEEKS ANSWERS
Alex Murdaugh arrives for a judicial hearing on Monday, June 29, 2026, at the Marc H. Westbrook Judicial Center in Lexington, S.C. (Tracy Glantz/The State via Pool)

Former prosecutor Joshua Ritter told Fox News Digital the strategy could backfire, saying the defense may have been better off leaving the DNA untested and using the unknown male profile to raise reasonable doubt at trial.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"They could make an argument, 'Hey, you found samples. It was unknown male DNA. That DNA did not come back to our client, correct? There's somebody else out there who could potentially be linked to this crime,'" Ritter said.

"Now, unless it comes back that it's a person who does have some reason to be suspicious, they've got a problem because if it comes back to a person with a rock solid alibi or a person with an innocent explanation as to why their DNA would end up underneath her fingernails, they've foreclosed any argument that they could have made.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Alex Murdaugh, right, is shown here with his family. (Fox News)
"It's one of those situations where sometimes it's better left unknown for the defense, but they seem to be determined to try to figure out who that DNA belongs to."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Murdaugh is due back in court Nov. 13.
Fox News Digital reached out to Murdaugh's defense team for comment.
Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

title: Hero dad who took down Oregon school shooter identified along with teacher, student both killed in attack
summary: The teacher killed in a shooting at a Bend, Oregon, school was identified by police Friday as 25-year-old Meghan Lambert. The hero who took down the shooter was Kaylub Giamanco.
story: Bend Police Department Chief Mike Krantz shares new details about Thursday's shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, during a news conference Friday.

The good Samaritan who police in Bend, Oregon, said "neutralized" the 16-year-old shooter who killed three children and a teacher Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School has been identified as 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, a law enforcement source confirmed to Fox News Digital.

During a news conference Friday, police identified the teacher who was killed in the shooting as 25-year-old Meghan Lambert, and also announced that among the youngest of the victims was 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. Police also revealed a school staff member threw a cellphone and tackled the attacker during the harrowing incident.

"Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. Her friends became her family," Lambert's family said in a statement read at the news conference.
ARMED BYSTANDER FATALLY SHOOTS SUSPECTED TEEN GUNMAN AFTER 3 CHILDREN, 1 ADULT KILLED AT OREGON SCHOOL: FEDS
"Yesterday was a terrible day for our community," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said during the news conference. "Five people succumbed to their injuries at the scene, including the suspect.

"The deceased at the school scene included three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and one 25-year-old teacher. One 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were transported by Bend Fire to Saint Charles Bend with critical injuries."
The 7-year-old is in serious but stable condition, and the 54-year-old teacher suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

Krantz said that, at 12:58 p.m., a witness who was driving by the school saw the suspect throw his gun over a fence and then climb the fence onto school property. He said the witness confronted the suspect, who then fired at his truck, hitting it at least three times. The driver, who was not injured by the gunfire, went down the street and made the initial 911 call at 12:59 p.m., he said.

Giamanco, who Krantz only identified as a "36-year-old man" during the briefing, drove into the school parking lot after seeing the suspect shoot at the truck, Krantz said, and saw the suspect shoot the glass panes on two double doors to get inside.
POLICE DISPTACH AUDIO RELEASED AFTER OREGON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL SHOOTING
Police tape is placed outside Silver Rail Elementary school after a shooting Thursday in Bend, Ore. (Joe Kline/AP Photo)
Once he was inside, the shooter went straight into the classroom that was to the left and fired as many as 15 rounds.
Krantz said the shooter used three types of ammunition and that all the victims were shot in the classroom.

Giamanco grabbed a .40-caliber pistol he legally kept in his car and went into the school through the same doors. After hearing the sounds of a shooting, he went into the classroom, where he saw the suspect struggling with a teacher, who had thrown her cellphone at and tackled the shooter.
Giamanco shot him multiple times.

"In addition to the 36-year-old man who bravely stepped in to stop the suspect, I want to highlight another person whose heroic action we need to recognize," Krantz said. "A teacher in the classroom threw her cellphone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him.
"She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed."
DEMOCRATS' LATEST GUN-CONTROL PUSH RUNS INTO INCONVENIENT FACT ABOUT HOW SCHOOL KILLER WAS STOPPED
Map locating Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., where three children and an adult were killed in a shooting on Thursday, according to federal law enforcement sources. (Fox News)

Police arrived at the school within minutes of the 911 call at 1:02 p.m. having been told that the "suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him, shooting him several times," Krantz said.
Earlier Friday, Kenda Freeman said in a statement that her son, Giamanco, intervened in the attack and shot the gunman who killed three students and a teacher, The Associated Press reported.
Giamanco, a local carpenter and dad, has two daughters who attend Silver Rail, his brother, Kyle Gianmaco, told NBC News.
Kyle shared that Kaylub is shaken by the event and doesn't want to speak to the public.
"We want the bystander who intervened to know we know he is going through a rough time, but we are grateful, and we think he is a hero," Lambert's family added in the statement.
"You selflessly put yourself at risk for others. We would like the other families to know they are in our thoughts and prayers. Meghan loved those children, and so we will show you love for her."
Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., Friday, a day after a deadly shooting. (Haven Daley/AP Photo)
The shooter forced his way into the school by firing a shotgun at locked doors, Krantz said, citing the initial investigation.
He said the shooter fired as many as 15 times and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed.

On Thursday, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek praised school staff, parents and first responders, along with the community member "who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life."
Silver Rail Elementary School is a public school in the Bend-La Pine Schools District with roughly 400 students, kindergarten through fifth grade, and approximately 40 staff members.
Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price, and Fox News' David Spunt and Bill Melugin contributed to this story.

title: Bryan Kohberger fights to remove judge who called him 'worst of the worst,' questioned his honesty
summary: Bryan Kohberger's new attorney accuses Latah County prosecutors of dodging key arguments in his motion to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler from the case.
story: Idaho prosecutors urge a judge to reject murder suspect Bryan Kohberger's attempt to withdraw his guilty plea, calling the defense's arguments a fishing expedition. Former federal prosecutor Jonathan Fahey joins to break down the latest legal maneuvers, the strength of the state's case and what lies ahead for the victims' families in the high-profile trial.
Bryan Kohberger's new lawyer is taking another swing at Idaho prosecutors in his fight to have the judge who called his client a "faceless coward" removed from post-conviction proceedings.

Court-appointed attorney Greg Rauch is accusing Latah County prosecutors of "regurgitating" rules rather than addressing concerns raised in his motion to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler from the case.
Hippler said Kohberger, 31, "slithered" into the victims' home before committing a crime that made him "the worst of the worst" after the killer admitted guilt last year.

At issue, according to Rauch, "is how [Hippler's] statements about counsel’s preparation and [Kohberger's] capacity for truthfulness bear on the disputes it may now decide, in combination with the myriad of other statements made."
KOHBERGER PROSECUTORS SAY NO AS IDAHO KILLER TRIES TO BOOT JUDGE WHO CALLED HIM A 'FACELESS COWARD'

Judge Steven Hippler of Idaho's 4th Judicial District in Ada County rejected the latest attempt by Bryan Kohberger's defense to drop the death penalty as a possible sentence if a jury convicts him of killing four University of Idaho students in 2022. (Katherine Jones/Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
And when addressing the fact that there would be no allocution or explanation from Kohberger, the judge also questioned whether Kohberger even possessed the capacity to say something truthful.

"Even if I could force him to speak, which legally I cannot, how could anyone ever be assured that what he speaks is the truth?" Hippler asked during sentencing. "Do we really believe, after all of this, he is capable of speaking the truth, or of giving up something of himself to help the very people whose lives he destroyed? Rather, I suspect the so-called reason would be dished out in enticing self-serving and aggrandizing untruthful bits, leaving people wanting more information, more insight, and thus enhancing even further the power he seeks to hold."
BRYAN KOHBERGER DIDN'T UNDERSTAND WHAT HE WAS DOING WHEN HE PLEADED GUILTY: UNSEALED MEMO

Bryan Kohberger appeared at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. Kohberger pleaded guilty in exchange for being spared the death penalty for the stabbing of four University of Idaho students nearly three years earlier. (Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)
Rauch wrote that "of course" judges can deny defense motions, "condemn terrible crimes," and go on to preside over post-conviction claims.
BRYAN KOHBERGER'S NEW LAWYER SAYS KEY QUESTIONS MAY SOON GET ANSWERS IN COURT
"The question is not whether someone might criticize the Court, but whether an informed, reasonable observer could question its impartiality in light of this connected record," he wrote.

And it's not just that Hippler tore into Kohberger at sentencing. He has also taken issue with a June scheduling order days before Kohberger surprised the country and pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty.

University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin were killed in a November 2022 attack at an off-campus house on King Road in Moscow, Idaho. (Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

"This motion does not rest upon one adverse ruling, one harsh statement, or the mere fact that the judge who presided over Bryan Kohberger’s criminal case has been assigned to his post-conviction proceeding," Rauch wrote in his initial 22-page motion on Aug. 27. "It rests upon the extraordinary convergence of all of them."

Hippler had rejected a request for more time for Kohberger's previous defense lawyer, Anne Taylor, and in a June 26 order, described her complaints about discovery as "ultimately empty" while suggesting she was simply trying to delay his trial.
IDAHO PROSECUTORS ACCUSE BRYAN KOHBERGER OF 'FISHING' TO FIND BETTER ARGUMENTS FOR BID TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA
Six days later, at a change-of-plea hearing, Hippler asked Taylor, "Have you been able to do all the discovery you feel necessary?"
"Yes, Your Honor," she replied.
Bryan Kohberger's lawyer, Gregory Rauch in Boise, Idaho. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)
BRYAN KOHBERGER WAIVED HIS APPEAL RIGHTS BUT PLANS ON PURSUING POST-CONVICTION RELIEF
Prosecutors, in an opposition to the motion filed earlier this month, wrote that Kohberger had failed to show Hippler "is biased."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Outgoing Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Bill Thompson, who announced his retirement earlier this week, and Deputy Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl wrote that Hippler's statements about Kohberger after he'd admitted to killing four innocent students were not unusual or out of line.
BRYAN KOHBERGER’S 2027 HEARING IS NOT GUARANTEED AS IDAHO SEEKS QUICK DISMISSAL
Latah County Prosecutor, Bill Thompson walks across the carpark at Latah County Courthouse, Moscow, Idaho, Friday, August 7, 2026. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)

"In our case, the sentencing remarks are not enough to show bias, and the required showing of perceived bias cannot be tied to this Court's capacity to fairly adjudicate any [post-conviction relief] claims alleged in this case but rather puts this Court in the best position to adjudicate them as the legislature and the Idaho Supreme Court's rules intend," they wrote.
BRYAN KOHBERGER'S POST-CONVICTION RELIEF BID ENABLED BY FLAWED PLEA DEAL, PSYCHOLOGIST ARGUES
Rauch also argued that Hippler could voluntarily recuse himself from the case to avoid any appearance of partiality.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

In the new 12-page filing, Rauch also argued that prosecutors have attributed concessions to his client that were never made, mischaracterized his initial motion and failed to address some of the arguments he did make in it.
Bryan Kohberger appeared at the Ada County Courthouse, Wednesday, July 2, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. (AP Photo/Kyle Green, Pool)
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
"The State’s Response does not resolve this motion by repeating the ordinary rule, supplying concessions Petitioner never made, or calling the disputed statements routine," Rauch wrote.

Kohberger is attempting to undo his guilty plea in the University of Idaho student murders that killed Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20, in November 2022.
GOT A TIP?
The former criminology Ph.D. student initially filed a handwritten petition for post-conviction relief in July.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Rauch was later appointed to represent him and has until Jan. 13, 2027 to file an amended petition that is expected to be much more in-depth than Kohberger's.
Bryan Kohberger arrived at Monroe County Courthouse in Pennsylvania in advance of an extradition hearing. (The Image Direct for Fox News Digital)
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
"A request for an impartial adjudicator is certainly not a request for a sympathetic one," he wrote. "Reassignment would change the judge, not the evidence or the governing law."
